Rainwater and hail lashed the carriage and forced commuters to flee.

News.title: James Cleverly quits shadow cabinet to run for London mayor and challenge Labour’s Sadiq Khan
News.content:
CLEVERLY’S BID James Cleverly quits shadow cabinet to run for London mayor and challenge Labour’s Sadiq Khan

JAMES Cleverly has quit his role in the Shadow Cabinet to run for Mayor of London.

The Conservative MP for Braintree and former Home Secretary will resign from his current role with immediate effect.

Cleverly explained that he decided he needed to make his position clear ahead of the Conservative Party conference in October.

It comes amid speculation that Cleverly was planning to stand in the race for London Mayor.





Kemi Badenoch will now need to fill the role of shadow minister for housing, communities and local government.

Labour has held dominance in the capital for a long time with Mayor Sadiq Khan now half way through his third term in the role.

Cleverly, 56, said he was looking to challenge Labour’s hold on the seat.

After he informed his party leader of his decision on Thursday, Cleverly said: “She took it very well.”



In an interview with The Sunday Times he continued: “Kemi has been very gracious.”

The Times reports that a source close to the Tory leader said: “Kemi is delighted that someone of his calibre wants to put himself forward to be Conservative nominee for mayor of London.

“She really wants someone to take on Sadiq Khan, as he is destroying the London she loves.”

Cleverly will now have to win the party’s nomination for the mayoral election before any of his colleagues can endorse him.



His Cabinet experience under Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak are likely to make him a favourite among his peers.

He said: “We need a credible big hitter putting themselves forward for mayor of London.”

Cleverly explained that he sees the route to success for the Tories begins in London.

He added that if they want to see Kemi Badenoch in Number 10 the party will need to win support in the capital.

His withdrawal from the shadow cabinet will likely lead to some speculation about a reshuffle.

News.title: Heartbroken mum of missing hiker, 18, reveals her cause of death after daughter’s body found in the woods
News.content:
MUM'S PAIN Heartbroken mum of missing hiker, 18, reveals her cause of death after daughter’s body found in the woods

The cause of death of a teen hiker has been revealed by her heartbroken mum after her body was found in the wilderness.

Lily Hooper, 18, was found dead after attempting a challenging solo hike in New South Wales, Australia.



She was missing for eight days before her body was found in dense bushland in the Nattai National Park.

It is thought she fell to her death on August 12, the day she went missing.





Her mother, Kirrily Hooper, told The Daily Telegraph: “Preliminary reports said Lily had a fall, she had an accident that first afternoon, she died the day she went missing and was found lying peacefully in dense bushland.”

Lily’s mum added: “In hindsight we now know she passed quickly and she didn’t suffer in the cold.

“That was the hardest part, not knowing if she was out there scared in the elements when we would come home at night and try to sleep.”

After her body was found, Lily’s parents spent a heartbreaking 18 minutes believing that she had been found alive but injured after a horrifying mess-up by Australian officials.



Lily was reported missing after she failed to show up at her boyfriend’s home after her planned hike.

A huge search effort was launched to find the teen.

Her dad Jim Hooper called her “unstoppable” and “fearless”.



He said: “She just loved the outdoors. She just had so many skills that, you know, we tried to install in her.

“She was just a clever kid who wasn’t afraid to take anything on. That was her free spirit.”

When Lily was discovered, her desperate family were tragically given false hope that she was alive but injured.

New South Wales Premier Chris Minns announced to parliament that the teenager had been found alive.

He corrected himself shortly after and said her body had been found.



It’s understood Lily’s family were also told the young hiker had been found alive.

The stomach-churning error is thought to have stemmed from confusion surrounding a code word used by rescuers to avoid alarming anyone listening to their radios.

Search crews sent a radio message saying “water bottle broken”, a message that was taken to mean Lily had been found alive but injured, according to The Daily Telegraph.

A rescue volunteer later clarified over radio that Lily had been found deceased.

New South Wales Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon apologised on Thursday afternoon for giving the family false hope.



“I unashamedly apologise for any additional trauma that may have caused Lily’s family,” he said.

“But certainly for the embarrassment and confusion that caused the miscommunication, obviously was born out of elation that Lily had been found.

“And certainly those at the command posts relayed, tragically, that miscommunication then led to a deflation, and obviously we know now an impact on her family.

Lily’s grief-stricken family were captured in photos hugging each other and sobbing after the tragic news broke.

The family have called for better bush safety education and the promotion of emergency tracking devices for remote hikes.



Dad Jim said: “We think it’d be good if there was a legacy that was left like a Skye’s Law, Jack’s Law… Lily’s Law.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“And that’s about the awareness of going out in the bush with EPIRBs, tracker devices, Garmin, Navman type devices.”

News.title: Moment paedophile martial arts teacher, 75, who raped and sexually abused girl is arrested as he’s caged for 25 years
News.content:
THIS is the moment a martial arts instructor is arrested before being jailed for a string of vile non-recent sexual assaults and rapes.

Anthony Swanson, 75, of Sidcup, London, was sentenced to 25 years behind bars at Woolwich Crown Court on Tuesday, July 7.



Video footage shows the moment officers from the Met Police storm Swanson’s home and bring him into custody.

The twisted abuser can be seen sitting calmly on his couch as officers explain that he is under arrest.



Officers read Swanson his rights as he continues to sit on the couch, saying nothing.

An investigation into the abuse was launched after a girl – who was in her early teens at the time of the abuse – came forward to report him in 2022.

The victim met Swanson in 2000 through martial arts lessons that he ran at a church hall in Beckenham.

Swanson groomed the girl before going on to sexually abuse her and rape her on several occasions.



One harrowing incident saw him rape her during a resident trip to Bath, Somerset.

The victim was also abused in the presence of her mum, who cannot be named for legal reasons.

Her mum pleaded guilty to three counts of sexual activity in the presence of a child at Woolwich Crown Court in September 2024.

She was subsequently sentenced to 16 months in prison, suspended for two years, at the same court yesterday.

Swanson was interviewed twice by detectives, both times denying that he had done anything wrong.



In an impact statement read to the court at Swanson’s sentencing hearing, the victim said: “When the abuse initially stopped, I locked it away in my mind and tried to forget and ignore what had happened. It was too traumatic.

“I came to realise through therapy that what he did happened, and that will never change.

“I will always have to live with the horrific acts of abuse he put me through.

“I am scared to bring children into the world knowing they could be hurt, abused or damaged at the hands of a paedophile like Tony Swanson, like I was.

“Swanson knows what he did to me and always has. He decided to abuse me again by pleading not guilty.



“He says I tried to ruin him. He has ruined me and shown no remorse.”

Swanson was found guilty of four counts of rape, four counts of indecent assault, three counts of engaging in sexual activity with a child, one count of inciting a child to engage in sexual activity and three counts of sexual activity in the presence of a child.

Detectives have appealed for further victim-survivors to come forward after Swanson was jailed.

Detective Constable Leonora Simpson, of the Metropolitan Police, said: “What happened to this young girl was awful. Anthony Swanson is an evil predator who thought nothing of taking advantage of the position of trust he held to carry out this vile campaign of sexual abuse.

“Based on the gravity of Swanson’s offending, we believe he may have other victims who have yet to come forward.



“We know that Swanson began teaching children’s martial arts classes in the Beckenham and Sidcup area in the early 2000s.

“He led residential trips to the West Country and Inverness in Scotland.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I am appealing to potential victims to come forward and speak to us about what happened.

“Any information will be treated extremely sensitively, and you will be supported by specialist officers.”

News.title: The rogue trade racket running riot at top UK tourist hotspot – as wheeler dealers brazenly laugh in the face of the law
News.content:
BRAZEN rogue traders are defying a blanket ban on street trading outside one of Britain’s tourist hot spots, despite being repeatedly slapped with court fines.

A Sun investigation found a racket of illegal vendors operating in plain sight on Westminster Bridge, flouting the law and absorbing the penalties as simply the cost of doing business.



Ice cream vans, hot dog stands and even vintage newspaper sellers are cashing in on the thousands of tourists who visit the world-famous landmark every day – seemingly undeterred by prosecutions.

One rogue ice cream vendor was caught selling his frozen treats to customers on the SAME DAY he was fined more than £2,600 for illegal street trading.



When Gjon Pjetri was confronted by our reporter over why he had returned to the bridge despite repeatedly being fined, he claimed he did not understand.

He then insisted he had a licence before brushing off our questions by asking: “You fancy ice cream?”

A council licensing officer previously told magistrates: “No one is granted a licence to trade on Westminster Bridge. It’s a prohibited area.”

Between April 28 and June 4 2025, Pjetri was caught illegally trading on Westminster Bridge and surrounding streets a staggering 16 times.



The 52-year-old, who required an Albanian translator in court, was hit with a £3,520 fine and more than £1,800 in costs and surcharges – with his barrister telling magistrates he made £35,000 a year from his van.

And this wasn’t his first time. He had already been slapped with a £2,640 fine after being caught illegally trading six times between December 2024 and March 2025 – landing him another £1,691 in costs and surcharges.

But despite the repeated crackdowns and hefty fines, the illicit trade appears to be booming.

A sightseeing bus ticket seller working nearby the illegal traders described the operation as “highly organised” and claimed six or seven of them rotate throughout the day.

He said: “Authorities try to move them on all the time… but they just come back later.



“As soon as the London Eye closes, they all disappear as the footfall slows down.”

For the millions of unsuspecting tourists who flock to Westminster each year, ice creams and cold fizzy drinks might seem like a welcome relief during the August heat – but few checked how much they paid.

None of the ice cream vans displayed prices in their windows and our reporter watched as customers simply tapped their bank cards or phones to pay.



Dan, 38, from Oregon, USA, was visiting Parliament with his wife and three children but confessed he had “absolutely no idea” how much he spent on three ice creams and two soft drinks from the vendor.

Moments later, the dad was forced to grab his son out of the cycle lane as a cyclist came hurtling towards him.

Our investigation found ice cream vans brazenly parked in bus lanes, with tourists buying their sweet treats spilling into busy cycle lanes.

Sue, from Luton, who was visiting Big Ben with her grandson, told The Sun: “If they’re causing a problem, like blocking a bus lane, they should move somewhere safer to operate.”

But when asked how much she paid for her two 99 Flakes, she admitted she didn’t know as she also blindly tapped her bank card.



Meanwhile, just metres away from the ice cream vans, rows of rickshaw riders were lined up in the bus lane touting for tourists.

And visitors unfamiliar with the capital could be in for a shock if they hopped aboard for a trip to Westminster Abbey.

The famous landmark is just 0.3 miles away – but riders were demanding £20 per person for the two-minute journey.



And when our reporter began asking questions on the bridge, the traders appeared to be keeping an eye out for one another.

One ice cream seller he quizzed over her prices alerted a nearby hot dog vendor to our presence.

And ice cream vans, hot dog stands and rickshaws weren’t the only illicit businesses operating on the bridge.

Lambeth Council public protection officers caught Vladadslada Tkach, 24, selling mock vintage newspapers on Westminster Bridge on November 28 2024.

As part of the scheme, tourists posed for pictures before Tkach printed their pictures on a souvenir vintage newspaper.



Pictures taken by Lambeth Council officers showed Tkach accepting a £20 note from a customer in exchange for a newspaper.



Tkach, who represented herself in her trial, claimed she was not breaking the law, citing an exemption for newspaper vendors under a specific law.

But magistrates rejected her argument and found her guilty of street trading without a licence, fined her £200 and ordered her to pay £675 in court costs

Yet illegal traders were still openly operating on the bridge when The Sun visited again this month.

Lambeth Council’s Jonathan Bartley, cabinet member for safer, thriving neighbourhoods, said: “These illegal traders exploit tourists, operate outside the licensing regime designed to protect the public and cause obstruction on one of the most iconic and busiest routes into our borough.

“Lambeth Council has taken significant enforcement action, including seizing ice-cream vans and prosecuting people for illegal trading. In the last month alone we have successfully prosecuted individuals for operating unlicensed vans and for selling without a valid street-trading licence.



“But the fact that some traders simply return after being moved on, fined or prosecuted shows that enforcement as it stands is not sufficient. This is a lucrative and persistent illegal trade, and we need to be prepared to look at what more can be done to disrupt it.

“People should not be able to treat fines and prosecutions simply as a cost of doing business. Westminster Bridge should be safe, welcoming and free from illegal trading.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Councillor Caroline Sargent, Deputy Leader of Westminster City Council and Cabinet Member for Enforcement said: “Westminster Bridge is a popular tourist hotspot, and we work closely with the Police and Lambeth Council to share intelligence and carry out enforcement on the bridge and surrounding area.

“Our teams have an excellent track record of enforcing against pedicab riders and unlicensed street traders who try to rip people off and we’ll continue to deter illicit street traders set on scamming unsuspecting visitors.”

News.title: Murder probe after man found dead alongside seriously injured child in Co Tyrone as PSNI confirm suspect in custody
News.content:
GRIM FIND Murder probe after man found dead alongside seriously injured child in Co Tyrone as PSNI confirm suspect in custody

A MURDER probe is under way after a man was found dead alongside a seriously injured child this morning in Co Tyrone.

The PSNI has confirmed that a man has been arrested on suspicion of murder and attempted murder after the grim discovery.



The body and the injured child were discovered in the Lisnahull Road area of Dungannon.

Earlier cops sealed off a terraced house in an estate, with a number of officers and police cars in the area.



A trampoline can be seen in the garden of the house.

The nature of the child’s injuries are unclear at this time. They are receiving treatment at Royal Belfast Hospital for Sick Children.



Cops from the Major Investigations Team are now investigating the shocking incident.

The Northern Ireland Ambulance Service said they were called to the scene at 11.08am.

One advanced care paramedic, two ambulance officers and three emergency crews rushed to the property.

A Hazardous Area Response Team and a helicopter crew, travelling in a ground vehicle, were also despatched.



Sinn Fein councillor Deirdre Varsani, who is also chairwoman of Mid Ulster District Council, said that there is a “strong sense of shock and trauma” in the area today.

She continued: “There is a strong police presence in the area today, trying to carry out investigations and find out and establish what happened.

“We never confirm any of the details until the police would give those full details, but certainly it is a long-standing member of the local community who have been here a good number of years.

“There appears to be a strong sense of shock and trauma and again we ask people to be respectful of the news that might be coming out, and if you have any information, even the smallest piece of information, to please pass that on to police.”

A PSNI spokesperson said that the force would provide a further update “in due course”.

News.title: Royal Navy warships and helicopter track Russian vessels for three days in ‘intense’ operation in UK waters
News.content:
SEA STANDOFF Royal Navy warships and helicopter track Russian vessels for three days in ‘intense’ operation in UK waters

ROYAL Navy warships and a helicopter tracked Russian vessels for three days in an “intense” operation in UK waters.

A task group was shadowed by Type 45 destroyer HMS Duncan, Type 23 frigate HMS St Albans and patrol vessel HMS Severn as it made its way from the North Sea through the English Channel.



Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko was watched escorting sanctioned cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta, with a Merlin helicopter extending the UK’s surveillance as the ships approached the Strait of Dover.

In response to the tracking, Russia deployed other military resources including the Neustrashimy frigate to guard the illegal shipment, UK officials said.



First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said there was “no room for complacency” as shadow fleet vessels continue to pose “an unacceptable risk” to maritime security and the environment.

“Alongside our allies, this approach is forcing Moscow to divert Russian warships away from their core purpose. That is because Russia knows we stand ready to act again, should it be required,” he said.

The Navy vessels handed over monitoring duties to a Nato ally off the coast of France near Ushant following the “intense” 72-hour operation last week, officials said.

Earlier this month, the Navy warned of increasing Russian activity around the UK’s waters after it spent 21 days in July monitoring Moscow’s ships.

Naval operations to monitor Russian activity increased 25 per cent in July compared to the previous year, with warships making repeated voyages through the Dover Strait and North Sea.

Moscow uses its shadow fleet of ageing vessels to evade international sanctions on its oil and fund the war in Ukraine.



The increase in Russian naval activity follows the seizure of the tanker Smyrtos by Royal Marines in June, the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel.

It comes after a week of repeated threats from the Kremlin to the UK following Andy Burnham’s visit to Kyiv, during which he announced Britain would provide Ukraine with blueprints for long-range Scalp missiles.

Western officials have sought to play down the prospect of a conflict between Russia and Nato, despite senior figures in Moscow accusing Ukraine’s allies, including the UK, of “playing with fire”.

Ex-Russian foreign minister Andrei Fedorov also said he could not “100 per cent exclude” the possibility of “semi-military” action against Britain in retaliation, raising the prospect of an attack on British drone factories from “unknown sources.”

On Friday, Western officials said the threats were “not a new phenomenon” but part of “long-standing Russian military doctrine” that seeks to use “hostile rhetoric” to “exploit fears” and influence decisions.



“We do need to be careful to distinguish what is real from what is rhetoric designed to scare and deter us. Replaying Russian threats and heightening a sense of crisis is exactly what the Kremlin wants,” they said.

“Our assessment remains that Russia isn’t seeking direct confrontation with Nato.”

News.title: Tory James Cleverly quits Kemi Badenoch's top team for London mayoral bid
News.content:
Tory James Cleverly quits Kemi Badenoch's top team for London mayoral bid

Ex-Cabinet Minister James Cleverly said he was quitting Kemi Badenoch's shadow cabinet to launch a bid to be London Mayor in May 2028

View 2 Images James Cleverly wants to run to be mayor of London (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

Top Tory James Cleverly has resigned from the shadow cabinet to allow him to be mayor of London.

‌



The former Cabinet Minister said he was quitting Kemi Badenoch's top team to launch a bid for City Hall in the May 2028 election. Labour's Sadiq Khan is serving his third term as London Mayor - but has not declared whether he will seek another term.

‌



In an op-ed for the Sunday Times, Mr Cleverly said: “I have told Kemi Badenoch that I will leave the shadow cabinet. Serving there has been a privilege, and I know there will continue to be strong voices around that table.

‌



“But to run the most effective campaign possible, I must be free to speak about every aspect of London’s future and concentrate fully on winning this race.”

Mr Cleverly is a much bigger name than previous Tory candidates for City Hall, which included controversial London assemblywoman Susan Hall who was trounced by Mr Khan in 2024. He must still win the Conservative nomination to enter the race.

Top Tory blasted for flogging £5 tickets to constituents who want to meet him READ MORE :

View 2 Images Kemi Badenoch is expected to shuffle her top team (Image: PA)

‌



Mr Cleverly, who lost out to Ms Badenoch in the 2024 Tory leadership race, served as Home Secretary and Foreign Secretary under Rishi Sunak and Liz Truss. He was also Education Secretary in Boris Johnson's zombie government in 2022 after fed up Conservative MPs forced the-then PM to announce his resignation.

But the gaffe-prone Tory has also made a string of unfortunate headlines. In 2023, he was forced to apologise after The Mirror revealed he'd joked about spiking his wife's drink at a Downing Street reception. He told female guests that “a little bit of Rohypnol in her drink every night” was “not really illegal if it’s only a little bit”.

It came only hours after he announced a Home Office crackdown on drink spiking. A spokesman later said: "In what was always understood as a private conversation, James, the home secretary tackling spiking, made what was clearly meant to be an ironic joke - for which he apologises."

Article continues below

Weeks earlier, the-then Stockton North MP Alex Cunningham accused Mr Cleverly of calling his constituency a s******* in PMQs. His team denied it, but later said: "He called Alex Cunningham a s*** MP. He apologises for unparliamentary language."

Mr Cleverly was also forced to deny he called his own Government's Rwanda deportation scheme “bats***” after Yvette Cooper told Parliament he had used the phrase.

His departure as Shadow Housing Secretary comes ahead of an expected reshuffle as Ms Badenoch battles to overhaul her party's toxic reputation. The Tory leader's personal popularity outstrips her party, which is dogged by ongoing anger at its failures in Government.

News.title: Big Church Festival live: Hero helped lift sign off victims after it came 'crashing down' killing man
News.content:
A huge wooden sign carrying the words “Everything’s Unmissable” fell on the man who died, according to an eyewitness.

One person has died after a sign fell on people at Big Church Festival in Steyning in West Sussex, with ambulance crews treating six people at the scene

Big Church Festival live: Hero helped lift sign off victims after it came 'crashing down' killing man

A 41-year-old man has died after a huge wooden sign came “crashing down” onto people at Big Church Festival in Steyning.

The sign, which reportedly carried the words “Everything’s Unmissable”, fell near a tented area at the Christian festival in West Sussex on Friday afternoon.

One eyewitness has since revealed he and his wife were walking just a few paces behind when the sign came down. He said they rushed to help lift it off those underneath and gave first aid alongside others until paramedics arrived.

Six people were treated for injuries following the incident at around 3.38pm. Sussex Police later confirmed a man from Eastbourne had died.

The festival, which had been due to continue until Sunday, has now been cancelled by organisers.

South East Coast Ambulance Service was called to reports of multiple people in need of medical attention, while an air ambulance was pictured leaving the scene.

This is a live news event. Please check for the latest updates below.

News.title: Everything you're entitled to if airline loses your luggage
News.content:
Everything you're entitled to if airline loses your luggage

Holidaymakers may be entitled to claim compensation when an airline loses, damages or delays their luggage

View 3 Images The compensation available from an airline is generally limited (Image: anyaberkut via Getty Images)

Holidaymakers facing the misery of lost, damaged or delayed luggage could be entitled to compensation from their airline - but they need to act quickly.

‌



Passengers arriving at their destination only to discover their suitcase has failed to make the journey with them have legal rights that can help them recover some of the costs. Citizens Advice says travellers have the right to claim compensation from an airline when checked-in luggage is delayed, lost or damaged. But there are important deadlines - and passengers should report a problem as soon as possible.

‌



The consumer advice charity warns that the rules for cabin baggage are different. You can generally only claim for a problem with hand luggage where the airline was at fault.

‌



Don't leave it too late

Citizens Advice says holidaymakers should report missing or damaged luggage to the airline straight away. At the airport, this will normally involve completing a Property Irregularity Report (PIR) at the baggage claims area.

Passengers should keep a copy of the PIR, or obtain written confirmation from the airline if they report the problem later. Making a report does not necessarily mean a compensation claim has been made. Passengers will normally still need to submit a separate claim unless the airline agrees to pay certain expenses upfront.

View 3 Images holidaymakers should report missing or damaged luggage to the airline straight away (Image: skynesher via Getty Images)

‌



There are strict deadlines

One of the biggest traps is assuming there is plenty of time to make a claim.

Citizens Advice says the usual deadlines are:

Damaged luggage: claim within seven days of receiving it.

Missing or damaged contents: claim within seven days of receiving the luggage.

Delayed or missing luggage: claim within 21 days of the flight.

Luggage not returned within 21 days: it is officially treated as lost, meaning passengers should make a claim as soon as possible.

‌



A suitcase that eventually turns up after several days does not necessarily mean a passenger has lost their right to compensation. Citizens Advice says it is still possible to claim for delayed luggage if it is returned within the 21-day period.

What can you claim for?

The compensation available from an airline is generally limited. For delayed luggage, this can include the cost of essential items needed while waiting for the suitcase, such as toiletries and underwear.

Passengers may also be able to claim some of the cost of repairing or replacing luggage and its contents if they are lost or damaged. If a traveller has to collect delayed luggage themselves, says they may also be able to recover reasonable transport costs.

‌



But holidaymakers should not assume they will receive the full replacement value of everything inside a suitcase. Airlines will often ask for receipts and proof of purchase, while Citizens Advice warns that they will not normally pay 'new for old' replacement costs.

There can also be restrictions around valuable, fragile or perishable items packed in checked luggage. Total compensation is generally limited to around £1,000 and is often considerably less.

Passengers cannot normally claim for stress or inconvenience caused by the luggage problem, or for knock-on problems such as missing a connection.

‌



View 3 Images You can generally only claim for a problem with hand luggage where the airline was at fault (Image: John Nordell via Getty Images)

Keep every scrap of evidence

Anyone making a claim should keep hold of their paperwork.

Citizens Advice says airlines will usually expect passengers to provide documents such as:

‌



their boarding pass;

luggage tags showing the identification number;

the PIR or written confirmation that the problem was reported;

receipts for emergency purchases made because of delayed luggage;

proof of purchase for lost or damaged belongings;

photographs showing damage; and

estimates for the cost of repairs where relevant.

Travellers should keep copies of their claim and the original documents.

How to make the claim

Passengers should check with their airline to find out how it wants compensation claims submitted. If there is no specific claim form, Citizens Advice says travellers may need to write to the airline's customer service department.

‌



The charity advises making clear that the claim is being made under the Montreal Convention. The claim should include details of the flight, including the date, flight number, departure point and destination.

Travellers should explain what happened, set out the amount being claimed and provide a detailed list of the luggage or contents that were lost or damaged. Any essential items bought because of the delay should also be listed, with copies of supporting receipts and other evidence.

What if several airlines were involved?

Passengers travelling on connecting flights operated by different airlines may be able to claim against any of them. However, Citizens Advice says most airlines expect the claim to be made against the last airline boarded.

‌



An airline cannot simply refuse to deal with a claim because another carrier was involved. If a passenger gets nowhere they can seek advice from the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA).

What if the airline rejects your claim?

Holidaymakers who are unhappy with an airline's response can take the matter further. Citizens Advice recommends first trying to resolve the complaint through the appropriate process.

The CAA can take up complaints against airlines or airports in certain circumstances, although its role depends on whether the airline or airport belongs to an approved alternative dispute resolution scheme. As a last resort, passengers can consider taking a case to the small claims court.

‌



A luggage claim can generally be taken to court within two years of the flight, although court action can be costly and time-consuming.

Check your insurance too

There is another option that could prove easier and more generous. Citizens Advice says that if luggage is covered by travel insurance or a home contents policy, making an insurance claim may be preferable.

This is because insurance can potentially provide more money and may be easier to claim through than pursuing the airline.

Article continues below

Passengers needing further help can contact the Citizens Advice consumer helpline on 0808 223 1133 or use its online service.

The charity also advises checking the specific rules applying to the airline, as individual procedures and deadlines can vary. More information here.

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Barcola signing imminent, Gakpo's message to Spurs, Man Utd get Chelsea deal
News.content:
The latest transfer news from the Premier League and further afield, including updates on Arsenal, Manchester United, Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and many more

Welcome to Mirror Football's transfer blog for Saturday, August 29.

Bradley Barcola's seemingly imminent transfer from Paris Saint-Germain to Liverpool has continued to dominate the headlines, as one of the most exciting sagas of the summer is set to come to an end. It is claimed that an agreement has been reached between the two clubs, and that the Reds will pay a total of £123million for the 23-year-old winger.

That's broken down into a guaranteed £106m, as well as £17m in add-ons. A move to Anfield is expected to be formalised in the coming days. Barcola isn't the only talent that could bolster Andoni Iraola's first-team in the coming days, however.

The Reds are also reportedly setting their sights on Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr, with Nicolo Schira claiming that an agreement in principle over a contract running to 2031 has been met between Liverpool and the player. A new bid is expected to come, after Palace rebuffed an initial offer of around £51m.

In the English capital, meanwhile, Arsenal are still chasing Julian Alvarez's signature, with his future with Atletico Madrid up in the air. The 26-year-old centre-forward has missed training thrice this week, albeit, citing illness as the reason for his absence, as the Gunners prepare to table a £130m bid to secure his signature.

Manchester United's search for a new left-back also runs on, having seemingly ditched their pursuit of Lews Hall as a result of Newcastle United refusing to sell the 21-year-old. While Alejandro Balde was considered an ideal candidate, the 22-year-old has now told Hansi Flick that he wants to fight for his place at Barcelona.

Stay tuned as we bring you all of the latest news in our transfer blog below...

News.title: Rain-soaked Reading Festival attendee realises 'big outfit mistake' too late
News.content:
Rain-soaked Reading Festival attendee realises 'big outfit mistake' too late

Reading Festival is taking place this weekend and thousands of music fans are descending on the city - but some of them have not come prepared for the downpours

View Image Reading Festival revellers battled downpours on Friday (28th August) (Image: Redferns)

Thousands of music fans have descended on Reading this Bank Holiday weekend for one of the UK's most iconic festivals, and despite the heavens opening up, the crowds are keeping their energy high. The event is being held at Richfield Avenue from August 27th to 30th, with a headline-grabbing lineup that includes Charli XCX, Dave, Fontaines D.C., Florence and the Machine, and Raye.

‌



Gates opened earlier in the week, giving eager festival-goers the chance to claim their patch of ground, set up camp, and soak up the atmosphere before Friday's opening full day of performances got underway. But as the festival began, so too did the rain - a sharp contrast to the dry, scorching summer many parts of the country had been experiencing in the weeks prior. It comes as flood warnings have been put in place for the festival, and many revellers find their tents full of water.

‌



As the downpours rolled in and the grass quickly gave way to mud beneath the feet of thousands of revellers, conditions underfoot became increasingly treacherous. And for one unsuspecting attendee, the deteriorating ground was about to expose a rather costly packing oversight.

‌



A woman named Phoebe took to TikTok to share a video diary of her Reading Festival weekend, but it quickly took an unexpected turn when viewers noticed something rather alarming about her choice of footwear.

Her footage showed the festival site's ground in a sorry state - a thick, waterlogged mess churned up by the combination of relentless rainfall and the constant footfall of festival-goers. It was, in short, no place for anything other than solid, sturdy footwear. Which made it all the more remarkable that Phoebe and her friend had shown up wearing flip-flops.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



The pair could be seen picking their way gingerly through the mud, each step a careful calculation to avoid a slip or, worse, losing a shoe entirely. At one point, Phoebe could be heard exclaiming she was "losing" her footwear as one of her flip-flops was almost claimed by the mud beneath her.

It didn't take long for commenters to pile in, with many branding the footwear choice a "rookie error" that seasoned festival-goers would never dare to make.

"This is going to be a BIG learning curve, girls," one viewer remarked.

‌



"Not walking around in flip-flops may help," offered another.

A third simply asked: "Really random, but why would you wear flip-flops to a festival?"

Anyone who has attended Reading Festival more than once will know that unsuitable footwear is a trap that tends to end in misery - and flip-flops are arguably the worst offender, whether the ground is muddy or not.

‌



Not everyone was unsympathetic, however. A number of commenters suggested the women make a quick trip into Reading town centre via shuttle bus to pick up a pair of wellies, or at the very least a more practical pair of trainers from a nearby shop.

Others noted that some traders within the festival grounds may well be selling wellies on-site - though they warned that, given the conditions, stock could already be running low.

If you are heading to Reading Festival on Saturday or Sunday, it is well worth keeping a close eye on the forecast before you leave the house. The Met Office is predicting rain throughout Saturday, with top temperatures of around 21°C. Sunday looks set to be similar in terms of warmth, though there is a slightly lower chance of showers - currently sitting at around 40% at the time of writing.

Article continues below

Either way, after two days of wet weather already this weekend, the ground is not going to get any drier. So maybe leave the flip-flops at home and opt for something more sensible.

News.title: 2027 bank holiday trick to turn 24 days leave into 56 days off work
News.content:
2027 bank holiday trick to turn 24 days leave into 56 days off work

If you're looking to make the most of your annual leave in 2027, there's a simple trick that could see you get 56 days off work using just 24 days of leave

View Image Here's how to maximise your time off next year (Image: Alexander Spatari via Getty Images)

With summer now drawing to a close, many of us will shortly be making plans for 2027. And if your annual leave resets on January 1, you may well be thinking ahead about how to make the most of it.

‌



How you choose to use your accumulated holidays is entirely up to you. Perhaps you want to spend quality time with family, catch up with friends, or simply enjoy some well-earned solitude, but whatever you decide, a clever trick could transform your standard 24 days of holiday into a whopping 56 days off work in some wonderfully lengthy stretches.

‌



It all boils down to bank holidays and some clever planning. Similar hacks have been available in previous years but, unfortunately for some, it only applies to those who don't work weekends, and are given bank holidays off as standard, or do not have to take them as annual leave.

‌



To begin, book Monday to Friday, January 4-8, off work to enjoy ten consecutive days off thanks to the New Year's Day bank holiday, using just five days of leave. Then in March, if you book off Monday to Thursday, March 22-25, you'll convert four days of leave into 10 days away from the office, thanks to Good Friday on March 26 and Easter Monday on March 29.

Your Easter break will then see you finish work on Friday, March 19, not returning until Tuesday, March 30. And later in the spring, there are two further opportunities to maximise your leave.

‌



Since the Early Spring Bank Holiday lands on Monday, May 3, if you request May 4-7 off, you'll secure nine days away from the office using only four days of annual leave. You can then replicate this approach later when the Spring Bank Holiday arrives on Monday, May 31 - request Tuesday-Friday June 1-4 off work to gain another nine days with just four days of annual holiday.

The Summer Bank Holiday in England and Wales lands on Monday, August 30, next year - so you can request Tuesday-Friday, August 31-September 3 off for another nine-day period using four days of annual leave.

And finally if you request Wednesday-Friday December 29-31 off work you can secure a substantial nine days off with only three days of holiday thanks to when the festive bank holidays land in 2027. Since Christmas lands on a Saturday, with Boxing Day on a Sunday, substitute bank holidays occur on the Monday and Tuesday, December 27 and 28.

Article continues below

Requesting the above days off at the conclusion of December would mean you're off work from Christmas Day right through to January 3.

Time off - days booked off

News.title: Britain's longest living child liver transplant patient is loving life - 36 years after op
News.content:
Britain's longest living child liver transplant patient is loving life - 36 years after op

Robert Blades had two liver transplants in 1989 when he was a child and is now the longest surviving child to have had operations in that field - it's a chance he hasn't failed to grasp

View 6 Images Robert Blades, longest surviving child liver transplant patient, with wife Emma

Robert Blades is a fit 47 year old father-of-two who lives life to the full enjoying rock climbing, swimming and surfing - he is also the longest surviving child liver transplant patient at 36 years and counting.

‌



Four decades ago, his parents were told he had a deadly liver disease, Alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency, that would kill him by the age of nine. He was just 18 months old.

‌



At that time there were no liver transplants for children and a list of those willing to donate their organs at death didn’t exist. Medics first realised something was wrong when Rob, a shipping consultant, was four weeks old and suffered internal bleeding that nearly killed him.

‌



View 6 Images Robert Blades in hospital for liver transplant as a child (Image: Supplied)

He recalls a childhood of hospital visits, during which a large needle was pushed between his ribs to get biopsy tissue from his liver. He said: “That was painful, but necessary, and the only way of assessing how much damage was being caused to my liver. Despite everything my family made a conscious decision - we were going to live as normally as possible.”

His parents took him rock climbing in Dorset and sailing on Cornwall, but the disease was always present. Robert said: “We spent as much time outdoors as we could. My parents did as much as they could for me. There was one memorable sailing visit to the Isle of Wight when I suffered a severe internal bleed. I had to be rushed ashore and taken to St Mary's Hospital in Newport where they operated and cauterized the bleeding.”

‌



View 6 Images Rob and his parents are celebrating his extra years

Rob, from The Witterings, Sussex, said: “There were hospital visits, scares, and the occasional emergencies, but life carried on. Now as a parent myself, looking back, I realise how much stress my parents must have been under.

“Every bump, every fall, every illness came with an extra layer of fear for them. But as a child, I just got on with it. What I now truly appreciate is that my parents have seen me at my best and at my worst, and I would not be where I am today without their stoic support.”

‌



By 1988, when he was eight Rob was getting weaker, he became jaundiced, struggled to eat, and had little energy. Out of the blue parents Peter and Heather received a call to go to Addenbrookes Hospital in Cambridge, a renowned liver treatment centre.

Rob recalls: “We met Sir Roy Calne, the eminent adult liver transplant surgeon and he introduced us to his transplant team. It was quite an experience for a sickly child. It was suggested, in a casual way, that a treatment might happen sometime in the future. It was that vague.”

View 6 Images For Rob, aged eight, the future seemed grim (Image: Supplied)

‌



Mum, Heather, 75, said: “When we went to Cambridge we had very little knowledge of transplants. We knew that they had been done in adults, but not, as far we knew, in children. Sir Roy was a brilliant man but a bit of an old-fashioned doctor. He didn’t say much and we left not knowing much more than we came. We were none the wiser about a transplant taking place.”

In February 1989 the Blades got a call to make their way quickly to Addenbrookes because a liver had been found for Rob. Rob’s nine hour operation was deemed a success. His donor was a 13 year old girl tragically killed in a car crash.

Heather, 75, said: “We were excited, but it was a trip into the unknown. We had no idea if it would work and if it did how long it would last. When they got him back from the operating theatre to ICU, we were relieved. He was in hospital for six weeks. But from early on the liver started to reject despite the use of powerful anti-rejection drugs.”

‌



By late summer Rob was sick again. He said “The anti-rejection drugs were unpleasant. But It was my failing liver that was making me jaundiced and unwell.”

Heather added: “We were told Rob needed another transplant, but could they find another liver in time? There was still no organ donor register. So sourcing organs was a bit of a lottery.”

View 6 Images Rob continues to enjoy life with his family

‌



Luckily for Rob seven months after the original transplant, in September, another liver was found. Again, the donor was a young girl killed in a car crash. The second op was a success - with medics assuming a five to ten year survival rate.

But 36 years on Rob is now happily married to wife Emma, 46, and dad to Megan,16 and Marilda, 12. He said: “At the time I wouldn’t have appreciated how lucky I was. Now I realise that in the absence of a national donor register other children would have died. Yet I got two transplants in less than a year.”

The family enjoys an outdoor life, surfing, windsurfing, sailing and climbing with their daughters - Rob even played rugby, knowing contact sports are frowned upon by medics because of the risk of damage to his transplant.

‌



He said: “The doctors would rather you were risk adverse but there’s no point in wrapping yourself up in cotton wool.”

Rob an advocate for Liver UK - said taking medication daily reminds him how lucky he has been. One reason survival rates are now so good is the anti-rejection drug, cyclosporin, which the late Sir Roy Calne helped develop.

View 6 Images Rob's mum said they weren't told a great deal ahead of the transplant

Article continues below

He said “You always remember your donors. I wrote to both of mine and got a thank you back from one. While there have been few problems with liver number two, it has started to show signs of rejection which can’t be controlled. I’ve had 36 years thanks to this liver but in recent years my body has started to reject it despite my anti-rejection drugs.

“You worry that should I need a third transplant, I might not get one. After all, I'm nearly 50. But I wouldn’t have been here today without that second transplant. And for that I am eternally grateful.”

News.title: Festivalgoers' misery as thousands drenched by pelting rain over bank holiday
News.content:
Festivalgoers' misery as thousands drenched by pelting rain over bank holiday

Flood warnings have been put in place at Reading Festival this weekend as pelting rain seeps through ticket holders' tents, leaving the fields thick with sticky mud

View 5 Images Revellers at Reading Festival have been soaked by torrential rain (Image: Geoffrey Swaine/Shutterstock)

Festivals across the country got off to a soggy start as relentless rain made a comeback for the Bank Holiday weekend.

‌



Reading Festival was one of the victims as thousands of fans had their spirits dampened by the gloomy weather. In glum scenes, music lovers were drenched by pelting rain while sloshing around in the mud to get to the stages.

‌



There were worse conditions in the camping sections as the alfresco sleeping arrangements as the ground turned to slush were thousands of tents were pitched.

‌



Flood warnings have been put in place at the festival as torrential rains seeps through ticket holders' tents. Sharing photos of the grim weather on Instagram, one person - sporting a poncho - mused: "Lovely weather for ducks at Reading".

Unfortunately for music fans, the deluge looks set to continue. Despite a three-day onslaught, which left many homes hammered by flood water, the Met Office has predicted the wet weather will continue throughout the weekend.

View 5 Images Flood warnings have been put in place at Reading Festival (Image: Jeff Moore/PA Wire)

‌



The forecaster issued a yellow warning across most of England and Wales for heavy showers and thunderstorms which was feared to cause travel disruption and flooding The showers will ease somewhat tonight with rain clearing from many central and southern areas, with a few showers following. On Sunday, the weather will remain unsettled but become somewhat drier late on Monday.

View 5 Images The Met Office has predicted the wet weather will continue throughout the weekend. (Image: Geoffrey Swaine/Shutterstock)

Also affected by the weather this weekend is Leeds Festival and Creamfields. Four-day dance festival, Creamfields, in Cheshire has been battered by severe storms, leaving some acts forced to flee their sets mid-performance.

‌



As things kicked off on Friday, DJ Vikkstar, better known as a member of YouTube collective The Sidemen, took to social media to share his disappointment after being booted off the stage.

Making his debut at the festival, Vikkstar shared videos of the fallout on his social media as he told fans "POV: Your Creamfields Debut gets shut down because of a thunderstorm."

View 5 Images Some party people soaked up the experience (Image: Jeff Moore/PA Wire)

‌



In a video shared online, fans could be heard chanting "keep on playing" and booing when the music stopped after the DJ appeared to have been told to press pause of proceedings.

“Creamfields robbed of some generational drum and bass tonight… next time," he shared.

Later though, he seemed to find the situation somewhat funnier as he shared on X: "Creamfields set shut down…Maybe I shouldn’t have worn a lightning tee. Appreciate you all."

‌



View 5 Images 'Classic UK weather betrayal!' (Image: Jeff Moore/PA Wire)

It is understood that all other sets were cancelled across the dance festival last night due to the severe weather disruption.

Taking to social media, sharing their frustration, one fan vented: "Of course! Months of perfect sunshine… then the moment Creamfields opens, the heavens decide to open too! Classic UK weather betrayal!"

Article continues below

However, despite the unfavourable conditions, some soaked up the experience and frolicked in the rain - laughing their heads off as they made the most of their weekend.

News.title: Christian festival 'devastated' as man dies after sign falls
News.content:
Organisers of a Christian festival say they are "devastated" after a man died and six other people were injured by a falling sign.

Sussex Police said it had been called to the Big Church Festival at Wiston Park, near Steyning in West Sussex, at about 15:38 BST on Friday.

It was later confirmed a 41-year-old man from Eastbourne in East Sussex had died.

The Archbishop of Canterbury said she was "sad and shocked" to hear about the fatal incident.

Dame Sarah Mullally said: "I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve. I pray for those receiving treatment, and the healthcare workers looking after them.

"And I pray too for the other festival goers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events.

"May the God of comfort and healing be with them all."

South East Coast Ambulance service said four of the six people injured were taken to local hospitals for further treatment, with two people having serious injuries.

The Big Church Festival, which describes itself as the UK's biggest Christian festival, was founded in 2009.

The festival began on Friday and was due to continue until Sunday, but a decision was made by organisers to cancel the remainder of the event after the incident.

"We are working with the emergency services, police and the Health and Safety Executive as they establish the circumstances surrounding today's incident," the organisers said.

"We are incredibly grateful to everyone who responded, and to our teams and community for the care they have shown one another."

News.title: Cleverly quits shadow cabinet to run for London mayor
News.content:
Conservative MP Sir James Cleverly has said he is resigning from the shadow cabinet to run for London mayor.

"I am putting myself forward to be the Conservative candidate for mayor of London, because our capital needs more than an administrator," he wrote in the Times.

Sir James said he has told Tory leader Kemi Badenoch he is stepping down as shadow housing secretary, saying: "I must be free to speak about every aspect of London's future and concentrate fully on winning this race."

The capital is not set to vote on a new mayor until May 2028. Labour incumbent Sir Sadiq Khan is yet to confirm whether he will seek an unprecedented fourth term.

A source close to Badenoch said Cleverly "is a formidable politician and will out-campaign Khan".

Sir James, who was foreign secretary under former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, wrote that he intended to make London a city to be proud of again.

"We must rebuild its reputation and make it, once again, the best place in the world to live, work, invest and build a business," he added.

A senior Conservative politician, Sir James has held a number of ministerial positions under three prime ministers - including roles as home secretary and education secretary.

The army reservist represented the Tories on the London Assembly before his election as MP for Braintree in 2015.

After rising through the backbenches, he unsuccessfully ran for Conservative party leader in 2024, losing out to Badenoch.

Reacting to Sir James's announcement, a source said Badenoch "really didn't want James to leave shadow cabinet", but believed "he will be a big asset in London".

Current London Mayor Sir Sadiq began his first term in 2016. Cleverly wrote that the capital has been "let down by Labour".

He accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of treating London as a "cash cow: somewhere to tax, regulate, raid and blame".

Sir James said: "Londoners need homes they can afford to buy or rent. Entrepreneurs need to be able to start and grow businesses without being strangled by cost and regulation."

The last time Londoners voted for their mayor in May 2024, Sir Sadiq beat Conservative rival Susan Hall by more than 275,000 votes - representing a swing of 3.2% to Labour.

The mayor won nine of the 14 constituencies including two gains from the Tories, and gained 43.8% of the vote share.

Reform UK revealed its candidate for the May 2028 election in January when it announced Westminster City councillor Laila Cunningham would be running.

News.title: Football fans pay tribute to crash death officers at Middlesbrough match
News.content:
Football fans and players have paid tribute to two Cleveland Police officers who were killed in a crash on Teesside.

PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough died in a head-on collision between their police car and a vehicle going the wrong way on the A66 near Middlesbrough early on 22 August. Five people in the other vehicle also died.

There was a minute's applause in their memory ahead of Middlesbrough and West Bromwich Albion's Championship match at Riverside Stadium, as pictures of the two men were displayed on a screen.

On Friday evening Hartlepool United also held a two-minute silence before their home National League game against Eastleigh.

Middlesbrough FC said in a statement prior to the match: "We are also showing our appreciation for the dedication and hard work of both men, and to Cleveland Police force in protecting and supporting our local community.

"The commitment shown by officers and staff, often in challenging and demanding circumstances, plays a vital role in keeping residents safe and helping people feel secure in their homes, neighbourhoods and local areas."

News.title: Sarah Ferguson expected back in the UK 'shortly', source says
News.content:
Ferguson is expected to move into the six-bedroom home "imminently", which could be as soon as next week, the Sun reported, external.

It is believed she has been spending her time out of the public eye at an Alpine chalet in Verbier, Switzerland, since leaving Royal Lodge. Her belongings were collected from Mountbatten-Windsor's home in Sandringham this week, the newspaper added.

She had been keeping a low profile since losing her titles alongside Mountbatten-Windsor after she became mired in the scandal about her connections to Epstein, and faced calls to speak to US authorities after last year's release of millions of documents shed new light on their relationship.

In one email exchange from 2011, she appeared to privately apologise for her public rejection of Epstein, saying: "You have always been a steadfast, generous and supreme friend to me and my family."

A spokesperson for the duchess previously said the email was sent after Epstein had threatened to sue her for defamation - in an effort to convince him not to.

Another email suggested Ferguson took her daughters to see Epstein in the US days after he was released from prison for child sex crimes.

The emails do not indicate any wrongdoing.

Epstein was also ultimately the downfall of Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his titles by the King because of "serious lapses of judgment" over his friendship with the late paedophile. Mountbatten-Windsor has always denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.

Ferguson lost her courtesy royal divorcee title and reverted to her maiden name, and also lost the freedom of the city of York after councillors voted unanimously to remove the honour over the scandal.

Her expected return comes just days after the Duke and Duchess of Sussex came back to Britain with their children to begin a new life after six years living in the US.

News.title: 97-year-old woman rescued after Nepali floods looked like 'a warrior'
News.content:
A 97-year-old woman pulled from flood debris in Nepal is recovering in hospital, according to her doctors.

Guna Maya Bohara's great-nephew, Dipak Bohara, has told BBC Nepali she looked like "a warrior" who had returned victorious from battle.

The operation to pull Bohara out of the rubble of her care home took four hours.

Bohara travelled from Kathmandu to help rescue his great-aunt.

Hundreds of people have been confirmed dead after Wednesday's flash floods, which scientists believe were triggered by a glacier collapsing in the Himalayan border region with Tibet.

Video produced by Mansi Kapur and Kamal Pariyar. Video edited by Suneth Perera, Jasmin Dyer and Andrew Webb.

More on this story here.

News.title: Satellite images reveal scale of flood devastation in Nepal villages
News.content:
New satellite imagery has revealed the scale of the devastation along Nepal's Trishuli River caused by Wednesday's deadly flash flood, triggered by a glacier collapse.

Before-and-after images show how sections of the valley, where a torrent of floodwater and debris surged through, destroyed villages, bridges and hydroelectric power stations.

Hundreds of people have been killed and thousands more are missing, Nepalese officials say.

Among the worst-hit locations reviewed by BBC Verify was a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing, which was engulfed by a rush of floodwater and captured on camera.

The satellite imagery from US-based intelligence firm Vantor, shows the site has been almost entirely washed away. Shocking CCTV footage showed the moment as the deluge of water swept over buildings as people tried to escape.

News.title: What we know about the 33 British nationals missing in Nepal
News.content:
Families are flying out to Nepal to help the ongoing search for 33 British nationals still missing after deadly floods hit the country.

The brother of Neetu Goyal Tiwari, one of the missing Brits who has not been seen since Wednesday, has appealed to officials to locate his sister.

"Please help us find her", Naresh Goyal told the BBC as he struggled to hold back his emotions.

On Friday, Nepalese authorities named 573 tourists who are still missing in the country and despite fears of a second wave of flooding, search efforts have continued.

To help, the UK is deploying a rapid deployment team to Nepal to support British nationals affected in the region.

The specially-trained crisis response team is expected to arrive in Kathmandu on Saturday, a move that follows Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge of Â£5m worth of humanitarian support for relief and recovery efforts.

And as rescue efforts continue in the aftermath of the disaster which killed at least 538 people, details of the missing are slowly emerging.

News.title: We're behind UK's emergency phone alerts - but question how they're being used
News.content:
The government's Cobra emergency committee met to discuss how to respond. After sign off from Prime Minister Andy Burnham's de facto deputy Louise Haigh, the alert was sent at 19:00 on 14 August.

It triggered a backlash on social media with some vowing to opt out of further alerts in their phone settings, domestic abuse charities and survivors saying victims with hidden phones were put at risk, and confusion about alerts sent multiple times.

Dowden's worry is that the wildfire alert was more like a public information campaign than an imminent threat to life across all of England and Wales.

"People need to know that when they receive an alert, it is a genuine imminent emergency," the Conservative MP says. "If that confidence is lost, people will simply ignore it."

A Cabinet Office report during trials in 2014 warned of this "cry wolf" effect, while pointing out there was strong support among the public for the alerts.

"Alerts should not be issued just because the government wants to be seen to be doing something," Dowden adds.

The National Fire Chiefs Council said the alert heightened people's awareness and public behaviour, while government insiders point out wildfire alerts are commonplace in many European countries.

"By following the guidance that was issued, people were able to take the necessary steps to keep themselves safe and front line services recorded a significant decrease in incidents in the following days," a government spokesperson said.

But Frazer Rhodes, who worked in government across a decade to help build the technology and devise high thresholds for the alerts, feels a review is now necessary to avoid future ones backfiring.

He was in a bar in Halifax, West Yorkshire, with his wife when the sound of pinging phones began echoing around.

"Everybody around was just going, 'what's this?' What's this?'" he tells us. "Then my wife shouted, 'he did that'."

His wife's joke aside, he said his "immediate thought" was whether it met the threshold for sending one. He explains: "At its heart are three criteria: urgency, severity and certainty. So, in simple terms, how bad, how soon, and how sure?"

Rhodes thinks the wildfire alert arguably met the bar for urgency and severity, but perhaps not for certainty of a threat to life.

"It should be very rare to get an alert," he points out.

News.title: Strong winds and thunderstorms kick off the bank holiday weekend
News.content:
After weeks of scorching heat and drought the summer's swan song is set to be one of frequent downpours as well as gales for some.

Areas of heavy rain and showers are expected to sweep across parts of the UK on each day of the weekend, which is a bank holiday for many.

This could make for some soggy moments at many of the festivals taking place over the coming days.

Strong winds and gales may also cause problems for travellers and holidaymakers in southern parts of the UK.

News.title: Royal Navy warships track Russian vessels for three days in UK waters
News.content:
Royal Navy warships and a helicopter spent three days tracking Russian Navy vessels and sanctioned cargo ships in an "intense" operation in the North Sea and English Channel.

HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn used radars to monitor four vessels last week, while a Merlin helicopter provided surveillance from the sky.

"Since that successful operation, we have seen Russian shadow fleet vessels increasingly forced to change their routes, imposing significant cost and delays to their journeys," Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord and Chief of Naval Staff, said.

It comes as data shows Royal Navy activity to monitor Russian movements is up 25% so far this year compared to 2025.

During the August operation, the Royal Navy warships including a Type 45 destroyer and a Type 23 frigate, tracked Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko as it escorted sanctioned cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta south through the North Sea and into the English Channel.

The Royal Navy said Russia was "forced" to respond with "costly military resources" including the frigate Neustrashimy.

A statement said a Nato ally then took over monitoring off the coast of France, without specifying the country.

The operation comes after Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in June.

Marines joined by National Crime Agency (NCA) officers, with the support of the RAF, intercepted and boarded the Smyrtos in a six-hour operation - the first of its kind by UK armed forces.

NCA officers arrested an Indian national, 38, on suspicion of sanctions offences under the Russia Regulations and he was taken into custody.

News.title: Mother backs calls to stop killers' early release
News.content:
More than 30 families have called on the government to stop killers convicted of any form of manslaughter being released early to ease prison overcrowding in England and Wales.

In a letter to Justice Secretary Alex Norris, the families said they felt victims were "being asked to bear the consequences of the prison capacity crisis".

Signatories include Emma Webber, whose son Barnaby was stabbed to death in the Nottingham attacks in 2023, and whose killer Valdo Calocane was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility.

Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, Bridget Phillipson, Minister for Women and Equalities, defended the early release scheme.

She said the government had faced "some really difficult and unpalatable choices" in dealing with prison overcrowding and that they had faced "the wholesale collapse of the criminal justice system".

The scheme, external aims to ease prison overcrowding in England and Wales.

The families of those affected by homicide have called for those convicted of any form of manslaughter to be excluded.

Those convicted of murder and those serving sentences for rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences are already excluded from the early release scheme.

News.title: Murder investigation after man found dead and child seriously injured
News.content:
A murder investigation has been launched after a man was found dead alongside a seriously injured child in County Tyrone on Saturday morning.

A male has been arrested on suspicion of murder and attempted murder and remains in custody.

The incident took place in Lisnahull Road in Dungannon.

The child was taken to the Royal Belfast Hospital for Sick Children.

Police are currently at the scene and have said the public should avoid the area while enquiries continue.

The Northern Ireland Ambulance Service (NIAS) said they received a 999 call at 11:08 BST on Saturday, following reports of an incident.

They dispatched a helicopter crew, three emergency crews, one advanced care paramedic, two ambulance officers and one HART (Hazardous Area Response Team) crew to the scene.

News.title: Woman detained in Egypt over 'sister's activism'
News.content:
A mother-of-four from Birmingham has been detained by the Egyptian authorities, with her husband and lawyer claiming it is due to her sister's online activism.

Eman el-Shazly, 45, from Handsworth Wood, was taken from her mother's house in Cairo in the early hours of Monday 17 August. Her husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, said this was 24 hours after Egyptian security forces "ram-raided" the property and told her: "You need to tell your sister to stop".

Three of el-Shazly's other siblings have also been detained, with her two brothers already being held when she was taken, and one of her sisters detained soon after.

The BBC has contacted the Egyptian consulate in London but has not had a response.

Moustapha said: "The family's a bit traumatised. [The children] are heartbroken.

"We really need the UK government to get their fingers out as quickly as possible."

A spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) said: "We are supporting the family of a British national detained in Egypt, and are in contact with the authorities."

News.title: Attempted murder arrest after man falls from balcony
News.content:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after a man fell from a balcony.

Police were called to reports that the man had fallen at flats on Liverpool Street in Salford shortly after midnight on Saturday, Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said.

Emergency services attended and the man was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries, where he remains in a critical condition, the force said.

A man in his 20s has been taken into police custody for questioning.

The incident has been referred to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) because the men had earlier contact with police, GMP said.

A blue forensic tent has been erected near to a building on the corner of Liverpool Street and Southern Street.

A local resident, who did not wish to be named, said she heard sirens overnight and saw the aftermath of the incident being live-streamed on social media.

She said: "I heard all the sirens, but I keep myself to myself so I didn't go out.

"I've seen it's all cordoned off and there's a blue forensics tent.

"It's sad, it's really sad. It's a bit close to home."

Ch Insp Lee Gridley said: "A man has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder, and he is currently being questioned in custody.

"Our officers are working at pace to establish the full circumstances, and a scene will remain in place whilst the investigation continues.

"We understand that incidents of this nature may cause concern within the community, however we believe this is an isolated incident and that there is no wider risk to the public."

An IOPC spokesperson said: "After being notified by the Greater Manchester Police of the previous police contact with the parties involved in this incident, we sent investigators to the police post-incident procedures in Manchester in assessment mode to gather further information.

"We continue to remain in assessment mode and will assess a GMP referral in due course."

News.title: Mountain of broken fridges growing across England and Wales
News.content:
A mountain of broken fridges is building up in waste centres across England and Wales, the Local Government Association (LGA) has warned.

This year's multiple heat waves have increased the numbers of white goods such as fridges and freezers breaking down and needing to be scrapped at specialist sites.

Dozens of councils have been forced to stop collections of white goods due to a major backlog, which has built up due to a national shortage of specialists needed to safely process the appliances.

Earlier this month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the latest crackdown on illegal waste dumps - and the LGA is now calling on the government to take urgent action on dealing with white goods too.

LGA Neighbourhoods committee chair Councillor Arooj Shah called on the government to force white goods companies to pick up the burden, help councils with the cost of extra storage, and prevent the same problems recurring in future.

"The backlog of defunct white goods is getting bigger by the day â they're at risk of becoming a mountain," he said.

"It is not right that residents who are trying to do the right thing can't take old or broken appliances to their local recycling centre due to failures elsewhere in the system."

Councils from Bradford to Gloucestershire, Durham and Nottinghamshire are among 26 to have suspended fridge collections this month.

A Department for Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) spokesman acknowledged the capacity issues and said short-term storage was being set up.

He said: "Our priority is to minimise disruption to household collection or proper disposal of fridges and other cooling equipment, and we are pushing producers of these items to take all necessary steps to achieve this and resolve any collection delays."

News.title: UK soldiers could get paragliders to drop behind enemy lines
News.content:
British soldiers could soon be given powered paragliders to enable them to fly up to 200 miles behind enemy lines.

The backpack-sized gliders mean Royal Marine and Parachute Regiment troops could fly into hostile areas during the night without the need to drop from aircraft.

Manufacturer Blakcro, which is based in Wiltshire, say the machines can be assembled in eight minutes and launched on foot.

The Ministry of Defence is spending Â£6m on the system, with trials set to begin "in the coming months".

Defence Minister Luke Pollard said the government was building a "more resilient, homegrown defence supply chain and ensuring our armed forces receive the pioneering equipment that can give them the edge on the battlefield".

The paragliders, which have a range of up to 200 miles, can carry body armour, night vision equipment and weapon mounts.

The manufacturers say the titanium-framed machines can be used to enter hostile territory covertly as they are more difficult to detect by radar or sound than traditional aircraft.

The gliders will be powered by a fan but pilots will be expected to launch them on foot.

The technology is currently being used by other Nato member countries.

Blakcro, which employs 11 people, was founded in 2023 and has received government support for two other projects.

The company also works with the US Department of Defense.

The government has said it wants to spend more on UK-made defence equipment and bring smaller companies into the supply chain.

Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to increase defence spending after he resigned from Sir Keir Starmer's government in protest at its investment plans.

As defence secretary, he accused Starmer's government of having no clear timetable to reach the target of spending 3% of the UK's national income on defence.

He is expected to increase spending further - but will not be setting out any plans in his first Budget in October.

Instead, a revised defence plan will be set out as part of a wider government spending review in the spring.

A government spokesperson said: "The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe.

"The prime minister and chancellor are committed to fully funding the defence investment plan.

"At the spending review we will set out a pathway to meet our NATO commitment of 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and will set a target date to hit 3% on that path."
