Sir James Cleverly is quitting the shadow cabinet to run for London mayor.

Announcing his decision, the former foreign secretary and Braintree MP said the capital needed “a champion, someone who understands its potential and is prepared to fight for its future”.

In an op-ed for The Sunday Times, he wrote: “I have told Kemi Badenoch that I will leave the shadow cabinet. Serving there has been a privilege, and I know there will continue to be strong voices around that table.

“But to run the most effective campaign possible, I must be free to speak about every aspect of London’s future and concentrate fully on winning this race.”

Sir James, who is the Tory party’s shadow minister for housing, communities and local government, will resign from the shadow cabinet with immediate effect.

Labour mayor Sir Sadiq Khan is halfway through his third term and has not confirmed whether he will stand again in May 2028.

open image in gallery Sir Sadiq Khan has been London mayor since 2016 ( PA )

In his op-ed, Sir James claimed Sir Sadiq “saw City Hall as his springboard into No 10” but that this ambition disappeared when Sir Keir Starmer became Labour leader.

He said: “London’s reputation has been allowed to slip, at home and abroad, while too many of its problems have been left to fester.”

The Braintree MP said that London’s success is driving the British economy and argued that “the route both to Britain’s economic recovery and to the next Conservative government runs through London.”

Speculation has rumbled for months that Sir James, who has held the shadow housing, communities and local government brief since last July, was considering a bid to run City Hall.

open image in gallery ‘I know I can beat whoever Labour puts forward,’ Cleverly wrote ( PA )

His move leaves an empty post ahead of an expected reshuffle of the shadow cabinet by Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch.

He wrote: “I have told Kemi Badenoch that I will leave the shadow cabinet. Serving there has been a privilege, and I know there will continue to be strong voices around that table. But to run the most effective campaign possible, I must be free to speak about every aspect of London’s future and concentrate fully on winning this race.

“The Conservative Party, and London, needs a credible candidate with the experience and confidence to win. I know this city. I know the job. I know I can do it. And I know I can beat whoever Labour puts forward.”

He also criticised prime minister Andy Burnham, claiming he treats the capital “as a cash cow: somewhere to tax, regulate, raid and blame” adding, “Other parties simply amplify every criticism of the capital, talking it down without offering either a credible plan or showing any real desire to make things better.”

open image in gallery Sir James lost the 2024 Tory leadership election to Kemi Badenoch ( PA )

Sir James has held a number of ministerial positions under three prime ministers - including roles as home secretary and education secretary.

He represented the Tories on the London Assembly before his election as MP for Braintree in 2015. After rising through the backbenches, he unsuccessfully ran for Conservative party leader in 2024, losing out to Badenoch.

A source close to Ms Badenoch told The Sunday Times, that she was “gutted” to lose Cleverly but was “delighted that someone of his calibre wants to put himself forward to be Conservative nominee for mayor of London.

The London Mayor’s office was approached for comment.

News.title: Tottenham v Newcastle LIVE: Marmoush handed Spurs debut but Savio absent for Premier League clash
News.content:
( Getty )

Tottenham and Newcastle could unveil fresh recruits as two new-look sides clash in the Premier League.

Spurs have signed Savio and Omar Marmoush in a double deal from Manchester City, following the hugely disappointing 3-0 defeat at Brentford in their Premier League opener last weekend. Savio scored on his debut as Roberto De Zerbi’s team beat Charlton in the Carabao Cup in midweek.

Newcastle have also been busy in the market and added an experienced midfielder in Nico Gonzalez as a replacement for Sando Tonali, who faces his former team this evening following his £100m switch to north London.

Matthias Jaissle was denied a first Premier League as Liverpool scored a late penalty in a thrilling 2-2 draw last weekend, with Yoane Wissa and Anthony Elanga among the attacking players who seem to be given a new lease of life under the new Newcastle boss.

Many Britons will get to enjoy a day off on Monday for the UK’s last bank holiday until December.

The summer bank holiday is the sixth of eight national holidays and falls on the final day of the month and the last day of summer this year.

While much of the UK is forecast to see rain and thunderstorms over the bank holiday weekend, the weather is expected to brighten up with sunny interludes for parts of the country on Monday.

Like other bank holidays, many stores will operate on reduced hours. This is when supermarkets are open on Monday:

Larger Tesco supermarkets in England and Wales will be open from 8am to 6pm, but express stores are expected to operate usual hours.

You can check your local store here.

You can find the specific opening times for your local store, using the store locator here.

Six-time grand tour champion and Vuelta a Espana leader Tadej Pogacar has abandoned the race after a nasty crash on stage eight.

The two-time world champion was the overwhelming favourite to win the Vuelta, the only grand tour he has yet to win, and won three stages in its opening week. He led the race by nearly four minutes from Movistar’s Enric Mas before his shock crash and abandon with 31km to go on stage eight.

The race leader appeared to hit a rock as he swerved suddenly while travelling in the midst of the peloton along a wide road. He crashed hard, with riders falling around and behind him.

He sustained a nasty wound to his left shoulder and the left side of his face, with blood pouring from above his eye and his shoulder, and was immediately attended to by medical staff.

The Slovenian got up unassisted and attempted to get back on his bike before shaking his head and sitting down again in evident pain, before he was helped into a waiting ambulance by staff and taken immediately to hospital.

This is the first time Pogacar has abandoned a grand tour in 10 attempts, the first time he has ever not finished on the podium, and his first withdrawal from a race since breaking his wrist in a crash at Liege-Bastogne-Liege in 2023.

The 27-year-old won this year’s Tour de France in dominant fashion and carried that form into an electric first week at the Vuelta, winning stages one, four and six on his way to establishing a seemingly unassailable lead.

But his crash on an innocuous-seeming stretch of road on the way to Xeraco - reminiscent of his rival Jonas Vingegaard’s unexpected crash on stage 15 of this year’s Tour - blows the race wide open.

Spain’s Mas now leads the overall standings by one minute from Slovenia’s four-time champion Primoz Roglic, with Giro d’Italia runner-up Felix Gall third at 1’11”. Britain’s Oscar Onley leads the best young rider classification and now sits fifth, 2’16” off the pace.

open image in gallery Pogacar won three stages in the opening week ( Reuters )

Pogacar’s withdrawal also entirely changes the dynamic of the race. His UAE Team Emirates-XRG squad will now target stage wins through the likes of Joao Almeida and Jay Vine, while Visma-Lease a Bike, who had largely been expected to aim for stages through Wout van Aert and British rider Matthew Brennan, may now prioritise the general classification hopes of Sepp Kuss. The American won this race in 2023 and now sits fourth overall.

Solo breakaway rider Xabier Mikel Azparren was caught with just 1.5km to go on the technical run-in to the line in Xeraco, with a huge crash bringing down riders all over the road in a chaotic final sprint.

Two-time stage winner Brennan was momentarily boxed in and had too much ground to make up in the finale as Bryan Coquard of Cofidis won the sprint from Lidl-Trek’s Mads Pedersen for his first-ever grand tour stage win.

The race continues on Sunday with a mountainous 187.4km ride in the Costa Blanca, from La Vila Joiosa to the category-one summit finish atop Alto de Aitana.

Generation Z employees are more likely to pull a sickie compared to workers aged over 55, a new poll has suggested.

The poll of 2,123 people showed just over four in five workers – 82 per cent – aged under 25 said they had taken a sick day in the past year when they had not been too unwell to work, compared to 43 per cent of staff aged between 55 and 64.

Carried out by Merlin Strategy for the centre-right think tank Centre for Social Justice (CSJ), the surveyors asked participants whether they told their employer they were too unwell to work when their symptoms were not, in fact, serious enough to prevent them from working.

The survey also found 39 per cent of under-25s reported taking sick days on at least five days in the past year compared to one in ten older workers.

Office for National Statistics published this year suggested sickness absence rates are overall higher in older working-age adults compared to under-25s.

The data, published in May, showed the sickness absence rate in 2025 was 1.3 per cent for those aged 16 to 24 years, compared to 1.6 per cent for those aged 25 to 34. 1.8 per cent for those aged 35 to 49 and 2.9 per cent for those aged 50 to 64.

The CIJ said the poll suggested a “striking” generational divide in the reasons workers use to pull a sickie. The poll found 79 per cent said being too tired had contributed to taking unnecessary time off work compared to 40 per cent of workers aged 55 to 64.

More than half of participants under 25 years old said attending a job interview or doing other work had played a part in their sickie, while 52 per cent cited social reasons such as a late night or hangover – compared to 12 per cent and 19 per cent respectively.

Other findings included 49 per cent saying they wanted to avoid work they did not want to do, against 15 per cent of older works. A total of 77 per cent cited burnout or needing a mental-health day, compared with 45 per cent of older workers.

The Vuelta a Espana 2026 is underway with another gruelling, mountainous edition of the year’s final - and often, most unpredictable - grand tour.

Tadej Pogacar had led the race by nearly four minutes before the six-time grand tour winner crashed out late on stage eight, blowing the race wide open.

Defending champion Jonas Vingegaard opted not not defend his title after crashing out of the Tour de France and ending his season early, leaving four-time champion Primoz Roglic, Spain’s Enric Mas and British rider Oscar Onley among the favourites.

As per usual this Vuelta is one for the best climbers and felt tailor-made for Pogacar, starting in his base of Monaco and winding through France and Andorra before crossing over into Spain.

There are four ‘sprint’ stages on the menu but six mountaintop finishes and another nine considered either hilly or medium-mountains, with two individual time trials; it’s also a very southern edition of the race, with much of the action taking place in the baking hot climes of Andalusia, adding yet another challenge.

open image in gallery ( Unipublic )

Stage 1: Monaco > Monaco (9.4km)

The Vuelta kicks off with what is essentially a prologue, a 9.4km jaunt of an individual time trial beginning by the Monte Carlo Casino, passing many of Monaco’s landmarks and the F1 racing circuit. The first couple of kilometres are slightly undulating before it flattens out entirely for a tricky, technical city-centre circuit. There are two very brief uphills right before the finish, which peak at 7% and could be a sting in the tail for some. The finish line will be familiar to F1 fans as it’s the same as for the Monaco Grand Prix.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 1 ( Unipublic )

Stage 2: Monaco > Manosque (214km)

From the shortest stage to the longest: stage two takes the riders from Monaco towards Nice and into the Provencal hills, and is tailor-made for a breakaway as the big guns are likely to preserve their energy for stage three’s summit finish. The climbing begins straight out the gate, with only two categorised climbs - the cat-three Col de Châteauneuf-Grasse and the Col de Saint-Andrieu - but it’s up and down all day before a narrow, technical finish in Manosque, with an uphill drag to the line.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 2 ( Unipublic )

Stage 3: Gruissan - Aude > Font Romeu (174km)

The first mountaintop finish of this year’s Vuelta. It’s a classic Vuelta route, flat all day - in this case passing through some lovely vineyards and skirting Perpignan - before a pair of climbs close together to finish, although not as brutal as the likes of the Angliru.

The double ascent of the category one Col de Mont-Louis and the final climb up the category-two Font-Romeu, 1800m above sea level, should give an early indication of the main contenders’ form and weed out some of the chaff.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 3 ( Unipublic )

Stage 4: Andorra la Vella > Andorra la Vella (104.8km)

Stage four starts and ends in the Andorran capital and is a real test for the GC contenders after yesterday’s first skirmishes. It’s short for a road stage but punchy: there are three category-one climbs on the agenda - expect UAE Team Emirates-XRG to make life difficult for everyone else - before the cat-three Alto de la Comella and and a 4km descent to the finish line, with the mountains coming back-to-back and little respite as each descent leads straight into the next climb.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 4 ( Unipublic )

Stage 5: Falset (Costa Daurada) > Roquetes (Terres de l’Ebre) (173.4km)

After four stages of a foreign Grand Depart the race enters Spain proper. It’s another hilly day out but in a race short on chances for the sprinters, the fast men may try to stamp their authority on this one.

There’s plenty of uncategorised climbing on the agenda bookending a flat middle third of the stage, with only the category-three Alto de Pauls to surmount in terms of official hills. That comes with 20km remaining for the sprinters’ trains to get themselves in order on the descent and flat approach to the line in Roquetes.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 5 ( Unipublic )

Stage 6: Alcossebre > Castello (177.4km)

Tadej Pogacar killed off the Tour de France competition on stage six this year; could he do the same in this Vuelta? There’s no Tourmalet on this stage six but there are four categorised climbs as the peloton turns inland from a coastal start in Alcossebre and winds through the dramatic ravines and limestone cliffs of Castellon. The main test of the day is the the cat-one Puerto El Bartolo, the last climb, which features 3km of dirt track for added jeopardy and difficulty.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 6 ( Unipublic )

Stage 7: Vall d'Alba > Aramon Valdelinares (149.8km)

The climbing continues on stage seven, which features the second-highest altitude finish of the entire race after the climb to Aramon Vadelinares. There are two category-two and two cat-three climbs to get over before then on another unforgiving day for the sprinters, before the riders head up to just shy of 2,000m above sea level at the summit of the final climb. This one could catch out some GC contenders.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 7 ( Unipublic )

Stage 8: Pucol > Xeraco (171km)

Stage eight should be another opportunity for the sprinters, with a flat finish, although the category two Puerto de Barx 22km from the finish could instead provide the springboard for a late attack. The stage begins near the coast on the outskirts of Valencia before heading inland and wending its way south and back out to the finish line on the seafront at Xeraco.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 8 ( Unipublic )

Stage 9: La Vila Joiosa > Alto de Aitana (187.4km)

The last stage of the opening week is the toughest to date, with more than 5,000m of elevation gain across six categorised climbs and more uncategorised rises. We’re into the mountains of the Costa Blanca, with the two major climbs of note the category-one Puerto de El Miserat, at around the halfway point of the stage, and the summit finish of Alto de Aitana.

El Miserat is about as miserable as the name suggests: it has multiple double-digit sections with the worst maxing out at 20%, averaging 10% for 5.2km, while the final 6km of Aitana rarely drop below 8%. The searing heat of Alicante in late August will also be a factor.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 9 ( Unipublic )

Rest day

Stage 10: Alcaraz > Elche de la Sierra (184.7km)

Not too taxing a first day back after the rest day, with three category-three climbs on a fairly long but otherwise not particularly remarkable day out. This should be one for the breakaway, while the heat as the race beds down in southern Spain will continue to be an important factor for teams to manage.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 10 ( Unipublic )

Stage 11: Cartagena > Lorca (151.3km)

A similar parcours to stage eight: in theory this is one for the fast men but the category-three Alto del Morron de Totana, which comes with just under 34km to go, could put some of the purer sprinters in difficulty. After that though it’s a gentle descent and flat approach to the line in Lorca, where we should get a rare bunch sprint.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 11 ( Unipublic )

Stage 12: Vera > Calar Alto (166.6km)

Stage 12 is another big summit finish after a couple of gentler days in the saddle. The climbs get tougher as the race barrels through eastern Andalusia, with an early pair of category three climbs followed by the category-two Collado Garcia before the double ascent of the category-one, 13km Alto de Velefique, which hits highs of 16%, and the summit finish atop Calar Alto, which rises more than 2,000m above sea level.

The first half of the Calar Alto regularly hits double-digit gradients before tailing off, with another nasty section closer to the top. Miguel Angel Lopez won here in the 2017 edition.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 12 ( Unipublic )

Stage 13: Almunecar v Loja (192.8km)

Stage 13 should be a day for the breakaway, with three classified climbs, the toughest of which is the category-one Venta de la Cebada inside the first 30km. The undulating terrain through the climbs of Granada will likely put paid to the pure sprinters’ chances, particularly after the gruelling stage 12, with the punchier fast men major contenders as the parcours flattens out after the final third-category climb, 38km from the line. We could see Wout van Aert and Mads Pedersen duking it out at the finish in Loja.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 13 ( Unipublic )

Stage 14: Jaen > Sierra de La Pandera (154.5km)

After one day’s respite for the breakaway we’re back into serious climbing territory as the race heads to Jaen, home of the Clasica Jaen and its treacherous gravel sectors through the picturesque olive groves of Andalusia. The scenery will be beautiful but the actual racing brutal: hot temperatures and blazing sunshine on the steep climbs will be important to manage once again.

From the provincial capital the race heads in the direction of another summit finish atop the category-one Sierra de la Pandera, 1,800m above sea level. Before that there are two category-two climbs to surmount and plenty more uncategorised climbing - nearly 4,200m of elevation gain in total - on another day for a general classification battle.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 14 ( Unipublic )

Stage 15: Palma del Rio > Cordoba (189.7km)

The second week of the Vuelta ends with a transitional stage which could well see a bunch sprint, if the fast men have recovered from their exertions. Otherwise, this could be a day for the enterprising escape artist. There are three category three ascents and a few more undulations on the way to Cordoba, with the descent towards the line a key moment to navigate, before a flat run-in to the provincial capital.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 15 ( Unipublic )

Rest day

Stage 16: Cortegana > La Rabida (Palos de la Frontera) (181.1km)

The final week of the Vuelta kicks off with a long stage of two halves: a hilly first half beginning in the Sierra Morena, leading to a flat run-in towards the southern coast on the outskirts of Huelva. For once there’s more descending than climbing, but the gradients are still fairly steep at points. The flat finish means we’re likely to be in for two bunch sprints in a row, separated by the rest day, although anything is possible this late in the race.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 16 ( Unipublic )

Stage 17: Dos Hermanas > Sevilla (185km)

A third bunch sprint in a row, in fact: stage 17 is a cookie-cutter sprint stage, the flattest of the entire race. Expect lots of aerial footage of beautiful countryside and much grasping at straws on commentary to find something to fill the time. Technical narrow streets will add some jeopardy, however, as will the city centre circuit through Sevilla to finish.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 17 ( Unipublic )

Stage 18: El Puerto de Santa Maria > Jerez de la Frontera (32km)

A second individual time trial of this year, but much longer than stage one, at 32km. This is another designed for the pure time-trial specialists, flat with long straights where aerodynamics and position will be absolutely crucial, although the Levante wind could cause some trouble. A big test for the general classification riders ahead of one final mountainous double-header.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 18 ( Unipublic )

Stage 19: Velez-Malaga > Penas Blancas (Estepona) (210km)

Back in the mountains for another long, hot day in the saddle. The first third of the stage is largely flat before a pair of category-two climbs, the Puerto de Las Abejas and Puerto del Viento, providing the perfect springboard for a breakaway.

The route wends its way along the coast past Malaga before swinging inland and uphill, before heading back towards the coast near Marbella for the final test of the day at Estepona: the category-one Penas Blancas, which regularly hits double-digits gradients and maxes out at 17% on the lower slopes. And that’s with 190km already in the legs.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 19 ( Unipublic )

Stage 20: La Calahorra > Collado del Alguacil (187km)

Landslides earlier this year have meant a late change to the route for stage 20, which has been shortened by nearly 20km and had one climb swapped out for another, but it remains a fearsome beast and the queen stage of this year’s race.

There are five categorised climbs on the menu, with the category-one Puerto de El Purche to be summited twice before a first-ever ascent of the Puerto de El Duque as the route weaves in and out of Granada into the Sierra Nevada. That is followed by the monstrous hors-categorie Collado del Alguacil (8.3km at 9.8%), which has never featured in the Vuelta before.

open image in gallery La Vuelta stage 20 ( Unipublic )

Stage 21: Granada > Granada (99.4km)

The Collado del Alguacil will have decided the general classification, but stage 21 is no procession, with four circuits of Granada, each featuring a short, sharp climb up to the Alhambra, to round off this year’s Vuelta.

The Vuelta loves a gimmick and this stage will start in the Granada Carrefour supermarket, a callback to a couple of years ago and a handy bit of product placement for the race’s main sponsor, before a gentle ride around the outskirts of the city en route to the city circuit itself. Narrow streets and sharp corners will make this a dramatic finale, which is likely to be contested by the punchier riders rather than sprinters.

News.title: South Africa v New Zealand LIVE: Kolisi extends Springboks’ lead in thrilling first half
News.content:
( Getty )

South Africa will bid to hit back and square the series as they face New Zealand in the second Test of the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry tour in Cape Town.

The All Blacks stunned the Springboks in the series opener at Ellis Park last Saturday, snapping the world champions’ 12-match winning streak with a 33-16 success. That defeat has prompted a recall for Siya Kolisi into the hosts’ back row, with the skipper back to lead South Africa as fellow flanker Pieter-Steph du Toit brings up a century of caps.

The two sides have again traded barbs in the build-up, with the scrum an area of particular focus. All Blacks boss Dave Rennie has accused South Africa of scrummaging illegally and failing to drive straight, with the Springboks defending their technique as they look to again gain advantage at a key battleground. Can they level things up at 1-1 with two Tests to come? Defeat would end their chances of series success....

News.title: Tom Hardy drops explicit verse referencing Kathy Bates and Stephen King on new rap album
News.content:

Tom Hardy has returned with his rap alias Frankie Pulitzer to deliver a new collaborative album, Czarface Meets Frankie Pulitzer, with the underground supergroup.

Czarface is made up of duo 7L & Esoteric and Wu-Tang Clan’s Inspectah Deck.

Fans in the know will already be aware of the Oscar-nominated British actor’s underground music career. In 2011 he spoke about recording “loads of stuff” that had never been released.

Well, now Hardy has surprised them by finally releasing his debut rap album, which features plenty of references to films and comic books – as well as an X-rated reference to Hollywood veteran Kathy Bates.

On “Raw Forever”, Hardy namechecks Martin Scorsese’s 1999 movie Bringing Out the Dead, along with Willem Dafoe’s depiction of the Green Goblin in 2002’s Spider-Man.

Meanwhile, on “Mad Technology” – also featuring Wu-Tang’s Method Man – he references Stephen King film adaptations Cujo and Misery, sandwiching them around his NSFW Bates mention.

open image in gallery Tom Hardy raps about Martin Scorsese, Marvel comics and Kathy Bates on his new album ( AFP/Getty )

“You s***-for-brain no-name lame, that bites like Cujo,” he raps. “I’d rather masturbate to Kathy Bates than hear you flow/ And you know that Misery, it loves company.”

Bates won the Oscar for Best Actress when she starred in the iconic 1990 film Misery, directed by the late Rob Reiner and based on King’s 1987 novel, as obsessive fan Annie Wilkes who holds famed novelist Paul Sheldon (James Caan) captive.

open image in gallery Kathy Bates as the psychotic nurse Annie Wilkes opposite James Caan as Paul Sheldon in Rob Reiner's 'Misery' ( Getty Images )

The Independent has contacted Bates’s representative for comment.

Other collaborators on the project include Run the Jewels’s LP on “Dragon Cannon”, Kendra Morris on “Frankie”, and Busta Rhymes on “Raw Forever”.

Hardy deploys his voice-acting skills across the record, sounding a little like his character Eddie Brock from Marvel’s Venom franchise as he raps: “I eat people, break ribs, throw bodies off the Golden Gate bridge/ And I get it how I live like a cannibal/ I talk sick, toxic, highly flammable.”

Meanwhile, on “Grim-Visaged War”, fans will be reminded of his famous performance as Bane from Christopher Nolan’s Batman film, The Dark Knight Rises, as he recites Shakespeare’s Richard III monologue.

Hardy has not spoken publicly about his work as Frankie Pulitzer, but has appeared on previous Czarface albums and also released standalone singles.

In 1999, he recorded and released a mixtape titled Falling On Your Arse, which resurfaced on Reddit back in 2018.

Speaking to the BBC in 2011, Hardy commented: “I used to be [signed] with the guy who managed Leela James and Lauryn Hill, Pras, the Fugees and all that. I worked out with [Grammy-winning producers] Warren Riker and Gordon Williams. I’ve recorded loads of stuff but it’s never been released.”

So far, the fan reaction to Czarface Meets Frankie Pulitzer has been hugely positive. Is there a Grammy nomination on Hardy’s horizon?

News.title: Munoz rescues draw for Liverpool as Iraola rages at bungling officials
News.content:
“I cannot explain because I don’t have an explanation,” Iraola said. “I wanted to make those substitutions about three minutes before. I mean, it was two, three, four times the ball had gone out. I still don’t know the reason why we couldn’t make the subs.

“I think [the fourth official] was having some problems with the board or something. It [the penalty] wouldn’t have happened if I had made the sub. I asked. I had complained the previous time. The supporters were shouting and they were aware of the situation.

“But I don’t know what happened and I don’t know why they have given the penalty.”

He did know, though, why Liverpool had needed to drag themselves off the deck again for the second week in a row. Solely looking at that incident in 99 minutes of play would be to create a diversion and Iraola has shown in his opening weeks on Merseyside that he is not someone who seeks excuses.

“A lack of intensity hurt us,” Iraola said with obvious disdain, and it was only down to a show of character in the second period that a slovenly first half did not enable Forest to win at Anfield for the third consecutive year, for all that the travelling fans thought it was “happening again!”

Forest, bruised after two defeats in four days to Leeds United, looked like an Oliver Glasner side. They were aggressive and well-organised, the only failing was that physically they couldn’t see the job through, but the Austrian insisted that will change in due course.

Once Glasner is settled in and he gets his transfer business done – “definitely one, possibly two and probably three,” was his mischievous reply to how the window will unfold – Forest will be a formidable proposition, especially if the first 45 minutes are a barometer.

They had been knocking on the door before Dan Ndoye eventually broke the deadlock, sweeping a left-footed drive past Alisson after Igor Jesus had won a header from a long clearance. It was a simple goal, marginally onside, but it was absolutely deserved.

News.title: Cherki magic helping Maresca to step out of Guardiola shadow
News.content:
Rumours of Manchester City’s supposed demise without Pep Guardiola appear to be much exaggerated.

They swept past Crystal Palace at Selhurst Park with a style of play under new manager Enzo Maresca that was just as swashbuckling as under his predecessor, with Rayan Cherki playing the role of chief architect. The Frenchman’s two goals included a captivating mazy dribble, which will long be remembered by those who had the fortune to see it.

City created enough space for themselves through clever movement. With Cherki zigging one way and Phil Foden zagging the other, they created even more by dribbling past a mesmerised Palace back three that became a back five at times and still could not cope.

Erling Haaland also scored twice. Even with the creative and unpredictable talents of those behind in a four-man attacking City midfield, Haaland remains irreplaceable with his ability to convert chances.

However, this night belonged to Cherki. Guardiola chided him publicly after he set up a City goal with a “rabona” cross last season. The thrust of Guardiola’s comments were that Cherki was not Lionel Messi. Of course not, but he possesses a genius all of his own, which Maresca would surely be foolish to rein in.

The jaw-dropping splendour of Cherki’s first goal drew a collective intake of breath at Selhurst Park.

Collecting a Foden pass, he attacked the Palace area on a diagonal path, slaloming between Jaydee Canvot, Takehiro Tomiyasu and Chris Richards, before having the spatial awareness and technique to flick his left foot at the ball to send it rolling on a perpendicular trajectory past Dean Henderson.

News.title: England light years ahead of lamentable Pakistan
News.content:
Who needs Ben Stokes? Actually, it is hard to think of any side that would need him against this Pakistan team.

After just five days of cricket, and despite their own limitations with the bat, England are on the cusp of a series victory at Lord’s with a 261-run lead and power to add thanks to the prowess of a seam attack that has emerged quickly from the shadow of its former captain.

It will take longer to feel the full effects of Stokes’s absence. When England need a spinner in the side, they will miss the seam-bowling all-rounder to balance the XI. There will be times when they are up against it on a flat deck on a boiling day and be desperate for Stokes’s sheer will to win. It is still hard to think he will not play some part in the Ashes next summer.

For the final two years of his career it was Stokes’s bowling that was top class, his batting having become ordinary. But with bowlers of the quality of Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson gelling, England are more than making up for Stokes’s retirement. This bowling attack against Pakistan’s batting was a complete mismatch.

Joe Root has stepped into Stokes’s shoes confidently, laying down the law off the field and tactically he has been spot on, although Pakistan have hardly stretched him. The only stir they have made since arriving was the stink they kicked up over Sky Sports’ interview with Imran Khan’s sons.

Conclusions are impossible to draw with any confidence against such poor opponents. Sri Lanka and West Indies two years ago put up a stronger fight in the first two Tests of their series. Tamim Iqbal scored two hundreds as Bangladesh at least landed some blows in 2010. Pakistan have managed one fifty in three innings and were bowled out for 171 and 135 at Headingley and a lamentable 110 here.

They were a batsman down at Lord’s because of a calf injury to opener Imam-ul-Haq, but only reached three figures because England dropped top scorer Azan Awais on eight; he went on to score 46.

England’s batting is hardly firing, but with a 180 first-innings lead, they could afford to be 13 for two without panic spreading. Losing Root for 24 kept Pakistan interested, but Emilio Gay toughed it out in the gloom to reach stumps unbeaten on 30; England 81 for three, light years ahead in the game.

Robinson’s astonishing figures of 13-6-11-4 set him on the way for a probable third man-of-the-match award in a row and continued his unexpected resurgence. Rarely did his pace go above 78mph, he just landed the ball time and again on a length and let movement off the seam do the rest.

News.title: I’ve lived in Norfolk for more than 30 years. Here’s how to explore England’s windswept east
News.content:
Norfolk’s vast sandy beaches are its chief draw for visitors: even on the busiest summer day there is always space for games, kite-flying or a family picnic in the dunes. Boating, crabbing, digging for cockles and wading in creeks provides hours of entertainment for all.

But there’s much more to Norfolk’s coast than its beaches. It’s also a landscape of dense pine forest and large expanses of salt marsh, which flush purple with sea-lavender in August. Birdlife is astonishingly rich, and wildflowers include yellow-horned poppies and lilac-flowering sea pea.

Inland, the undulating countryside and sleepy flint-built villages are perfect for gentle cycling, walking or touring by car. Grand stately homes make enjoyable days out, and almost every village has a sublimely beautiful medieval church at its centre.

Lively Georgian towns such as Burnham Market and Holt offer quirky shopping – and, wherever you are, you’re never far from an atmospheric pamment-floored pub serving local ales, or an excellent delicatessen selling the region’s specialities. Look out for pungent cheeses, smoked fish and salt-marsh flavoured honey.

News.title: Telegraph Fantasy Football tips: Game Week 2
News.content:
As the Telegraph Fantasy Football season heads into 2026-27, the award-winning experts at Fantasy Football Hub ccontinue to bring you the very best in fantasy football knowledge, tips and tools to help you rise up the ranks and win your mini-leagues.

Join the Hub and get access to all their great resources and expert tips.



Welcome back

We would like to start by thanking everyone for playing Telegraph Fantasy Football for the 2026-27 season.

If you are a new player, we really hope you enjoy the game. Telegraph Fantasy Football has been running for over 30 years and is widely regarded as the purest form of fantasy football. No captains, no wildcards and no gimmicks.

For the returning players, we apologise for the delay with getting the game live. We had to rebuild it from scratch following the World Cup and, in order to have a game ready in time for the new season, several features are still being worked on, including updated iPhone and Android apps.

Please be aware that there are ongoing issues with the android app that will not be fixed until later in September. Instead use a web browser on these devices. You can also try adding a shortcut to your homescreen for quick and easy access.

Rest assured we are working through the site improvements and, if you have any feedback, please use the Contact Us chat on site.



Telegraph Fantasy Football: last week's insights

Champions open with a win

Mikel Arteta’s side kicked off the new campaign in perfect fashion: three goals, a clean sheet and three points in north London. Captain Martin Odegaard (£5.2m) netted and looked back to his best, but it was the full-backs Riccardo Calafiori (£4.4m) and Ben White (£4.1m) who really stood out with a clean sheet and an assist each.



Tigers humble Manchester United

Many TFF managers started with Red Devils’ assets with the Manchester club opening up with back-to-back fixtures against newly promoted teams, but they were duly shocked as Hull City outfought and at times outplayed the 13-time Premier League champions. Ollie McBurnie (£2.9m) is one to keep an eye on for when the Tigers’ fixtures turn.



Chelsea attacking flair

A fully fit Cole Palmer (£6.2m) has sparked TFF managers to rethink their set-ups, as his 11-point haul on Monday night has put non-owners on red alert. The Blues’ talisman returned a goal and an assist, and an injury-free season should have the ex-Manchester City midfielder challenging at the summit of the points scoring charts.



Visit the Telegraph Fantasy Football Stats Centre for all player points >



Telegraph Fantasy Football Tips: Game Week 2



The Telegraph Fantasy Football player list has been analysed ahead of the upcoming games, and these look like the best players to transfer in:



1. Christos Tzolis (£4.0m)

Despite not delivering any attacking returns in his first game, the Gunners’ summer recruit impressed onlookers and Arsenal fans alike with his performance. The price point, the Monday night entry point and the fixture itself all point to the 24-year-old being an astute acquisition.



2. Marcus Tavernier (£3.1m)

The midfielder netted at the Etihad on Sunday, and forms part of an attractive Cherries attacking line-up that should continue to score many goals this season. It’s home comforts this weekend for their No.16 and he could be a great option to transfer in for any newly injured players in your starting XIs.

3. Enzo Le Fée (£3.3m)

The Black Cats underwhelmed in their opener, but with Fulham looking defensively vulnerable on Monday night, the French penalty-taker could take advantage this weekend.

City’s other games do not look easy either but they should be defeating teams such as Sporting Lisbon and Porto – at least they would be expected to under Pep Guardiola.

Verdict The San Siro was where Arne Slot began to turn results around last season and Iraola getting a win there would be a big statement. Atlético staged a comeback at Anfield in 2020 and the repeat fixture will be tight. But there are enough winnable games there for Liverpool to reach the next round.

News.title: England return to proper Test cricket with gritty batting performance
News.content:
Cox unfurled some fine drives and assessed conditions like a veteran, scoring quickly to a run-a-ball 38 but only six more from his next 48 as Pakistan knocked over partners at the other end. It was vital Cox stayed in to stabilise the innings. It is the job of a No 3 to attack or defend; calibrate their game to what is required at the time. Cox, when he played briefly for England in New Zealand two winters ago and before injury cut short his tour, looked to be a player drunk on the Bazball fumes. He was out in a warm-up match against a New Zealand XI in Queenstown hooking and flailing at the ball. This was his second mature performance in a row, an innings of 55 to follow his 73 at Leeds and this was made in much harder circumstances.

Pakistan were better after their Headingley horror show. Mohammad Abbas must feel more at home on a dank London day than he does in Sialkot, and can earn a place on the honours board if he nicks the last England wicket after taking four for 56. Mohammad Ali bowled some jaffas, and some rubbish, for three for 67 and spinner Usman Ali kept it tight and found some turn before losing control as Smith went after him. England still scored at 4.4 an over a reflection of some of the wasted deliveries by Pakistan and 10 no-balls.

Inevitably they were a mixed bag in the field. Three dropped catches were redeemed by a run out and a world-class grab at slip by Salman Ali Agha – captain last week, left out here – to dismiss Cox when he lost his shape trying to hit the ball too hard.

News.title: Ebola response shifts to Congo’s river network
News.content:
Stacked with logs and crammed with hundreds of passengers, the giant barges are nudged day after day along one of Africa’s greatest waterways.

The weeks-long voyage looks sedate, but the tugs are pushing their heavily-laden charges along an unstoppable aquatic superhighway.

Sharing the Congo river with these trade behemoths are canoes, fishing boats and smaller wooden cargo ships.

The river connects the wild east of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to the capital Kinshasa, in a vital economic artery and transport corridor nearly 1,100 miles long.

The waterway is a lifeline for passengers, timber, produce and goods. Roads are rare and unreliable, and airfares are far too expensive for most.

Now there are concerns the river risks becoming a conduit for something else heading to the capital of nearly 18 million people: the deadly Ebola virus.

Sports.title: Ex-Premier League referee questions whether Nottingham Forest penalty should have been OVERTURNED due to Delap throw-in
Sports.content:
FORMER Premier League referee Mark Halsey has questioned whether Nottingham Forest’s penalty against Liverpool should have been overturned after raising concerns over Liam Delap’s throw-in.

Forest were awarded a penalty during their clash with Liverpool at Anfield after goalkeeper Alisson came out to challenge Forest’s Neco Williams.



The decision was checked by VAR but the penalty stood with Halsey agreeing that the on-field call was correct.

However, the former Premier League official believes there was a separate talking point moments earlier involving Delap’s throw-in.



Halsey told SunSport: “Liverpool were unhappy with the award of a penalty to Nottingham Forest at Anfield, where you can see that Alisson comes out, he challenges Williams, and for me, clearly makes contact with Nottingham Forest’s Williams.

“Now, Liverpool were unhappy because before the incident they wanted to make a triple substitution and fourth official Tim Robinson wasn’t ready, obviously, because he didn’t have the board ready.



“So yes, it does take some time with one man operating two boards.

“It looked like he was a bit flustered.

“But looking at the incident itself I think it was a penalty.

“VAR looked at it, they’re not going to get involved because some people may say it’s subjective.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

“But going back to the throw, I think there could be a bit of controversy there because was the throw taken correctly in accordance with law?

“When a throw is taken, you have to have both feet on the floor behind the line.

“Now Liam Delap, it looks like he has one foot in the air but it obviously isn’t conclusive.

“But for me it is a big talking point.”

Halsey’s comments come after Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola was left furious by the delay to his triple substitution.



The Reds manager is still searching for his first win as Liverpool boss and was particularly frustrated that the changes could not be made when he wanted.

Iraola argued after the match that had the substitutions been completed earlier, Liverpool may have been able to prevent the penalty.

The former Bournemouth manager also took aim at the fourth official over the amount of time it took to process the changes.



He said: “A professional fourth official cannot take three minutes.

“I was already angry because in the previous stop we couldn’t make it.

“And before the throw-in I said that we would do it now and then I don’t know, they will have to explain it, but it’s taken ages.”

Liverpool were unhappy with the sequence of events as Forest went on to benefit from the penalty decision.

But while Halsey believes the contact between Alisson and Williams justified the spot-kick, he has raised a fresh question over whether the build-up to the incident should have been examined more closely.



The key issue is whether Delap was correctly positioned when he took the throw-in.

Under the Laws of the Game, a player taking a throw-in must deliver the ball from the point where it left the field and use both hands, bringing the ball from behind and over their head.

Both feet must also be on or behind the touchline when the throw is taken.

Halsey stressed that the footage was not conclusive enough for him to say definitively that the throw was illegal.

But he believes it remains a significant talking point from a dramatic sequence at Anfield.

Sports.title: Munoz rescues point for Liverpool as Iraola's wait for a win goes on
Sports.content:
Victor Munoz thumped in a deflected leveller to rescue a point for Liverpool in a 2-2 draw with Nottingham Forest.

Andoni Iraola was heading towards defeat in his first Anfield Premier League game in charge of Liverpool when Morgan Gibbs-White converted a debatable penalty with 20 minutes to play. But summer signing Munoz put an otherwise frustrating first appearance in front of his new home fans behind him with an emphatic equaliser.

A first win with Liverpool still remains elusive for Iraola, having seen his side also come from behind to draw 2-2 at Newcastle last weekend. He will hope the seemingly imminent arrival of £120m Bradley Barcola can kickstart their season.

Winger Munoz had moved to the right flank just a few minutes before his strike, after Cody Gakpo, who had impressed on that side despite transfer links with Tottenham and Man City, was subbed off. The Dutchman's low cross through the six-yard box had been tapped in by the otherwise anonymous Alexander Isak earlier in the second half as Liverpool put a poor first 45 behind them.

Image: Liverpool's Alexander Isak celebrates scoring their first goal of the game

Iraola's side struggled to deal with the direct approach of Forest for much of that opening period, with a long ball from Matz Sels proving their undoing in the build-up to Dan Ndoye's opener.

Image: Dan Ndoye scores to make it 1-0 to Nottingham Forest

The defending from Liverpool for that goal was poor but Forest boss Oliver Glasner will ultimately rue missed chances in that half, with a stunning stop from Alisson just before half-time to push Igor Jesus' shot onto the bar proving key.

It was an entertaining, action-packed draw - but a frustrating one for both sides, who continue to look for their first league wins of the season.

More to follow...

The key moments from Anfield

12: BLOCK! Dan Ndoye nods down Ola Aina's back-post cross but Igor Jesus' attempt to turn it in is blocked by a big stretch from Liverpool centre-back Jeremy Jacquet!

19: CLOSE! Ndoye meets James McAtee's cute, clipped cross at the back post but steers his header across goal and wide of the other stick.

24: GOAL! Ndoye finishes across Alisson after Jesus latches onto a long ball from Matz Sels and feeds Morgan Gibbs-White to find Ndoye in the box.

33: GOAL RULED OUT! Florian Wirtz thinks he's pulled Liverpool level after intercepting a McAtee pass and converting from Jeremie Frimpong's pass - but a VAR check judged Frimpong offside before he made the assist.

39: WHAT A SAVE! Cody Gakpo crosses from the right but Wirtz's good header is tipped over the bar by Sels.

Gakpo starts despite transfer uncertainty Cody Gakpo - who started and scored last weekend at Newcastle - started again for Liverpool despite doubts over his future at the club.



Victor Munoz replaced Rio Ngumoha on the right and Alexis Mac Allister came into midfield for Ryan Gravenberch.

45: OVER! Munoz bends one narrowly over the bar! He had to hit the target.

60: GOAL! Alexander Isak taps in Gakpo's low cross from close range to equalise.

70: GOAL! Gibbs-White sends Alisson the wrong way with a penalty to restore Forest's lead after the goalkeeper brought down Neco Williams after a quick throw from Liam Delap.

Image: Liverpool's Victor Munoz scores their side's second goal of the game

82: GOAL! Munoz thumps in an equaliser off the underside of the bar, with the help of a deflection off Murillo. Wirtz with the pass into him and the assist.

85: CLOSE! Dominik Szoboszlai so close to a free-kick winner but whips his shot past the post.

Gibbs-White delivers again In 2026, only Bruno Fernandes (4 goals, 14 assists) has been involved in more Premier League goals than Nottingham Forest’s Morgan Gibbs-White (13 goals, 4 assists), with Gibbs-White’s 13 goals the most of any player this calendar year.

Analysis: Was the Forest penalty call correct?

Mike Dean on Soccer Saturday:

"He's knocked it over the goalkeeper and Alisson has caught him slightly.

"There's not much else he can do. It's like a coming together.

"But once it's given, it's not going to be overturned because it's not a clear and obvious error from the referee."

Clinton Morrison on Soccer Saturday:

"I just thought it was a shot going wide. It's harsh. I don't think there's a lot of contact.

"There's nothing he can do. He's coming out to get the ball."

Hutchinson not involved for Forest Omari Hutchinson was not in the Forest squad. Sky Italy reported this week that AC Milan are exploring a deal to sign him.



Xaver Schlager started in midfield instead of Ibrahim Sangare, who was not involved at all.

Iraola: First half not good enough

Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola to TNT Sports:

"Not the result you want. Two very different halves. We were poor in the first half. Even being unlucky with their goal slightly VAR offside, the goal we score is slightly offside.

"The intensity was different [in the second half]. A lot more intense, a lot more threatening. I was happy with the second half but it was late for winning the game.

"First half has been poor, it's definitely not good enough. When you go 1-1 the momentum is with you. We concede another one and everything becomes difficult. And we couldn't finish the comeback."

Analysis: Will Liverpool cash in on in-form Gakpo?

Sky Sports' Peter Smith:

Cody Gakpo has attracted interest from Tottenham and Man City and with Deadline Day fast approaching his future is far from certain. The impending arrival of Bradley Barcola has also fuelled talk that the Dutchman will be heading for the exit.

But at the same time, Gakpo has been one of Liverpool's best performers during their stuttering start to the season. He scored at Newcastle last weekend and could have had more. On Saturday he put Isak's goal on a plate with a sumptuous cross after getting in down the right.

The switch of flanks from his favoured left side didn't deter him and he was Liverpool's brightest spark during the first half when they otherwise struggled. That versatility is a trait which is important to Iraola with the way he likes his wingers to operate.

This early-season good form from Gakpo, though, could soon be continued in a different club's shirt, should Liverpool receive an offer and opt to cash-in before 11pm on Tuesday. His impactful performances could convince his admirers to make their bid.

Glasner: Proud of performance, disappointed with result

Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner:

"Overall the performance was top, especially first half, creating so many chances here at Anfield. I really loved the reaction after we conceded the equaliser, we still played forward and were rewarded with the penalty.

"We feel proud of the performance - but also disappointed with the result. This tells us a lot. A lot of positives to take but still a lot of work to do."

Sports.title: Swansea cruise to away win at struggling Derby
Sports.content:
Swansea remained unbeaten in this season's Championship after goals from Joseph Opoku, Eom Ji-sung and Ronald secured a convincing 3-0 win at Derby.

Opoku netted for the second time following his summer move from Belgian outfit Zulte Waragem, while Eom - the architect of that opener - then got on the scoresheet himself just before half-time with only his second league goal since November. Ronald added a deserved third in second-half stoppage time.

The routine victory meant Vitor Matos' men have collected seven points from a possible nine, while out-of-sorts Derby are still waiting for their first win of the new campaign.

Earlier, Ryan Hedges had the ball in the net for the hosts after just 18 seconds, but that was the nearest John Eustace's men would get to the Swansea goal during a sluggish opening half-hour in which they did not muster a single shot that counted.

Image: Swansea's Ji-Sung Eom celebrates scoring their second goal

The visitors, meanwhile, struck from for their first attack in the second minute. Eom was allowed to run unopposed with the ball through the left channel before pulling the ball back for Opoku, whose deflected 12-yard drive spun into Jacob Widell Zetterstrom's bottom-right corner.

The Ghanaian attacker almost added a second when his acrobatic volley just cleared Zetterstrom's crossbar following Stephen Welsh's floated ball into the six-yard box.

Derby will have been relieved to see Opoku exit the action midway through the half due to injury. But the Swans continued to threaten down the right, with Zetterstrom unconvincingly spilling a Melker Widell shot to safety and Adam Idah flashing a far-post effort wide.

The Rams finally offered a response but Max Johnston could only find the side-netting from an unfavourable angle and Eom made it 2-0 in the 44th minute.

The South Korea international followed up to roll the ball into an unguarded net from a yard out after Zetterstrom had saved well down to his right to keep out Idah's header from Widell's right-wing cross.

An unhappy Eustace made a triple substitution at half-time and Derby briefly rallied, with Lewis Travis and Charlie Taylor both seeing long-range attempts deflected away from goal.

But soon afterwards, Zetterstrom made two saves to keep his team in the contest. First, Swans sub Zan Vipotnik should have done better when he shot straight at the Swedish international after Moussa Yeo had combined brilliantly down the left wing with Eom.

Then, Zetterstrom kept out a near-post Yeo drive after Lawrence Vigoroux's long forward punt had sent him sprinting clear through the right channel far too easily.

Ronald went on to wrap up matters when he fired into Zetterstrom's bottom-right corner from the edge of the box after Stephen Eustaquio's shot had been blocked.

Toothless Derby were booed off at the final whistle, having failed to score for the first time in 24 league games at Pride Park - a run stretching back to last September.

The managers

Derby's John Eustace:

"I can understand the fans' frustrations 100 per cent because the performance was unacceptable and I'm really disappointed," he said.

"We are lacking in confidence at the moment so conceding that first goal so early on didn't help, and while we huffed and puffed and had some little moments, to then concede the second just before half-time was a kick in the teeth.

"We then made three changes at half-time. I didn't want to because none of the players are fit yet and that showed with the way we dropped off the pace in the final 20 minutes, but we had to try and make something happen.

"We couldn't really put together any sustained attacks or give their keeper any problems, though, and things just seemed to fizzle out a bit and we're probably lacking a bit of quality in certain areas, which we are crying out for.

"The only thing that disappointed me in the second half was that the body language of some players wasn't great. But I'll take full responsibility for the performance and result. I pick the team, coach the players and give the tactics out."

Swansea's Vitor Matos:

"We started the game really well and scored. There were moments when Derby pushed us back but we coped with their threat, and after we scored the second goal that gave us the comfort to control the game how we like to.

"Derby made a really strong start to the second half and pushed us back again, but we stayed controlled and calm and then had a number of chances to score. We were maybe a bit too anxious to get a third to kill the game off but I'm really pleased with the maturity of the team, how the new players are fitting in and the desire and energy they are showing.

"We have a group of players who are enjoying playing together. We have the same mindset whether we're playing home or away and we're happy to have put on a good performance for our fans.

"We're showing we can compete against teams with different styles of playing, but it's only one game and we have a difficult run of fixtures coming up."

What the result means and next fixtures...

Sports.title: Wolves ease to victory against Stoke
Sports.content:
Wolves came from behind to beat Stoke 4-1 and continue their unbeaten start in the Sky Bet Championship.

Sam Gallagher's stunning second-minute goal gave Stoke the perfect start at Molineux but two goals in three minutes from Rodrigo Gomes turned the game on its head before half-time.

Raul Jimenez's penalty made it 3-1 after 55 minutes before substitute Jordan James scored on his home debut with six minutes remaining.

Mateus Mane also went close for Wolves in a convincing performance from Cesar Peixoto's side, who went top following the lunchtime fixtures.

Gallagher shocked Wolves with a superb goal for the visitors. The forward held off Marshall Munetsi before curling a tremendous shot into the top corner from 25 yards, giving goalkeeper Jose Sa no chance.

It was the 30-year-old's first goal since March and came about from a sloppy square pass by Wolves attacker Fer Lopez.

Gallagher went close to making it 2-0 when his shot was blocked by Sa after an early pass from Bae Jun-ho. Sorba Thomas should have buried the rebound only to fire wide.

After surviving that scare, Wolves equalised in the 20th minute from their first serious chance and then took the lead three minutes later - both goals coming from Gomes, and both rebounds.

The Portuguese attacker was ideally placed to stab home after goalkeeper Viktor Johansson parried Jimenez's side-footed effort after a heavy touch by Eric Bocat.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rodrigo Gomes finds the net twice inside four minutes to give Wolves the lead against Stoke at Molineux.

Mane did brilliantly for Wolves' second goal. The 18-year-old beat Ben Johnson and Gallagher before holding off Bosun Lawal and his cross was parried by Johansson before Gomes fired high into the unguarded net.

Wolves had a couple of opportunities to break following the restart but found their way halted by some resolute Stoke defending.

Jimenez had a shot blocked but he won a penalty when he was impeded by Johnson at the far post challenging for Hugo Bueno's corner.

The Mexican needed no second invitation from the spot, firing home his second goal of the season as he coolly sent Johansson the wrong way.

Mane was denied a fourth when his curling shot was tipped wide by Johansson, who smothered an angled drive from the same player.

Very little had been seen of Stoke's attack in the second half but Bocat screwed wide with a tame effort late on.

James, who replaced Gomes in the 77th minute, started and finished the move for Wolves' fourth.

The Wales international swept home Lopez's square pass from the right from 12 yards inside Johansson's left-hand post. James' crossfield pass had released Lopez out wide to start the move.

Substitute Tawanda Chirewa's curling effort was deflected over as Wolves looked for a fifth goal.

The managers

Wolves' Cesar Peixoto:

"We conceded a goal but the reaction was very important for us. We showed personality and character to fight and after that, we scored four goals and could have scored more.

"We played well and were organised in terms of defensive organisation, and with offensive organisation we could have scored more.

"I talked to the players before the game to have the right shape and the right body language to bring our supporters to support us.

"We did that. The players showed character, personality and quality when we had the ball - they found the right spaces and we defended well, not conceding a lot of chances."

Stoke's Mark Robins:

"We scored a brilliant goal then contrived to shoot ourselves in the foot. We started really well and scored a 'worldie' and got our noses in front.

"We then had some really decent play, from the goalkeeper's close kick all the way to Gallagher, who won a header and we got runners off him into the box.

"We started to gather momentum but then we decided to do something different.

"Instead of doing those things that got us success, we played it to Eric Bocat, who tried to take on a man and lost the ball in a really dangerous area and they had the weight of numbers to score.

"That changed the whole momentum because we gave them a second one and they hadn't had to work for it.

"We've been the authors of our own downfall for the second week running."

What the result means and next fixtures...

Sports.title: Champions League fixture schedule confirmed
Sports.content:
The Champions League fixture dates for Arsenal, Manchester City, Manchester United, Liverpool and Aston Villa have been confirmed.

Last season's European finalists Arsenal will play Real Madrid and Bayern Munich in this year's Champions League league phase.

The Premier League champions will also face Borussia Dortmund and Napoli in their bid to finish in the top eight automatic places, having topped qualifying with a perfect record last term.

Meanwhile, both Man City and Aston Villa will host holders PSG. The Villa Park fixture will be a repeat of the recent Super Cup, which PSG won 2-1 in Salzburg.

Final: 5 June 2027 - Wanda Metropolitano Stadium, Madrid

How does the league phase draw work?

A total of 36 teams will enter the competition at this stage after 29 qualified at the end of last season. The remaining seven places were determined by the qualifiers.

In the new format, which is entering its third season since being implemented, teams now play fixtures against eight different teams - two teams from Pots 1, 2, 3 and 4.

Half of the eight league-phase matches are at home, with the other half away.

Who qualifies for the knockout rounds?

The top eight sides in the league will qualify automatically for the round of 16, while teams finishing 25th or lower are eliminated and do not drop into the Europa League.

The teams finishing in ninth to 24th place compete in a two-legged knockout-phase play-off. Teams finishing between ninth and 16th are seeded, meaning they will face a team in 17th-24th with the return leg at home.

The eight clubs who win their knockout-phase play-off each meet one of the seeded top-eight finishers in the league-phase table for a place in the quarter-finals.

Champions League knockout-phase match dates and schedule

The draw for the two-legged knockout-phase play-offs is yet to be determined.

Knockout-phase play-offs: February 16/17 and 23/24

Round of 16: March 9/10 and 16/17

Quarter-finals: April 6/7 and 13/14

Semi-finals: April 27/28 and May 4/5

Final: June 5

When and where is the final?

The final will take place at the Estadio Metropolitano in Madrid, Spain, on June 5 2027.

Sports.title: Víctor Muñoz rescues Liverpool to deny Nottingham Forest another Anfield win
Sports.content:
A malfunctioning electronic board will not have been on anyone’s bingo list of Liverpool complaints for the first Anfield game of Andoni Iraola’s tenure, but others sounded all too familiar. A slow start, a lack of intensity and defensive shortcomings were again evident as Liverpool salvaged a point against Nottingham Forest, while showing stronger foundations are required along with the excitement of £123m Bradley Barcola.

In front of some of the billionaires behind Liverpool, Iraola’s opening act on home soil offered more food for thought than the feast they may have been expecting. Forest were good value for the second 2-2 draw of the new Liverpool head coach’s reign and created enough clear openings to justify their frustration at the final outcome. A superb finish from Liverpool’s summer signing Víctor Muñoz cancelled out Morgan Gibbs-White’s penalty, after Alexander Isak had done the same to Dan Ndoye’s opener.

“I’ve got two emotions,” said Oliver Glasner. “I’m very proud of the performance and how many chances we created, but I’m disappointed with the result. It could and should have been a win, but after 60, 65 minutes our defending was not as clinical.”

Iraola’s irritations veered from his team’s first-half display to the bizarre situation of being unable to make a triple substitution because the assistant’s electronic board would not work. Liam Delap, Forest’s new record signing who made a good impression, took a quick throw that led to the visitors’ second goal while Ryan Gravenberch, Rio Ngumoha and Kostas Tsimikas waited to come on.

Watching on from the directors’ box were Liverpool’s prospective new vice-chair Amit Bhatia and his father-in-law, the Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal. Bhatia and Mittal, who has given financial backing to 1892 Holdings acquiring a 38% stake in Liverpool, were the invited guests of John W Henry. Jeff Bezos and Eduardo Saverin, other billionaire members of the consortium, were not in attendance.

The club’s principal owner was present to witness the start of a brave new era. Turns out it looked very much like the old one, even down to Dominik Szoboszlai ending the game at right-back.

After a rousing tribute before kick-off to Kevin Keegan Liverpool were soon exposed by the pace and movement of the Forest attack. First-time long balls released Ndoye behind the defence twice in the opening six minutes and, while the attacking midfielder lost his footing on both occasions, Liverpool failed to deal with the source of their problems.

View image in fullscreen Víctor Muñoz marks his first league start with Liverpool’s equaliser. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA

Forest carried the only consistent threat in the first half with Igor Jesus, thwarted by Jérémy Jacquet’s fine intervention, Ndoye and Jesus again having chances before the breakthrough. Having cleared a Forest corner, Liverpool were undone by Matz Sels’s long clearance back over their defence to Jesus.

The striker, just onside, held up the goalkeeper’s delivery despite the close attentions of Jacquet and Alexis Mac Allister to find Gibbs-White, who rolled a simple pass to the unmarked Ndoye. The Switzerland international steered a precise finish low beyond Alisson’s left hand.

Anfield erupted shortly afterwards when Florian Wirtz swept a smart finish on the turn inside Sels’s right post. A much-needed goal for Liverpool and their £116m playmaker, however, was disallowed by the video assistant referee for offside against Jeremie Frimpong in the buildup.

Patience in Frimpong is in short supply at Anfield judging by the exasperation that greeted his poor crossing and defensive toils. Iraola would replace both of his full-backs before the afternoon was over.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Liverpool were indebted to Alisson for denying Forest a second goal on the stroke of half-time. Ola Aina flew past Muñoz before picking out Jesus near the penalty spot. Alisson produced a superb, crucial save to turn the striker’s first-time shot on to his crossbar.

View image in fullscreen Morgan Gibbs-White restores Nottingham Forest’s lead from the penalty spot. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA

The Brazilian’s intervention assumed greater significance when Liverpool levelled on the hour. Cody Gakpo, a transfer target for Manchester City and Tottenham, gave a timely reminder of his quality when receiving Wirtz’s pass and spinning away from two defenders, Neco Williams and Murillo, in one movement. He then supplied a perfect pass across the face of the goal for Isak to tap home.

Delap’s quick-thinking caught Liverpool cold – Jacquet and Frimpong in particular – as his throw-in released Williams into the area with the defenders asleep. The former Liverpool full-back flicked a shot high and wide of the goal before being felled by the keeper, who was booked for protesting the harsh penalty decision. Gibbs-White swept an emphatic penalty kick to the keeper’s right as Alisson dived left.

Liverpool, improved by the substitutions, fought back for a second time when Wirtz pierced the defence with an excellent pass behind Murillo to Muñoz. The £34.5m summer signing from Osasuna marked his home debut with a brilliant finish off the underside of the crossbar to rescue a point for Iraola’s work in progress.
