World.title: Germany, extreme hot summer ripens grapes faster and advances wine harvest several weeks
World.content:
Germany, extreme hot summer ripens grapes faster and advances wine harvest several weeks

29th Saturday, August 2026 - 13:23 UTC Full article

“This was the earliest start to the harvest ever in all wine-growing regions,” Wine Institute spokesman Ernst Büscher said

Germany's main grape harvest takes off earlier than ever recorded following on the country's exceptionally hot summer which accelerated the ripening process in vineyards, according to the German Wine Institute

The record-early harvest (September) continues a trend seen in recent decades, with higher temperatures affecting when grapes ripen, as well as their sugar and acidity levels.

“This was the earliest start to the harvest ever in all wine-growing regions,” institute spokesman Ernst Büscher said. “Some winegrowers even cut short their holidays because of it.”

Harvesting is already underway across Germany’s wine regions, from Saxony in the east to Lake Constance in the south.

The harvest has already included not only grapes for Federweisser — partially fermented young wine — and sparkling wine, but also first grapes destined for premium wines.

The main harvest is expected to begin “on a large scale” in the first week of September. Compared with recent years, the main harvest has begun around one to two weeks earlier, according to Büscher.

“Compared with 30 or 40 years ago, it is certainly four weeks earlier,” he said. The hot, dry summer caused grapes to ripen unusually quickly, while many varieties are reaching maturity at roughly the same time.

That means the harvest is also expected to proceed rapidly and could be completed by the end of September.

“This will be a very fast harvest because almost all varieties are ripening at the same time,” Büscher said.

However climate change has brought some advantages for Germany's wine industry over the years. Warmer conditions have allowed growers to experiment with grape varieties better suited to warmer climates and have made wine cultivation possible in some new areas.

But increasingly long and frequent periods of heat and drought also pose challenges.

Growers are closely watching both sugar and acidity levels. Leaving grapes on the vines too long in hot conditions can push sugar levels higher, producing stronger wines with more alcohol.

High temperatures can also reduce the fruit acidity that gives many German white wines their characteristic fruity freshness. Growers are pleased with the quality of the grapes harvested so far.

“The grapes are still very healthy,” Büscher said, adding that this pointed to aromatic white wines. Producers are also expecting deeply colored red wines.

Nevertheless the overall harvest is expected to be below average because dry conditions have left grapes smaller than usual. Significant rainfall in the coming weeks could accelerate the harvest even further.

World.title: Royal Navy turns to amphibious ships; sells HMS Bulwark to Brazilian Navy
World.content:
Royal Navy turns to amphibious ships; sells HMS Bulwark to Brazilian Navy

29th Saturday, August 2026 - 13:01 UTC Full article

Based at HMNB Devonport, Based at HMNB Devonport, HMS Bulwark served as the Royal Navy’s Fleet Flagship between 2011 and 2015served as the Royal Navy’s Fleet Flagship between 2011 and 2015

HMS Bulwark is to be sold to the Brazilian Navy, ending more than two decades of service with the Royal Navy, as UK focus turns to the future of amphibious assault ships.

HMS Bulwark, one of the Royal Navy’s two Albion-class amphibious assault ships, was commissioned in 2005 and went on to play a central role in operations around the world, including amphibious deployments, humanitarian assistance missions and multinational exercises with allies and partners.

Her sister ship, HMS Albion, remains alongside at HMNB Devonport pending disposal.

The transfer comes as the UK and Netherlands confirmed a new £2.4 billion maritime partnership in July 2026 to deliver a fleet of new amphibious transport ships, replacing the capability provided by the Albion class.

The future ships will be built in UK shipyards, working alongside Dutch industry, as part of a programme that is expected to sustain hundreds of highly skilled UK jobs. At 160 meters in length and displacing 15,000 tons, they will be capable of transporting troops, vehicles and equipment, including drones, wherever they are needed.

Minister of State for Defence, Lord Coaker said: “HMS Bulwark served this country and our allies with distinction for over two decades, and I’m pleased that she will continue her story in Brazilian service, with a nation that has long stood alongside us as a defence partner.

“This partnership with the Netherlands marks a real step forward for our Armed Forces, giving our personnel the modern, interoperable capability they need to operate alongside our allies for decades to come. It’s also a vote of confidence in British shipbuilding, backing the skills and shipyards that will keep our industrial base strong and our nation secure.”

Based at HMNB Devonport, HMS Bulwark served as the Royal Navy’s Fleet Flagship between 2011 and 2015, supported civilian evacuation operations from Lebanon in 2006, and provided maritime security for the Sailing Regatta at the London 2012 Olympics.

The flight decks of the future UK-Dutch amphibious fleet are being designed to operate current and future long-range drones and autonomous systems, supporting the Royal Navy’s transition to a hybrid Navy and the wider ambitions set out in the Defence Investment Plan to integrate uncrewed and autonomous technology across the fleet.

The program will form the backbone of a strengthened UK-Netherlands amphibious force, with each nation set to operate four vessels, delivering a shared and interoperable capability that reinforces NATO’s northern and Atlantic flanks.

World.title: The US will control 55% of output from the new oil company in Venezuela
World.content:
The US will control 55% of output from the new oil company in Venezuela

29th Saturday, August 2026 - 04:58 UTC Full article

“We have secured majority US control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American taxpayer,” Trump wrote

US President Donald Trump announced on Friday an agreement with Venezuela's interim government granting Washington majority control over more than 65 billion barrels of proven Venezuelan crude reserves, around 21% of the country's total. Acting president Delcy Rodríguez confirmed the deal.

According to a US official who asked not to be identified, the arrangement is structured through a joint venture between the US government and a private operator based in Venezuela whose identity has not been disclosed. Rodríguez granted that company 100-year concessions over fields containing some 63 billion barrels. Washington will control 55% of effective output, split between an equity stake and the right to buy crude at cost. The same official described the new company as the world's second-largest corporate holder of proven reserves, after Saudi Arabia's Aramco.

“We have secured majority US control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American taxpayer,” Trump wrote on his social network, adding that the transaction “more than doubles American oil reserves.” US proven crude reserves stand at around 48 billion barrels, though the reserves being added lie in Venezuelan territory and are controlled through a corporate stake.

The Venezuelan government's statement puts the deal at the development of 17 strategic fields, with investment exceeding 100 billion dollars and more than 209 billion in taxes for the state. Rodríguez said the aim is “to consolidate our position as an energy-producing power, putting our immense reserves at the service of national development.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who negotiated the agreement alongside Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, called it a victory for both sides. According to The Wall Street Journal, Chevron and the services provider Halliburton are involved so far.

The announcement comes two months before the US midterm elections, with the average price of petrol above four dollars a gallon and the country's strategic reserves at their lowest level since the early 1980s, after six months of war with Iran that have disrupted a fifth of the world's crude supply.

The deal comes almost nine months after US forces captured then president Nicolás Maduro in Caracas and transferred him to New York, where he awaits trial on drug trafficking charges. Rodríguez assumed the acting presidency and in January enacted a reform allowing private companies to manage extraction. The US Treasury subsequently eased sanctions on the sector.

Venezuela's annual inflation runs at around 600% and the minimum monthly income, some 240 dollars, covers less than half of a basic basket costing more than 500.

World.title: The US waives beef tariffs for Brazil and Paraguay, but not for Argentina and Uruguay
World.content:
The US waives beef tariffs for Brazil and Paraguay, but not for Argentina and Uruguay

28th Friday, August 2026 - 19:35 UTC Full article

For Brazil, the largest beef supplier to the US market, the measure removes for three months the out-of-quota duty of 26.4% it has paid since mid-January

US President Donald Trump signed a proclamation on August 26 temporarily waiving tariffs on imports of up to 300,000 tonnes of lean beef trimmings, a measure that excludes countries already holding their own quotas in the US market, among them Argentina and Uruguay. The main beneficiaries will be Brazil and Paraguay.

The text, titled Further Ensuring Affordable Beef for the American Consumer, invokes section 404 of the Uruguay Round Agreements Act, which allows a president to widen a tariff-rate quota temporarily. The expansion will run for 90 days from September 1, with a maximum of 100,000 tonnes a month allocated on a first-come, first-served basis in three tranches until November 30.

The exclusion stems from a technical point. The proclamation allocates the entire additional volume to the statistical category of “other countries or areas,” which does not include exporters holding country-specific quotas. That leaves out Argentina, Uruguay, Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom, which obtained its own 13,000-tonne allocation on January 1, as well as Canada and Mexico, covered by the free trade agreement.

For Brazil, the largest beef supplier to the US market, the measure removes for three months the out-of-quota duty of 26.4% it has paid since mid-January. Paraguay qualifies through the same channel: it shipped 23,497 tonnes in January, though it has since remained below 5,000 tonnes a month.

Argentina holds its own quota, historically 20,000 tonnes a year, which a proclamation on February 6 raised to 100,000 for this calendar year. Mario Ravettino, president of the ABC Export Consortium, confirmed the country is excluded along with Uruguay, Australia and New Zealand, and that the only beneficiary would be Brazil. “We are analysing it,” he told the newspaper La Nación.

The scale of the loss is debatable. Colin Carter, professor emeritus of agricultural economics at the University of California, Davis, said Argentina is not currently a significant supplier of the product covered by the programme, lean trimmings intended to be blended with US beef to make ground beef. In Brazil, the exporters' association Abiec said its members could benefit, though the requirement to sell those cuts at a discount of around 25% limits margin gains.

The White House justified the decision on the decline of the US cattle herd, which it places at its lowest level in 75 years, and on restrictions on live cattle imports from Mexico over the New World screwworm, drought and wildfires. The Department of Agriculture projects production will fall by around 4% compared with 2025. Trump warned he could revoke the measure to prevent a windfall for foreign producers if the discount does not materialise.

World.title: The Pope says states struggle to control the concentration of artificial intelligence
World.content:
The Pope says states struggle to control the concentration of artificial intelligence

28th Friday, August 2026 - 18:56 UTC Full article

The pontiff called for acting so that “the good of the human family is not sacrificed to private interests,” and raised a question about the pace of technological development

Pope Leo XIV warned on Friday of the difficulty states face in overseeing artificial intelligence, which in his view is concentrated in the hands of a small number of major economic and technological players, and called for the use of such tools to be governed by ethical criteria.

“It is important that a certain ethics be established to accompany the use of these important tools which, unfortunately, are concentrated in the hands of major economic and technological players, and which the state finds it hard to control,” he said during an audience in the Clementine Hall of the Apostolic Palace with members of the Institut International des Sciences Administratives, a Brussels-based body, at the close of its annual conference held in Rome.

The pontiff called for acting so that “the good of the human family is not sacrificed to private interests,” and raised a question about the pace of technological development: “The speed at which innovations relating to artificial intelligence are developing leads us to ask whether in future it will be possible to control these machines, whether humanity does not risk becoming the victim of its own inventions.” He added that one of the grave problems of the present is seeing that “decisions about human life are entrusted to machines.”

Leo XIV defended what he called the irreplaceable character of human intelligence in the face of these tools and argued that the work of experts can help authorities take decisions in the field. He closed by encouraging participants to work towards the humanisation of digital technologies, “so that they serve life and peace.”

The address draws on Magnifica humanitas, the encyclical the Pope devoted to safeguarding the human person in the age of artificial intelligence, and comes a week after another audience on the same subject. On August 21, before some two hundred members of the International Catholic Legislators Network gathered in Rome, he warned of the risk that technological innovation could become “another instrument of ideological or economic colonialism,” a “subtle form of domination” capable of increasing poorer nations' dependence on richer ones.

On that occasion he argued that every technological achievement poses a moral question that is not confined to “what we can do, but what we should do,” and cautioned against the temptation to build “a new Tower of Babel where power, efficiency and control obscure the face of the human person.”

Artificial intelligence has been a central concern of the pontificate from its outset. Leo XIV, the first pope born in the United States, also holds Peruvian nationality after decades as a missionary and bishop of Chiclayo. He did not name any specific company.

World.title: Washington negotiates stakes in Venezuelan oil fields with leases of up to a century
World.content:
Washington negotiates stakes in Venezuelan oil fields with leases of up to a century

28th Friday, August 2026 - 14:15 UTC Full article

The negotiation covers around a dozen fields holding some 90 billion barrels of proven reserves, close to a third of the roughly 300 billion Venezuela has certified, the world's largest

The United States government is negotiating with Venezuela's interim administration to acquire stakes in a group of the South American country's oil fields, under arrangements that would include leases of up to a hundred years, the outlets Axios and Bloomberg reported on Thursday citing unnamed senior US officials.

Neither side has confirmed the talks. The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the Department of Energy, which did not respond. Nor did Venezuela's oil ministry, the state oil company PDVSA or the information ministry, and hydrocarbons minister Paula Henao could not be reached.

According to the sources cited by Axios, the negotiation covers around a dozen fields holding some 90 billion barrels of proven reserves, close to a third of the roughly 300 billion Venezuela has certified, the world's largest. A list of 17 fields seen by the Reuters news agency includes new areas in the Orinoco Belt and mature fields in Lake Maracaibo, some currently operated by a Chinese company under a contract signed during Nicolás Maduro's tenure.

The scheme under discussion would give Washington an ownership interest in designated fields, with private companies, including American ones, brought in to modernise and operate them. Venezuela would receive higher revenues from increased output. The talks are led by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and acting president Delcy Rodríguez, and there is no timetable for a final agreement. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has considered travelling to Venezuela next week. “Calling this deal huge would be an understatement,” one of the officials told Axios.

The move also responds to domestic pressures. The administration faces rising petrol prices ahead of November's midterm elections and is seeking to replenish the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It fits a recent pattern too: the US government has taken stakes in companies including Intel, MP Materials and Lithium Americas, and in what Bloomberg calls the so-called Donroe Doctrine of extending American influence across the hemisphere.

In parallel, Bloomberg reported that Caracas is considering leaving the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, which it helped found in 1960 and whose quotas it has failed to meet for years. The United Arab Emirates announced its departure in April and Iraq raised the possibility in June before dropping it. Venezuela currently produces around 1.25 million barrels a day.

The talks follow the hydrocarbons law reform Rodríguez enacted on January 30, less than a month after Maduro's capture by US forces, and the easing of the oil embargo by the US Treasury. Officials cited by Axios acknowledge the acting president could face accusations of handing over the country's natural resources.

World.title: A flavorful, vanilla-scented hideout awaits along Mexico’s Gulf Coast
World.content:
You may have seen it: a group of high-flying performers, dressed in a colorful array of traditional garments, climbing a 100-foot-tall pole in a group of four, before diving into the air, upside down, to spin as a human cyclone — held only by a rope tied to their feet — while a fifth member sits atop the pole, performing a ceremonial dance and song with a flute and small drum.

The UNESCO-recognized tradition can be traced back to Tajín, an archaeological site that once served as the capital of the Totonac Mesoamericans from A.D. 800. Today, it is one of Mexico’s most celebrated and active Indigenous rituals, known as the “Danza de los Voladores,” or “Dance of the Flyers.”

Interestingly, the Totonac did not invent the dance — that was likely the Nahua of Central Mexico — but they have preserved it, inextricably linking the practice to their history and culture in the process.

Ancient traditions in the modern world

These airborne avatars of the Totonac people are native to the northern region of Veracruz, where the modern Pueblo Mágico of Papantla can be found, roughly four hours northeast of Mexico City. They are famed throughout the country, with representatives performing their millennia-old routine in tourist centers such as Mexico City’s Bosque de Chapultepec and Xcaret Park in Playa del Carmen.

The voladores maintain their practices and Indigenous language through generations of flyers and community-supported programs, including the Escuela de Niños Voladores in Papantla. They are one of Veracruz’s greatest cultural exports and have inspired an inside joke among Mexicans, who sometimes shout “Papantla, tus hijos vuelan!” when something funny or unexpected happens in daily life.

And yet, as impressive and fun as the voladores are on a sweltering summer day, the region has also gifted Mexico, and the world, even more than its high-flying customs: Papantla is the global cradle and origin of vanilla.

I drove four hours north of Xalapa along the Gulf Coast to Papantla — admiring the decaying majesty of its tropical vastness and curving, mountainous shoreline — to visit the historical ruins and learn about its contemporary tastes.

‘The city that perfumed the world’

Papantla, a town of 55,452 inhabitants according to national census data, was once the global leader in vanilla exports. From 1870 to 1910, the modest pueblo in Veracruz state — located on steep, labyrinthine roads in the middle of a tropical forest — became the epicenter for vanilla, one of the most expensive spices in the global market. Much of it was exported to Europe and the United States, and the region was dubbed “the city that perfumed the world” for the sweet, refreshing scent that vanilla emits.

Sadly, naturally grown vanilla from Papantla — which a researcher at UNAM designated as one of Mexico’s greatest contributions to global cuisine, along with cacao, amaranth, chile peppers and tomatoes — is no longer what it used to be. Nowadays, artificial vanilla dominates, and the market value of small-batch vanilla bean production from Papantla is nowhere near what it once was — in many ways a metaphor for the greater significance of Veracruz as a state.

The rise and fall of the vanilla trade

Historical documents reveal that vanilla cultivation dates back to the Totonac peoples, who gathered the fruit of orchid plants in surrounding areas before any other known society. Writing in her journal article “The History and Ecology of Vanilla,” Dr. Mariana Hernández Apolinar, a biologist and faculty member in UNAM’s science department, notes that for more than 200 years, “Mexico was the world’s only supplier of vanilla, bringing the country considerable profit.”

That declined in the mid-19th century when Europeans intervened. According to Hernández Apolinar, “it was discovered that vanilla flowers could be fertilized manually. This made it possible to produce the fruit on plantations outside its natural area and led to intensive vanilla cultivation in different tropical regions, making its production intensely commercial.”

Fast-forward to today, and the vanilla economy has been at risk for more than a decade. As NPR reported in 2019, local farmers have found themselves the target of robberies and violence at the hands of organized criminal gangs. In addition, a group of Mexican professors and biologists have outlined how issues of deforestation, soil erosion, shifting weather patterns and the marginalization of rural communities have negatively impacted modern vanilla productivity in the region.

At the same time, efforts to restore vanilla’s potential within the Mexican agricultural sector have been underway, including Papantla’s growing tourism sector.

Exploring ‘The Vanilla Route’

Originally known as “xanat” or “xanath” in the local dialect, the region upholds a proud legacy of vanilla. Vanilla tours are widely available, allowing visitors to tour nearby plantations that grow the spice. Family-owned shops abound, selling everything under the sun with an added touch of vanilla: ground coffee mixed with vanilla extract, vanilla-flavored cigarillos, vanilla sodas, horchata with vanilla, bottled vanilla concentrate, vanilla-scented candles, vanilla perfumes, vanilla liqueurs and more. Each shop explains the benefits and uses of its products. For example, vanilla’s aroma is considered an effective aromatherapy treatment for stress, while eating it is believed to offer digestive and anti-aging properties.

For a deeper immersion, there are excursions like “The Vanilla Route,” which spans two days of history and includes guided visits to the Xanath ecological park, a 54-acre plot of land that is preserved for sustainable vanilla growing, as well as a visit to a family-owned vanilla farm, where guests can witness firsthand how vanilla is turned into artisanal products.

Savoring local gastronomy

I made it a point to find as much local gastronomy as I could during my visit. I stayed at a small hotel with classical architecture dating back to the 18th century, less than a block away from the town’s main plaza, which stays abuzz at all hours and where street vendors sell goods and regional treats, such as homemade vanilla ice cream and atole morado, an iced, purple corn beverage to stave off the jungle’s humidity.

For breakfast, a trek up the nearby hillsides led to Saberes Ancestrales de la Vainilla, a family-owned business with two locations, one of which offers a vanilla museum and sweeping vista of the town. “Saberes” is the Spanish word for “knowledge,” and embodies the spirit of the restaurant and museum, which was founded to preserve the culinary essence of vanilla in its multitudinous forms.

Here, I began my self-guided tour of Papantla with a café de olla, a traditional coffee brewed in a clay pot and doused with natural vanilla, giving it a rich, natural sweetness to balance the drink’s dark bitterness.

Indigenous flavors and regional dishes

To eat, we had bocoles, a Huastecan dish featuring girthy tortillas made from bean or chicharrón masa stuffed with a protein of choice, as well as espolvoreadas de pipián, a lard-rubbed heap of thick tortillas, served in a pancake-style stack, and topped with ground pumpkin seed powder. The dish is simple, but in its simplicity, the orchestra of corn, pumpkin and oily grease is a representation of Mexico’s indigenous flavors without any unnecessary pomp.

The meal was so good that my family and I returned to Saberes Ancestrales de la Vainilla’s original location near our hotel in the main zócalo, where I ordered a chicken breast simmered in a smoky vanilla-pepper sauce. It was tangy and piquant, reminiscent of an American Southern barbecue dish, but in a tropical context.

For dinner, we visited Nakú, a restaurant named in honor of the Totonac word for “heart.” Its outdoor eatery offers tours and artisanal products, while highlighting an indigenous diet specific to northern Veracruz.

Art, history and unforgettable flavors

There are hard-to-find dishes like zacahuil, served on Sundays only, and pulaklh, which are regional varieties of tamales with ingredients such as sesame seeds and acoyo, popularly known as hoja santa. Other unique offerings include tachula xa talhtsi, a bowl of buttery beans coated with crumbled pumpkin seeds; liwa xalak kakwin, rabbit in a spicy al chiltepín salsa; and pollo en salsa de vainilla y pulque, chicken bathed in a chilpaya, pulque and vanilla sauce, served with steamed vegetables and a stack of espolvoreadas de pipián.

Any visit to Papantla and nearby Tajín should include more than vanilla. One highlight that may surprise tourists is the murals and work of Teodoro Cano García, a Papanteco sculptor, painter and muralist who was mentored by Diego Rivera and who gifted the town a massive mural depicting the historical evolution of the Totonac people in the town square, to go along with a monument of the voladores de Papantla.

An overlooked attraction

In addition, the small but impressive Teodoro Cano Museum offers a rare contemporary art space in the pueblo, housing his paintings alongside Totonac artifacts, and is open to the public for free. Regardless of interests, Papantla is a historically significant, if not overlooked, part of Veracruz’s — and Mexico’s — rich past, and remains a culturally informative, intensely flavorful visit that will not break your bank.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: What I learned from our two summer interns: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Part of our team’s passion for journalism extends to making sure that we do our part to help inspire the next generation of journalists. This summer, the MND team had two students working with us in our San Miguel office — Jared and Zella. The two have completely different life experiences, different personalities and different passions, so it was fun to have them both on the team.

Jared grew up in the Chicago area and is about to start his senior year at the University of Washington in Seattle. He is a journalism major and is passionate about sports journalism. Although he had been to Europe several times with his family, he had never been to Mexico. Despite having taken five years of Spanish in school, his speaking skills were quite “rusty” (to put it mildly). Jared is very much a self-proclaimed introvert.

Zella was born in Manhattan and moved to San Miguel with her family when she was six months old. She then lived in SMA until she was 15 years old, though her freshman year in high school. For the final three years of high school, she is going to a boarding school in California (her parents still live in SMA). For her upcoming senior year, Zella will be the editor-in-chief of her high school paper. She is completely bilingual and very extroverted.

As many people on our team do not have children, it presented an interesting opportunity for us to work with two kids at different phases of their “journalism journey.” At some points this summer, our office in San Miguel had team members aged 17, 21, 27, 28 and 32 (my wife’s and my ages are confidential!). The following is a list of what I learned from our two interns this summer, offered less as a verdict on them and more as a snapshot of the moment their generation is navigating.

1. Artificial intelligence presents a real dilemma for them. On one hand, they see how easy it can make their life, yet on the other hand, they also realize that it can make them overly dependent on it and lazy. It’s like the ultimate superpower, but at the same time you know it carries real risks. We made it clear to them that at MND we would allow zero AI in their writing, but that it is perfectly fine to use for research purposes.

2. Neither one of them wanted to think too much about what AI could do to the journalism profession, the news industry or their career prospects in general. It was refreshing, albeit somewhat concerning, to see them so … naive? In denial? Innocent? … about what AI could mean for them in the future. They didn’t really want to talk about it, so I didn’t push it much.

3. It’s troubling to see how few actual books they read. TikTok or Instagram videos are the new version of reading. Which, of course, is concerning. This isn’t unique to Jared and Zella — it reflects a broader shift in how information is consumed across most of their peer group.

I asked Jared when he last read a non-fiction book, to which he replied, “I don’t think I ever have read one.” So I promptly gave him two books to read: The first was “The Last Emperor of Mexico” by Edward Shawcross, a great book about Maximilian and a fascinating part of Mexican history. He loved it. The second was “Comfort Crisis” by Michael Easter, which is about the mental and physical health benefits of embracing discomfort. I have written previously about how important I think embracing discomfort is, and how important it was to me as I studied abroad years ago. I also see the benefits in it from my wife’s journey to the U.S. from India, as well as from many other immigrants. I don’t think he appreciated the book yet — these things sometimes take time to land — but I find it very unfortunate that many in society seem to be somewhat giving up on expecting kids to read books, especially non-fiction. That is not a good trend.

4. It was fascinating to see how both interns’ faces literally lit up when they were writing. For both of them, writing is clearly a “happy place.” I loved seeing that. I truly believe that writing is a wonderful demonstration of comprehension, communication and logic. If someone is unable to put something in writing, they likely will not be able to communicate it well. And if someone relies too much on AI to do the writing, they likely haven’t comprehended much. Both interns loved writing, loved putting their thoughts into the written word. Seeing this made me equally happy and saddened. Happy to see the passion stirred up in them. Sad to think about how quickly our society is seemingly deprioritizing the importance of reading and writing — crucial tools to create a generation of young people who are well-informed and can intelligently communicate their thoughts and ideas. It left me wondering: Who will read the great writings of this new generation of journalists?

5. American parents and administrators: Relax!! I was shocked at the monitoring, tracking, guiding and checking in that Jared seemed to be subject to. Zella’s parents, having lived in Mexico for years, were much more chill. Just a generation ago, a study abroad experience was a true adventure — a chance to get uncomfortable and disconnect from family, friends and authority. Every family navigates this differently, and there are good reasons parents stay closely connected today that didn’t exist a generation ago. Still, it’s worth asking whether some of today’s students are being given less room than earlier generations had to grow through that kind of independence.

We look forward to welcoming interns again next summer, giving them a chance to learn from our team — and giving us a chance to learn from them.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: ‘Confidently Wrong’ podcast: What one man’s heart surgery story reveals about healthcare in Mexico
World.content:
“Confidently Wrong” is back with a new episode from Mexico News Daily, and this time we are doing a deep dive into the realities of receiving urgent healthcare in Mexico. In an earlier episode, we tackled one of the most asked — and most misunderstood — topics: healthcare in Mexico. We reviewed the Expat Healthcare Survey results, digging into the responses of over 700 foreigners actively using healthcare in the country.

You can see the results of the survey here: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/mnd-intelligence/mnd-mexico-healthcare-experience-survey-1/

And you can see the episode of the podcast here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=drRwz5bIuOE&list=PLejJ221QSkEk&index=4

After the usual questions about safety and life in Mexico, the conversation almost always turns to healthcare. Do you have a doctor? Is it affordable? Can you trust the system? In that episode, we broke down those questions using real data and real experiences.

The MND team surveyed foreigners living across Mexico to better understand what healthcare here is actually like. From routine dental cleanings to major procedures like heart surgery, respondents shared insights on cost, accessibility and quality of care. While no single survey can cover everything, the results offer a grounded, firsthand look at the system.

In this episode, we do a much deeper dive into the nitty-gritty of the healthcare system. We review the real-life example of George Reavis, my co-host, and his recent heart surgery in Mexico. We discuss the entire process including interactions with doctors, the procedure and health insurance. We also review what went well and what he thinks he should have done better.

I’m sure you will find, as I did, his story extremely insightful and helpful to better understand how to navigate the healthcare system in Mexico. It’s filled with unbiased, real-life anecdotes relevant to anyone wanting to learn more about the realities of receiving urgent healthcare in Mexico.

Check it out below.

World.title: Mexico nets 2 Gold Medals at World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam
World.content:
Mexico made history at the 2026 World Rowing Championships, winning two Gold Medals and a Bronze at the event in Amsterdam.

Aylín Ibarra and Melissa Márquez started things off Thursday with a victory in the women’s lightweight double sculls to become the first Mexican rowers to win a Gold Medal at a senior World Championships.

ESPN reported that the duo — which won gold last month at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games — dominated from the outset and resisted attacks from Greece, the reigning under-23 world champion, to claim victory with a time of 7:10 minutes.

Mexico had never before won a Gold Medal at this event and its rowers had never won more than one medal at a single World Championships.

Kenia Lechuga helped turn that history around by winning the lightweight race, capturing the world title that had eluded her until now. Lechuga — Mexico’s most decorated rower — won silver in this event in 2023 and came home with a Bronze in 2025. She won gold in this event at the 2019 Pan American Games.

On Thursday, the 32-year-old Nuevo León native took the lead from the start aboard her signature pink boat and maintained control to the finish line. She completed the standard 2,000-meter course in 7:29 minutes

“We are competing fearlessly against the European monarchs,” Lechuga said afterward.

It is believed that this year’s World Championships was the last time Lechuga will compete in the lightweight category as she is expected to focus on the individual sculls leading up to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

Lechuga competed in the 2016 Rio Games (finishing 12th), the 2020 Tokyo Games (finishing 16th) and participated in the open weight category at the 2024 Paris Games.

Finally, Alexis López earned a bronze medal in the men’s lightweight individual sculls, completing the 2,000-meter race in 6:52 minutes, placing him third behind Greece’s Petros Gkaidatzis and Uruguay’s Felipe Kluver. Gkaidatzis, is the reigning European champion and Kluver was world champion in 2025.

López, a native of San Felipe, Baja California, won four medals at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games — two gold (individual and mixed double) and two silver (men’s double and men’s quadruple).

With reports from ESPN, Aristegui Noticias, El Universal, La Jornada and Zeta

World.title: The Mexican peso’s strong run hits a snag following US inflation worries
World.content:
The peso climbed above 17 to the U.S. dollar on Friday after U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh expressed concern about inflation.

Mexico’s currency closed on Thursday at 16.9752, but the spot exchange rate reached 17.0151 shortly after Warsh’s speech at the Fed’s annual Jackson Hole (Wyoming) symposium, his first since being confirmed as Fed chairman on May 12.

“We must be certain that core inflation is heading toward our target, clearly and at a sufficient pace,” he said. “Otherwise, we have work to do. That is our task.”

As the market digested the chairman’s comments indicating that the Fed still has work to do, the dollar strengthened.

Warsh said the most recent inflation data did not point to a change in trend and the Fed must move to ensure prices are clearly converging toward its 2% target, especially since the July Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index rose more than expected.

A day earlier, senior Fed officials had admitted that there are concerns about the inflation outlook.

Warsh’s speech prompted the futures market to reflect an increase in bets on a rate hike.

The peso, which began the day with moderate gains, retreated after Warsh’s Friday remarks and those made by other Fed officials on Thursday.

For the first time in eight days, the exchange rate rose above 17 pesos, trading within a range of 17.0467 and 16.9440. By noon Mexico City time, the Mexican currency was trading at 17.0463, a loss of 7.51 centavos, or –0.44%.

For several weeks, the peso has been one of the best-performing emerging market currencies despite sluggish economic growth and persistent trade tensions with Washington.

Earlier this week, the Reuters news agency revived talk of the “super peso,” while warning that it had begun “squeezing the margins of some exporters,” while lowering costs for importers.

The peso surge has been attributed to “lower ​trade-risk premia, political stability and solid macroeconomic conditions,” not to dollar weakness.

Following Warsh’s admission regarding U.S. inflation, investors are likely to demonstrate confidence that the Fed will raise its interest rate at the September meeting. This would then contribute to further depreciation of emerging market currencies, including the peso.

Higher U.S. interest rates also reduce the relative appeal of “carry trades,” a profit-seeking strategy based on investing in higher-yielding currencies. Carry trades have been one of the factors driving the peso’s appreciation.

With reports from El Economista and El Financiero

World.title: Mexican exports hit record $81B in July, up nearly 44% on AI-driven manufacturing boom
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico’s foreign trade set new records in July as exports surpassed US $80 billion for the first time ever, the performance driven by sales of computer and electronic equipment to the United States.

Merchandise sales abroad totaled US $81.4 billion last month, according to information released by national statistics agency INEGI on Thursday.

The surge in exports in July — up 43.7% year-on-year, the biggest leap in five years — comes amid a boom in investments related to artificial intelligence infrastructure.

This is the largest growth for any month since May 2021, when exports soared 125% as the country recovered from the most acute phase of the crisis triggered by the Covid-19 pandemic.

Disregarding the statistical rebounds in 2021 and May 2010 (the +43.8% bump that month was part of the recovery from the Great Recession of 2008-2009), July’s record represents the largest increase since at least 1993.

At the same time, imports totaled US $82.3 billion, increasing by 45.7% year-on-year. This represents the best growth rate since August 2021, though it resulted in a deficit of US $847.5 million, a month after June’s trade surplus of US $4.1 billion.

The strong export performance is primarily attributed to the 64.9% rebound in non-automotive manufacturing, which totaled nearly US $60 billion and represented 73% of total foreign sales.

“This data reflects a context wherein U.S. companies are demonstrating high demand for inputs to develop data centers associated with artificial intelligence,” Enrique Covarrubias, chief economist and director of analysis at Actinver investment bank, told El Financiero newspaper.

“It also comes at a time when the United States is tightening trade restrictions on the import of such inputs from Asian partners,” he added.

Analysts at Grupo Financiero Monex concurred, saying the advance in exports was driven by greater dynamism in non-automotive manufacturing, where shipments of electrical and electronic equipment and machinery stood out.

The total value of exported manufactured goods was US $76.3 billion, representing a 45.7% year-on-year increase.

The most significant advances were observed in exports of electrical and electronic equipment and appliances (134.0%), mining and metallurgy products (27.3%), machinery and special equipment for various industries (13.9%), plastic and rubber products (13.3%) and automotive products (2.4 percent).

Non-oil exports to the United States, which account for 84.5% of the total, surged 49.8% year-on-year in July and an improvement over the 35.9% growth reported in June.

In contrast, oil exports slowed their growth trend to 6.8% year-on-year in July, well below the 42.6% reported the previous month.

Conversely, sales in the extractive industry accelerated to 87.1%, up from 37.3% in June and marking 13 consecutive months of double-digit growth.

Agricultural products were the only export category that failed to achieve year-on-year growth, posting a negative-8.6% rate in July.

Meanwhile, the jump in imports can be attributed to the 56.3% increase in imports of intermediate goods, which accounted for 81.6% of total purchases. Also noteworthy was the 9.9% increase in imports of capital goods, the largest in 27 months.

The resulting trade deficit was Mexico’s first since February. The biggest factors were an oil trade balance that showed a deficit of US $3.7 billion, whereas the non-oil trade balance showed a surplus of US $2.8 billion.

Analysts at Banamex forecast a surplus of US $14.2 billion for the full year, anticipating 22% growth in exports and 20% growth in imports.

For its part, Monex says Mexico’s foreign trade will continue to be closely linked to the evolution of negotiations between Mexico and the United States, as part of the annual review of the USMCA, North America’s free trade agreement.

With reports from El Financiero, El Economista, La Jornada and Expansión

World.title: New winter flight routes will connect Guadalajara with New York while boosting Mexico links
World.content:
Winter will offer new connectivity options for national and international travelers with the addition of a nonstop route between Guadalajara and New York, a new flight between Tuxtla Gutiérrez and Oaxaca city, and increased flight frequencies between Mexico City and Querétaro.

These recently announced developments will occur during a period of high demand associated with the December holidays, family gatherings, and year-end tourism.

Guadalajara – New York

Guadalajara, a top Mexican aviation market, will have a daily, nonstop connection to New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport. The Aeroméxico flight will operate from December 17, 2026, through January 3, 2027, on a Boeing 737 with a capacity of 166 passengers.

Departure times and flight duration have not yet been made public, but the new flight will offer an alternative to passengers who currently need to stop over in Mexico City, Monterrey, or airports in the United States to travel between Guadalajara and New York City.

It’s also an opportunity to attract U.S. tourists during the peak season, as well as to meet the demand from business travelers and Mexicans living in the northeastern U.S. who travel to the country during the holidays.

The seasonal route adds to the growth of Guadalajara International Airport’s network, which will expand from 66 to 71 destinations during the winter season.

Tuxtla Gutiérrez – Oaxaca

Authorities in the southern state of Chiapas announced a new air link between the state capital, Tuxtla Gutiérrez, and Oaxaca. According to the announcement by Governor Eduardo Ramírez, the new route will be operated by Viva on Mondays and Fridays, starting October 30.

The service will improve mobility between two states known for their cultural, natural and culinary attractions, as well as facilitate business travel.

Mexico City – Querétaro

In central Mexico, Aeroméxico will expand its operations between Mexico City and Querétaro starting October 25. The airline is adding an extra flight on Sundays and Mondays, increasing the route’s frequency from three to four daily flights on those days.

The additional flight will depart Mexico City at 3:25 p.m. and arrive in Querétaro at 4:34 p.m. The return flight will take off from Querétaro at 5:10 p.m. and land in the capital at 6:20 p.m.

With this addition, the route’s monthly capacity is set to rise from approximately 16,000 seats in September to 23,000 in November—an increase of nearly 40%.

Beyond serving travelers between the two cities, the new service will provide Querétaro with greater connectivity to domestic and international flights departing from Mexico City International Airport.

With reports from El Economista, El Momento and A21

World.title: El Jalapeño: Jalisco residents fear real-life Guillermo del Toro horror movie following discovery of ‘zombie fungus’
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

GUADALAJARA, Jalisco — State health officials in Jalisco addressed public concern Thursday by detailing the specific, highly improbable conditions under which the newly discovered Ophiocordyceps deltoroi zombie fungus could theoretically jump to human hosts, confirming a real-life cinematic nightmare would require a blend of atmospheric humidity, Victorian-era interior design and deeply tragic family lore.

The announcement follows wide fascination over the University of Guadalajara’s cataloging of six ant-parasitizing “zombie fungi” species in the forests of San Sebastián del Oeste. Given that one species was named after Guadalajara-born director Guillermo del Toro, researchers spent the week answering press inquiries regarding how an actual cinematic-style biological spillover could unfold on Mexican soil.

“To cross the species barrier, the microscopic spore would need a host possessing a very specific physiological profile,” explained Dr. Arturo Mendoza, lead bio-risk consultant for Jalisco’s Ministry of Health. “The ideal human candidate must be an orphaned heiress, wear a yellow velvet gown with massive leg-of-mutton sleeves, and reside in a crumbling, 19th-century hacienda where red clay continuously seeps up through the floorboards.”

According to mathematical models developed by Mendoza, the infection process would not involve aggressive biting or rapid viral decay. Instead, the mutated spore would infect a human host only after they spend several minutes staring intensely into an ornate, gilded mirror while listening to a haunting lullaby played on a broken, mechanical music box.

Mendoza added that secondary transmission would rely almost entirely on dramatic pacing. “If a human were to inhale the spores, they would not transform overnight. They would spend three weeks coughing delicate flecks of blood into a linen handkerchief while lingering near a dimly lit spiral staircase, ignoring clear visual warnings from a glowing, translucent ancestor.”

University of Guadalajara mycologists concur with this assessment, and have reassured the public that despite the rich narrative potential, the real-world probability of a human outbreak remains very low.

“Human biology is simply too warm, our immune systems are too active, and most modern apartments in Guadalajara lack the damp, oppressive Gothic archways necessary for spore incubation,” confirms Inés Santos, one of the researchers who discovered the Guillermo del Toro fungus. “Unless you happen to be keeping a mysterious, lock-bearing trunk hidden beneath your floorboards, the fungus will remain strictly interested in forest ants.”

World.title: Colombia Lifts Glyphosate Ban but Spray Planes Stay Grounded
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Colombia · DRUG POLICY

Key Facts — Instrument Resolution 0006 of 2026 repealed the 2015 order suspending aerial glyphosate spraying.

— Signed Vice-Minister Carlos Gónima Díaz-Granados signed the text on 18 August 2026.

— Not yet The resolution says the repeal does not mean automatic resumption of flights.

— Conditions Environmental plans, prior consultation and a health opinion must all be completed first.

— Coca Colombia had 261,000 hectares of coca at the end of 2024, the United Nations says.

Resolution 0006 of 2026 ends a decade-old prohibition without clearing any aircraft to fly.

Colombia’s National Narcotics Council has repealed the 2015 order that halted aerial glyphosate spraying over coca fields. The repeal does not restart the flights, and several legal conditions remain unmet.

A crop-spraying aircraft. Colombia’s spray programme still needs an environmental permit to fly.

What the government actually changed

Colombia’s National Narcotics Council signed Resolution 0006 of 2026 on 18 August. The text became public on 28 August, after it appeared in the official gazette.

The resolution repeals Resolution 6 of 2015, which suspended spraying with the herbicide nationwide. Carlos Gónima Díaz-Granados, vice-minister for criminal policy and restorative justice, signed the new text.

The council is known in Spanish as the Consejo Nacional de Estupefacientes. It sets national drug policy and governs the eradication programme flown by the police.

The document states plainly that the repeal does not imply automatic resumption of the programme. That single clause is the difference between a headline and an operational change.

The 2015 order that has now gone

Resolution 6 of 2015 was signed on 29 May 2015 by justice minister Yesid Reyes Alvarado. It ordered a nationwide halt to aerial glyphosate spraying over illicit crops.

The trigger was a finding by the cancer agency of the World Health Organization. Its International Agency for Research on Cancer had called glyphosate probably carcinogenic to humans.

A second order followed from the environmental regulator on 30 September 2015. Resolution 1214 suspended the spraying programme itself under the precautionary principle.

Together the two orders grounded the fleet and ended two decades of chemical eradication from the air. Ground application of the herbicide was allowed again from 2016.

Why the aircraft cannot fly yet

The new resolution leaves every judicial and administrative hurdle standing. It removes a prohibition without granting an authorisation, and that difference matters.

Five requirements must be met at the same time before aerial glyphosate spraying can restart. Colombian outlets that have read the text list them consistently.

The environmental regulator must hold an active general environmental management plan for the activity. It must also formally lift the precautionary suspension imposed in 2015.

Each target area then needs its own specific management plan approved before any flight. The council’s technical secretariat must verify that every step has been completed.

The National Institute of Health must also issue a favourable opinion on health risk. Without that opinion the secretariat cannot clear work in any sector.

The conditions the Constitutional Court set

Sentencia T-236 de 2017 is the ruling that shaped this whole debate. It did not ban the practice, but it imposed demanding safeguards on the state.

The court required risk rules written by a body independent of the spraying programme. It also demanded continuous risk evaluation and rigorous, impartial scientific research.

A later ruling, Sentencia T-413 de 2021, added further duties on the government. It called for updated data, evaluation of each target polygon and genuine farmer participation.

Prior consultation with Indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities is compulsory in their territories. That duty flows from Convention 169 of the International Labour Organization, adopted by Law 21 of 1991.

The court has also policed compliance through follow-up orders, among them Auto 387 of 2019. That order stressed voluntary substitution and manual eradication before any return to the air.

Where the environmental licence stands

The National Environmental Licensing Authority, known by its Spanish initials ANLA, holds the file. Its management plan for the programme dates back to Resolution 1065 of 2001.

ANLA modified that plan in April 2021 in a resolution running past 500 pages. The agency said at the time that the general plan by itself authorises nothing.

In September 2025 ANLA tightened the terms again through Resolution 2257. It added farming zones to the exclusion list and lowered permitted herbicide residues in water.

In December 2025 the agency said no new environmental instrument was needed. It is waiting for a calibration and drift study endorsed by an inter-institutional technical committee.

ANLA authorised ground application of the herbicide back in December 2016. A drone based method also exists, but it needs clearance from the same technical committee.

The coca numbers behind the decision

Coca planting is the reason this question keeps returning to the cabinet table. United Nations monitoring counted 261,000 hectares in Colombia at the end of 2024.

That was a rise of 3.5 percent from 253,000 hectares a year earlier. The figure comes from the survey published in June 2026 by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.

The same report left out its usual estimate of potential cocaine output. Its authors cited methodological problems identified during technical reviews in April 2026.

Manual eradication has slowed in recent years and remains dangerous for the teams involved. Supporters present aerial glyphosate spraying as the faster instrument available.

Washington, money and the wider strategy

President Abelardo de la Espriella took office on 7 August 2026 promising to restart fumigation. He spoke of last-generation herbicides rather than of glyphosate itself.

The United States Department of State announced a security package worth US$1 billion around the inauguration. That money still requires approval by the United States Congress.

Washington removed Colombia from its list of fully cooperating countries on 15 September 2025. The decertification was the first in about three decades and stung in Bogotá.

Officials have also floated a pilot using glufosinate ammonium in place of glyphosate. No location or start date for that pilot has been made public.

What to watch next

The first measurable signal will come from the environmental regulator rather than the presidency. Any move to lift the 2015 precautionary suspension would be the real trigger.

The second signal is the prior consultation calendar in the departments where coca concentrates. Those processes are slow and are routinely challenged in the courts.

Legal challenges to Resolution 0006 of 2026 are likely from environmental and farming organisations. None had been formally filed when this account was written.

For investors the practical question is timing rather than principle. A first flight under aerial glyphosate spraying could still be months or years away.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can Colombia spray coca fields with glyphosate from the air now? No. Resolution 0006 of 2026 removes the 2015 prohibition, but aerial glyphosate spraying still needs environmental, health and consultation clearances. What exactly did the government repeal? It repealed Resolution 6 of 2015 of the National Narcotics Council. That order had suspended spraying nationwide after a World Health Organization cancer classification. Which court rulings govern any restart? Sentencia T-236 de 2017 and Sentencia T-413 de 2021 both apply. They require independent risk rules, continuous evaluation, prior consultation and updated evidence.

World.title: Peru Asks Congress for 120-Day Legislative Powers Over Tax and Security
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Peru · POLITICS

Key Facts — Request Peru’s legislative powers bill covers 66 measures and reached Congress on 28 August.

— Duration The government asks for 120 calendar days to issue decrees.

— Growth The finance ministry now projects 3.4% expansion in 2026 and 2027.

— Watchdog The Fiscal Council calls the growth path demanding and the fiscal numbers referential.

— Seats Fuerza Popular holds 41 of 130 deputies and 22 of 60 senators.

A 66-item request lands in a bicameral Congress where the governing party lacks a majority.

Peru’s legislative powers request reached Congress on Friday, 28 August 2026. The bill asks for 120 days to legislate on 66 separate matters.

Peru’s Congress in Lima, which has yet to vote on the 120-day delegation of powers.

What Peru’s legislative powers request contains

Prime Minister Luis Galarreta presented the bill to Congress on Friday, 28 August 2026. The Council of Ministers had approved it the previous day under President Keiko Fujimori.

The text groups 66 separate requests across eight policy areas. They range from citizen security and prisons to taxation, customs, mining, housing and labor rules.

Ministers will defend their own chapters before deputies, and the Senate reviews the text afterwards. Nothing has been granted yet, and no vote has been scheduled.

Delegated powers are a standard Peruvian instrument, not an emergency decree. Congress hands the executive a defined list of subjects for a fixed period.

How long the powers would run

The bill asks for 120 calendar days from the moment any delegation law takes effect. That would carry decree-making authority into late December or early January.

Peru switched to a two-chamber Congress in 2026, after a constitutional reform. A request for Peru’s legislative powers now travels from the Chamber of Deputies to the Senate.

The Senate’s constitution committee has up to 90 working days to report on the bill. Peruvian press reporting points to a decision in the second half of September.

A simple majority carries the bill in the Chamber of Deputies. In the 60-seat Senate, 31 votes are needed to change or reject the text.

The arithmetic in a divided Congress

Fuerza Popular, the president’s party, holds 41 of the 130 seats in the Chamber of Deputies. It holds 22 of the 60 Senate seats, the largest bloc in both chambers.

Neither figure is a majority, so the government needs partners on every chapter. Juntos por el Perú, Renovación Popular and smaller blocs hold the balance.

Delegation bills are often narrowed before approval, with chapters struck out. That makes the tax and interest-rate items the most exposed parts of Peru’s legislative powers package.

Tax, customs and the interest-rate cap

The tax chapter asks for power to simplify Peru’s small-business tax regimes. Finance Minister Elmer Cuba says those schemes are more than thirty years old.

One is the Régimen Único Simplificado, a flat monthly levy for micro traders. Another is the Régimen Especial de Renta, a simplified income tax track.

The government also wants to widen the works-for-taxes mechanism to disaster risk and rural housing. That scheme lets companies build public works and offset the cost against income tax.

A separate item would repeal the ceiling on lending rates set by Law 31143 of 2021. The central bank has estimated that about 500,000 people lost access to credit under the cap.

Peru’s legislative powers request also covers customs and a ban on imports made with forced labor. Officials link that item to a United States tariff increase from 10% to 12.5%.

Security, prisons and El Niño

Interior Minister César Astudillo says the security chapter would place armed forces in prisons and border zones. The package also covers criminal law, the prison system and migration.

Agriculture Minister Marco Vinelli described faster emergency procedures routed through the civil defense agency. That body is the Instituto Nacional de Defensa Civil, known as INDECI.

Peru is preparing for a global El Niño event that forecasters call strong. The framework expects primary sectors, including fishing and farming, to shrink 1.4% this year.

A new growth forecast published the same week

The Ministry of Economy and Finance published its Marco Macroeconómico Multianual for 2027 to 2030 on 28 August. The multiyear macroeconomic framework projects 3.4% growth in 2026 and again in 2027.

That lifts the ministry’s own April projection of 3.2% for both years. It sits just below the 3.5% Minister Elmer Cuba floated in public remarks on 7 August.

For 2028 to 2030 the framework pencils in 4.0% average growth. President Keiko Fujimori‘s platform had promised 5% by 2028 and 6% near the decade’s end.

Private investment carries the forecast, at 10.5% growth in 2026 against 5.5% assumed in April. Mining investment is put above US$7 billion a year, with a pipeline over US$20 billion.

The deficit path runs from 2.2% of gross domestic product in 2025 to 1.8% this year. It then falls to 1.4% in 2027 and 1% from 2028.

What the Fiscal Council actually said

The Consejo Fiscal, Peru’s independent fiscal watchdog, issued its opinion on 28 August. Its press note carries the reference number 03-2026-CF and is signed in Lima.

The council says the framework’s fiscal projections should be treated as referential. The government has announced changes to the fiscal rules, yet the numbers follow the current path.

It calls the growth projections demanding, citing El Niño risk and a smaller mining pipeline. It also warns that delayed project execution could undercut the 4.0% medium-term path.

The council links this year’s revenue surge to high export commodity prices, which can correct abruptly. It says the recent deficit fall is not proof of stronger structural collection.

Its closing line is blunt about design alone not being enough. A better framework, it says, will fail without credible commitment to compliance and sustainability.

Why the fiscal rules are in play

Minister Elmer Cuba said on 7 August that the government is weighing looser fiscal limits. He mentioned lifting the debt ceiling from 30% to 32% of output.

He also floated a 2028 deficit target of 1.2% rather than 1%. Cuba pointed to spending not budgeted for 2026, including El Niño costs and military pensions.

Peru’s legislative powers request does not itself rewrite the fiscal rules. Those changes would come separately, and the council will issue a prior opinion on them.

The 2026 public budget was approved at 257.562 billion soles (US$76.93 billion). That uses 3.348 soles per dollar, the banking system selling rate reported by Peru’s central bank for 27 August 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Congress granted the delegation yet? Not yet, and no vote has been scheduled. The bill reached the Chamber of Deputies on 28 August 2026. What would the 120 days cover? Tax and customs, citizen security, prisons, migration, labor rules, mining, housing and administrative reform. Peru’s legislative powers request lists 66 separate measures. What did the Fiscal Council object to? It called the growth path demanding and the fiscal projections referential. It warned that a commodity-driven revenue rise is not a structural improvement.

World.title: Brazil Court Clears Braskem Extrajudicial Recovery Filing
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Brazil · RESTRUCTURING

Key Facts — Ruling The São Paulo bankruptcy court admitted the Braskem extrajudicial recovery on 28 August 2026.

— Debt About US$10.9 billion of unsecured financial debt sits inside the case.

— Support Creditors holding 39.6 percent of that debt had signed when Braskem filed.

— Deadline A non-extendable 90 day window applies to reach a majority of each class.

— Shield Executions and asset freezes stay suspended for 120 days, minus 60 already used.

The court admitted the Braskem extrajudicial recovery for processing, and a 90 day clock now runs on creditor support.

A São Paulo court has let Braskem’s out-of-court reorganization proceed, shielding the petrochemical group from creditor claims. The 28 August 2026 ruling covers about US$10.9 billion of unsecured financial debt.

A Braskem petrochemical plant. The company filed with 39.6 percent of creditors behind the plan.

What the São Paulo court decided

The 2nd Bankruptcy and Judicial Recovery Court of São Paulo let Braskem’s out-of-court reorganization proceed on 28 August 2026. Braskem confirmed the ruling to the market the same day.

In Portuguese the court is the 2ª Vara de Falências e Recuperações Judiciais da Comarca de São Paulo. The procedure is a recuperação extrajudicial, an out-of-court reorganization run under court supervision.

The decision is a deferimento do processamento, which means the case may now run its course. It is not the homologação, the final court confirmation of the plan itself.

That distinction matters for bondholders and shareholders alike. The case has been admitted, not approved on its merits.

How the case reached the court

Braskem asked the same court for protection on 25 June 2026, before any restructuring plan existed. The judge granted an injunction the next day, freezing executions against the group for 60 days.

That shield was due to run out in late August, which set the timing of everything that followed. The board approved the filing on 24 August 2026 and the petition went in the same day.

The petition covers Braskem itself together with a set of controlled companies. Their obligations were suspended as a block under Brazil’s insolvency law.

Weak petrochemical margins worldwide had squeezed the group’s cash generation for two years. Legacy liabilities tied to the Maceió ground collapse added to the strain.

What Braskem does. Braskem S.A., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the manufacture, sale, import, and export of chemicals, petrochemicals, and fuels in Brazil. The company supplies electricity and other inputs to second-generation producers; sells utilities, such as steam, water, compressed air and industrial gases; industrial services; and engages in the production, supply, and sale…

The debt inside the Braskem extrajudicial recovery

Braskem placed roughly US$10.9 billion of unsecured financial debt inside the proceeding. Brazilian filings and local coverage put the same pile at R$56.29 billion (US$10.82 billion).

Conversions here use the Central Bank of Brazil PTAX venda rate of 5.2005 reais per dollar. That was the official rate for 28 August 2026, the day of the ruling.

The perimeter is financial only, and it covers bonds plus loans from international banks. Supplier invoices, customer contracts and payroll sit outside the case and continue on normal terms.

Bondholders hold roughly two thirds of the affected debt, according to Brazilian market reporting. Foreign banks hold most of the remainder.

Why one third of creditors was enough to start

Brazil’s insolvency statute is Law 11.101 of 2005, reformed in 2020. Article 163 normally demands signatures from creditors holding more than half of each class covered.

A later paragraph of the same article opens a second door. A debtor may file with one third and then has 90 days to reach the majority.

Braskem filed on 24 August 2026 with 39.6 percent of the affected debt already signed. That cleared the one third bar but not the majority the plan finally needs.

The Rio Times reported that creditor tally on 25 August 2026. Citi and Santander, together with two ad hoc bondholder groups, led the early support.

The gap between 39.6 percent and the required majority is the whole story of the next three months. Every percentage point has to be won class by class, not in a single vote.

What the plan would actually do

The framework published so far is deliberately loose. It contemplates longer maturities, a grace period with interest paid in kind, and possible conversion of debt into equity.

No haircut on principal has been announced. Braskem has not confirmed any write-down of face value inside the Braskem extrajudicial recovery.

New money is the sharpest open question. Distressed funds have pushed for a capital injection of up to US$4 billion, which the company has not accepted.

Collateral for creditors and the scale of shareholder dilution also remain unsettled. Those four points are the substance of the negotiation now beginning.

Braskem has said the process is meant to rebuild a sustainable capital structure. It has published no target leverage ratio and no dated schedule for the new terms.

Who controls the company now

Petrobras holds 36.1 percent of Braskem’s total capital and 47 percent of the voting shares. The state oil company confirmed those figures with a new shareholders agreement in April 2026.

Novonor, the former Odebrecht group, agreed to hand its controlling block to the manager IG4 Capital. Brazil’s antitrust authority cleared that transfer without restrictions earlier in 2026.

The buyer is a credit fund managed by IG4 Capital, which absorbed about R$20 billion (US$3.85 billion) of Novonor bank debt. Petrobras and IG4 Capital are set to share control of the board.

Shared control makes any debt for equity swap a negotiation between two owners rather than one. That raises the political stakes of the Braskem extrajudicial recovery.

The 90 day clock and the fallback

Braskem must now show the court a majority of each affected class within 90 days. The statute describes that window as non-extendable.

Missing it would end the out-of-court route without confirmation of any plan. Brazilian analysts read a full judicial reorganization, the heavier recuperação judicial, as the fallback.

The 120 day stay is shorter in practice than it sounds. Sixty of those days were already consumed by an injunction granted on 26 June 2026.

Dissenting creditors may still challenge the ruling through Brazil’s interlocutory appeal, the agravo de instrumento. Such a challenge would not by itself stop the case from running.

What investors in Brazil should watch

Braskem’s preferred shares traded at R$4.37 (US$0.84) on 28 August 2026, up 3.55 percent. The market read the ruling as procedural relief rather than a cure.

Cash flow remains the binding constraint for the resin maker. Petrobras extended a commercial credit line worth R$2.35 billion (US$452 million) for feedstock purchases through 31 December 2026.

Legacy liabilities sit outside the financial perimeter of this proceeding. Brazil’s federal public defender’s office filed a fresh claim over the Maceió salt mine collapse in August 2026.

Those environmental claims are not restructured by the current case. Investors should read the case as a financing fix with a separate liability tail.

The next hard date is the close of the 90 day window for creditor signatures. Until then the Braskem extrajudicial recovery is a negotiation with a court stamp, not a settled outcome.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly did the São Paulo court approve? It allowed the case to be processed, not the plan itself. Final confirmation still requires a majority of each affected creditor class. Does the case affect Braskem’s suppliers and customers? No, the proceeding covers only unsecured financial debt. Trade payables, customer contracts and wages continue on their normal terms. What happens if creditors never reach a majority? The Braskem extrajudicial recovery would lapse and the creditor shield would fall away. A full judicial reorganization under the same law is the usual next step.

World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Key Facts — The Ibovespa, Brazil’s main stock index closed at 175,665 points, up 0.30% — an eighth straight gain.

— The real, Brazil’s currency weakened 0.67% to 5.1965 per US dollar.

— Petrobras shares, PETR4 and PETR3 each rose 2.0% and led the index higher.

— Negative breadth meant more stocks fell than rose, even as heavyweight oil shares carried the index higher.

— The index remains about 12% below its record close of 198,657 points, set on April 14.

Today’s Focus Brazil’s stock market extended its winning streak on Friday, with the Ibovespa index adding 0.30% to close at 175,665 points. The gain came despite more shares falling than rising on the São Paulo exchange. Petrobras — the state-controlled oil giant — did the heavy lifting. Its common and preferred shares each rose 2.0% and led the index’s advance. The real weakened against the dollar, closing at 5.1965. The fate of a 12% crude-oil export tax — suspended by a federal court on Thursday, then extended by the government hours later — kept oil producers and the currency in focus. Homebuilders and retailers struggled, with MRV falling 5.1% and Magazine Luiza down 4.6%. What matters today. A narrow advance led by Petrobras masked broader weakness, with interest-rate and political uncertainty continuing to steer domestic sectors.

São Paulo, home of the B3 exchange where the Ibovespa trades. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

01 The session in one read

The Ibovespa — Brazil’s main stock index, which tracks the largest listed companies — closed Friday’s session at 175,665 points, up 0.30%. That was an eighth consecutive gain and left the benchmark about 12% below its record close of 198,657, set on April 14.

The advance was narrower than the headline number suggests. Trading data showed negative breadth, meaning more stocks fell than rose, while a handful of heavyweights — led by Petrobras — carried the index into positive ground.

On currency desks, the real — Brazil’s currency — weakened 0.46% against the US dollar, closing at 5.1965 reais per dollar after touching 5.2308 earlier in the day. The move left the currency about 1% weaker on the week, tracking a firmer dollar globally.

Oil traders spent the session digesting a fast-moving legal fight over the 12% tax on crude-oil exports. A federal court ordered the levy suspended on Thursday, and the government responded within hours by extending it to November 6 — leaving the tax in limbo and Petrobras shares higher.

Assessment — Petrobras masks an uneasy market MEDIUM The session’s positive close tells only part of the story. Negative breadth and sharp falls in rate-sensitive homebuilders and retailers suggest underlying caution, even as export-linked heavyweights buoy the headline index. The court-ordered suspension of the oil-export tax — and the government’s rapid counter-move — is a concrete, verified catalyst behind Petrobras strength. The variable to watch is whether oil-sector gains continue to paper over weakness in consumer and construction names in coming sessions.

03 Why it moved — an oil tax in limbo and a wary market

The session’s clearest theme was the legal battle over the 12% tax on crude-oil exports. The levy was created by a provisional measure in March and re-imposed on July 10 by Camex, the government’s foreign-trade chamber, after that measure lapsed.

On Thursday a federal court ordered the tax suspended, siding with producers who argued the levy was legally flawed. Hours later the government extended the tax to November 6, leaving its status unresolved — a standoff that kept oil shares bid through Friday’s close.

Petrobras, Brazil’s dominant crude exporter, gained the most from the uncertainty lifting in its favor. Its preferred shares (PETR4) rose 2.0% to R$43.55 (US$8.38) (US$8.38) and its common shares (PETR3) also added 2.0%, closing at R$48.25 (US$9.28) (US$9.28).

Beyond oil, the market looked uneasy. Falls in homebuilders such as MRV (−5.1%) and retailers such as Magazine Luiza (−4.6%) pointed to concern about domestic interest rates, which remain high by international standards.

Politics added a layer of noise. The most recent Vox Brasil poll, fielded July 26 to 28, put President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s disapproval at 50.3% against 48.9% approval.

The gap sits within the survey’s 2.15-point margin of error.

04 The day’s movers
