Petrobras set the tone, with both share lines up 2.0% as the oil-export tax fight turned in producers’ favor. Exchange operator B3 and Santander Brasil also posted solid gains.

At the other end, homebuilder MRV slumped 5.1% while retailer Magazine Luiza lost 4.6%. Both are sensitive to borrowing costs, reflecting investor caution about the interest-rate outlook.

05 The regional scoreboard

Index Country Change Ibovespa Brazil +0.30% IPC Mexico −0.53% IPSA Chile −0.22% Merval Argentina −0.72% COLCAP Colombia −1.28%

Brazil stood alone in the region’s positive column. The Ibovespa gained 0.30%, while Mexico’s IPC fell 0.53% and Chile’s IPSA slipped 0.22%.

Argentina’s Merval dropped 0.72%, and Colombia’s COLCAP was the region’s weakest, down 1.28%.

06 The technical picture

The Ibovespa’s session range ran from 173,894 to 176,421, with the close of 175,665 near the upper end of the daily band. The benchmark opened at 175,137, just above Thursday’s close near 175,135.

At 175,665 points, the index is about 12% below its record close of 198,657, set on April 14. An eighth straight daily gain has put that record back on traders’ radar.

Traders will be watching whether the index can hold above the mid-170,000s, a level that has repeatedly marked near-term resistance. The week’s steady grind higher suggests buyers are active, but the narrow breadth warrants caution.

07 What to watch

Oil-export tax case: Whether Thursday’s court-ordered suspension survives the government’s move to extend the levy to November 6 — a decision that directly affects Petrobras earnings and government revenue.

Whether Thursday’s court-ordered suspension survives the government’s move to extend the levy to November 6 — a decision that directly affects Petrobras earnings and government revenue. Selic interest-rate path: Brazil’s benchmark rate guides borrowing costs for homebuilders and retailers, the session’s biggest losers.

Brazil’s benchmark rate guides borrowing costs for homebuilders and retailers, the session’s biggest losers. US dollar strength: A firmer dollar pushed the real to 5.1965; sustained strength could weigh on Brazilian assets.

Background: Brazil Markets Rise as Court Halts Oil Export Tax.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Ibovespa?

The Ibovespa is Brazil’s main stock index, tracking the largest and most-traded companies listed on the B3 exchange in São Paulo.

Why did Petrobras rise on August 28?

A federal court ordered the 12% tax on crude-oil exports suspended on August 27, though the government moved hours later to extend the levy. Petrobras shares rose 2.0% as the case turned in producers’ favor.

What does a weaker real mean?

A weaker real means it takes more reais to buy one US dollar — on August 28 the rate closed at 5.1965. This can help exporters but raises the cost of imports and inflation.

Why did homebuilders and retailers fall?

Companies like MRV and Magazine Luiza are sensitive to high interest rates, which raise borrowing costs for consumers and developers. Investor caution about Brazil’s rate outlook weighed on them.

World.content:
Weekly Edition · Saturday, August 29, 2026 · Issue #19

The Latin America Defense Monitor: military moves, arms deals and security policy across Latin America and the Caribbean, in plain language

Executive Summary The Big Picture: This week’s Latin America Defense Monitor opens in Colombia, where the new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, turned three weeks of promises into action. On Thursday the air force bombed camps of the FARC-dissident faction run by alias “Calarcá” in the southern department of Guaviare — Operation AMÓN — killing at least eight fighters in a strike led by Kfir jets and Super Tucano turboprops, followed by commandos on the ground. It is the second airstrike since he took office on August 7, and part of a first-100-days plan built around 15 “beta operations” against armed-group leadership. The week before, De la Espriella had flown to Panama City to sign Colombia up to the Shield of the Americas, the US-led security alliance pushed by Donald Trump — and named a brand-new military high command to run the offensive, recalling a general that Gustavo Petro had pushed out. Washington is now talking about joint US–Colombian military operations and a proposed $1 billion assistance package. Elsewhere, the US military used a high-energy laser for the first time in anger on the Mexican border, burning three cartel drones out of the sky over the Rio Grande Valley. An Ecuadorian official confirmed US Special Forces are operating inside Ecuador, with two US warships on the way. A US aircraft carrier moved into the Caribbean near Venezuela, and another suspected drug boat was hit at sea, killing four. And in Argentina, the combined exercise Fraterno XXXIX with Brazil ended with an open sales pitch: Brazil parked its brand-new Tamandaré frigate and Riachuelo-class submarine at Mar del Plata and invited the Argentine Navy to shop. The Bottom Line Up Front: The region’s center of gravity has shifted to Colombia. The De la Espriella government is fighting armed groups with airstrikes, a fresh high command, a US alliance, and the prospect of a billion dollars of American help — all within its first month. The laser shootdowns in Texas mark a real first: directed-energy weapons are now an operational tool in the cartel fight, not a test. Ecuador’s confirmation of US boots on the ground makes the American military footprint in the region the deepest it has been in decades. And Brazil’s quiet showroom visit to Mar del Plata shows the region’s biggest defense industry chasing its biggest potential customer.

Latin America Defense Monitor: Where Things Stand

Country Status What’s Happening Colombia High Operation AMÓN airstrike in Guaviare kills 8+ fighters of Calarcá’s FARC-dissident bloc; second strike of the new government; 15 “beta operations” planned for the first 100 days; new high command named; joins the Shield of the Americas. US–Mexico border High US Army uses a high-energy laser operationally for the first time, downing three “cartel-linked” drones in the Rio Grande Valley; Sheinbaum warns over sovereignty. Ecuador Elevated Official confirms US Special Forces are operating inside the country; two US warships arriving to support anti-cartel campaigns. Caribbean / Venezuela Elevated US carrier arrives in the Caribbean in a buildup near Venezuela; another boat strike kills four, taking the campaign’s reported toll past 195. Argentina / Brazil Active Fraterno XXXIX combined exercise concludes; Brazil showcases the Tamandaré frigate and Humaitá submarine at Mar del Plata as candidates to renew Argentina’s fleet. Bolivia Watch Political tension around President Paz’s inner circle; a March photo with Rubio at the Escudo summit resurfaces in a domestic scandal.

01 The Week’s Key Stories Aug 22–29, 2026

COLOMBIA 1. New government bombs Calarcá’s camps in Guaviare, its second airstrike in three weeks President Abelardo de la Espriella announced Thursday that the armed forces carried out Operation AMÓN in the early hours against camps of the Jorge Suárez Briceño Bloc — the FARC-dissident structure commanded by alias Calarcá — in rural El Retorno, Guaviare. Initial reports put the dead at eight or more. Troops seized over a dozen rifles and five machine guns. The operation, run by the Joint Special Operations Command, opened with a precision aerial bombardment by five Kfir fighter jets and six Super Tucano aircraft, followed by a commando assault. Troops remain in the area and the offensive is continuing. The target matters. Calarcá’s Estado Mayor de Bloques y Frentes is fighting a territorial war against Iván Mordisco’s rival dissident faction across Meta and Guaviare — a fight that, according to the military, includes the forced “registration” (carnetización) of rural civilians. It was precisely General Erik Rodríguez Aparicio’s public warnings about that practice that got him pushed aside by Petro. De la Espriella has now brought him back as commander-general of the armed forces. What it means: This is the new government’s theory of victory in miniature: air power first, special forces second, territory held after. Two airstrikes in three weeks matches the campaign promise of a 90-day shock plan to kill or capture ten top commanders. The choice of Calarcá as the first big target is deliberate — he is the dissident leader most associated with coercing civilians during the election. The risks are just as clear: Guaviare is contested by two armed groups, civilians are trapped between them, and every airstrike in Colombia carries the memory of past bombings that killed minors. The government is betting that speed and precision will hold public support. Watch the human-rights scrutiny.

COLOMBIA 2. A new high command, a new alliance — and $1 billion of US help on the table Days before the strike, De la Espriella stood in Barranquilla and presented his complete new military leadership. General Erik Rodríguez Aparicio — 35 years of service, removed under Petro after flagging forced civilian registration in Meta and Guaviare — returns as commander of the armed forces, with the confidence of Defense Minister (retired general) Jorge Mora. The appointment followed Colombia’s formal adhesion to the Shield of the Americas at a ceremony in Panama City — the US-championed security bloc launched at the Doral summit in March. According to reporting by Finance Colombia, the government still owes the public a full explanation of three US announcements: joint US–Colombian military operations, the Escudo membership itself, and a proposed $1 billion US assistance package. Not everyone is on board. A Medellín judge is reviewing the legality of Colombia’s foreign military operations — an early sign that the courts intend to watch how far the alliance goes. What it means: Colombia is pivoting, fast, from Petro’s “total peace” negotiations to a Washington-anchored war footing. The Escudo gives De la Espriella money, hardware and political cover; it gives Trump a flagship ally in the hemisphere’s oldest drug war. The open questions are the terms: what do “joint operations” mean for Colombian sovereignty, what conditions come with the billion dollars, and whether the Medellín court review — or Congress — slows any of it down. Fifty years of Plan Colombia history says the money arrives faster than the accountability.

US–MEXICO BORDER 3. A laser weapon downs three cartel drones — a first for the US military Late Tuesday and early Wednesday, Joint Task Force–Southern Border used the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser (AMP-HEL) — a system developed by AeroVironment — to shoot down three drones it said were operated by Mexican cartels in the Rio Grande Valley. NORAD and US Northern Command confirmed it Thursday. Officials called the drones “hostile,” said they posed a physical threat to troops and Border Patrol agents, and declined to say whether the engagements happened over US or Mexican soil. “Cartel networks are increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human-smuggling and actively spy on our personnel,” said task-force commander Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor, who thanked Mexico’s government and military for their cooperation. It is the first confirmed operational use of a directed-energy weapon in the US cartel fight — and a redemption story of sorts. In February and March, the same laser family caused chaos: CBP zapped what turned out to be Mylar balloons near El Paso, soldiers shot down a CBP drone near Fort Hancock, and the FAA twice closed Texas airspace. A Pentagon–FAA safety agreement followed. This week, the system worked as advertised. Separately, JIATF-401 last month awarded CACI up to $500 million for the SkyValor jammer. What it means: The counter-drone war on the border has gone from experiment to doctrine. Hundreds of drones cross near the border daily; lasers and jammers are now the standing answer. Two things to watch: the sovereignty question — President Sheinbaum has called any unilateral US action on Mexican soil a grave breach, and the military pointedly won’t say where the drones were when they were hit — and escalation, as cartels adapt with cheaper, more numerous drones. The border is now the live-fire test range for the technology every military in the region will want.

ECUADOR 4. US Special Forces confirmed operating inside Ecuador, warships en route Ecuadorian officials confirmed this week that American special-operations soldiers are working inside the country in the fight against cartels, and that two US warships are arriving to support military campaigns (Task & Purpose, Aug 25). The confirmation formalizes what had been visible for months: Ecuador, whose port cities have become some of the most violent places on earth as cocaine routes shifted to the Pacific, is now the most forward-leaning US security partner on South America’s west coast. What it means: With Colombia’s Escudo membership, US forces in Ecuador, a carrier group in the Caribbean and a laser-armed task force on the Mexican border, the US military posture in Latin America is now the deepest since the Cold War — built around cartels and migration rather than communism. For President Noboa, US boots deliver capability his forces lack; they also hand his opponents a sovereignty argument. The practical test will be whether joint operations dent the flow of cocaine through Guayaquil — and whether any US casualty in Ecuador changes the politics overnight.

CARIBBEAN 5. Carrier in, another boat destroyed — the campaign at sea grinds on A US aircraft carrier arrived in the Caribbean this week in what Defense News described as a buildup near Venezuela, replacing the long-deployed USS Abraham Lincoln — which, after a record nine months at sea, was relieved in the Middle East and is heading home via a historic port call in Thailand. On Wednesday, the US military struck another boat it said was smuggling drugs in the Caribbean, killing four — the latest in a campaign whose reported death toll passed 190 in July and keeps climbing. The strikes continue even as, inside Venezuela, high-stakes political negotiations proceed under the new government. What it means: Two tracks, one theater: warships and lethal strikes offshore, diplomacy ashore. The carrier adds visible pressure while Washington negotiates with Caracas — a familiar combination, but a volatile one, especially with the region’s governments split between Escudo members and skeptics. Peru’s July proposal for a shared, regionally commanded anti-drug fleet — raised at the Cusco ministers’ meeting — remains the standing alternative: same target, different chain of command.

ARGENTINA / BRAZIL 6. Fraterno ends with a Brazilian showroom at Mar del Plata The combined Argentina–Brazil exercise Fraterno XXXIX wrapped up with a notable port call: the frigate Tamandaré (F200) — the most modern surface warship built in South America — and the submarine Humaitá (S-41), second of the Riachuelo class, docked at Mar del Plata and opened their hatches to the Argentine Navy. Brazil’s naval-projects agency EMGEPRON briefed Argentine commanders on the MEKO A-100/Tamandaré program (built with TKMS, Embraer and Atech) and on PROSUB, the submarine program developed with France’s Naval Group. The context is plain: Argentina’s MEKO 360 destroyers are down to three tired hulls, its submarine force needs replacing, and Argentina has been evaluating the Scorpene design that underpins the Riachuelo class — including a letter of intent with Naval Group. What it means: This is Brazil’s defense industry making its move at exactly the right moment. Argentina’s fleet renewal is inevitable; the only questions are money and supplier. Brazil offers regional supply chains, no Washington strings, and kit designed for South Atlantic conditions. If Argentina buys Brazilian frigates or submarines, it would be the biggest intra-regional arms deal in South American history — and would make Brazil, not the US or Europe, the southern cone’s arsenal. Financing and political will remain the obstacles, as they have for a decade of similar courtships.

PERU 7. Lockheed offers Peru a $1.8bn sweetener for its F-16s Lockheed Martin has proposed an industrial and social partnership package worth $1.8 billion to Peru, attached to its F-16 Block 70 offer (Airforce Technology, Aug 29). The bid lands three months after Peru’s fighter scandal — the $3.5 billion deal signed in April without the president’s knowledge, $462 million already paid, still under congressional investigation — poisoned the procurement well. What it means: After the April debacle, no Peruvian government can sign a jet deal in the dark. Lockheed’s answer is to make the offer about more than jets — industrial offsets and social spending that a new administration can defend in public. Peru still needs fighters, and the competition (Gripen, F-16, others) will now be fought on transparency and offsets rather than quiet signatures. Whichever way Lima goes, the scandal has permanently raised the bar for arms deals across the region.

02 What’s Being Bought

Country The Deal Where It Stands Why It Matters Peru F-16 Block 70 + $1.8bn industrial/social package (Lockheed) Proposed Aug 29 Post-scandal reset of the region’s most troubled procurement Argentina Frigates & submarines (Brazil’s Tamandaré / Riachuelo among candidates) Brazil pitching after Fraterno XXXIX Would be the biggest intra-South American arms deal ever Colombia $1bn US assistance package under the Shield of the Americas Announced; terms unexplained Funds the new offensive; sovereignty terms unclear Colombia Petro-era $12bn plan (17 Gripens, helicopters, boats, vehicles, rifles) Gripen survives; rest under new-government review Successor government inherits — or trims — the region’s biggest buy US (border) AMP-HEL lasers + $500m SkyValor jammer (CACI) Laser now operational; contract awarded July Counter-drone kit the whole region will copy Ecuador US security assistance, Special Forces presence Confirmed this week Deepest US footprint on the Pacific coast in decades

03 The Big Powers

United States The week’s through-line. Lasers on the Mexican border, special forces in Ecuador, a carrier in the Caribbean, another boat strike, the Escudo alliance growing, a $1bn package for Colombia, and Lockheed pitching Peru. Washington’s hemispheric posture is now organized, funded and kinetic — and increasingly the framework every regional defense decision is made inside. Brazil Playing a different game: industrial statecraft. While the US sells security, Brazil sells ships. The Mar del Plata showroom was aimed at Argentina but broadcast to every navy in the region — buy from the neighborhood, keep the value chain at home. Brazil is at last building its own warships. Now it wants to export them. France Naval Group remains the quiet winner behind Brazil’s submarine success — and holds a letter of intent with Argentina. If Buenos Aires picks Scorpenes built under a PROSUB-style arrangement, French design DNA will sit in both of South America’s southern fleets. China / Russia No direct moves this week. Russia’s exit from the regional market, sealed when Colombia moved to replace its Russian helicopters, stands. China’s footprint stays commercial — trade and drones — while the security architecture hardens around US and regional suppliers.

04 What to Watch Next 7–30 Days

COLOMBIA The next “beta operations” after Guaviare; casualty and civilian-harm reporting from AMÓN; the Medellín court’s review of foreign military operations; terms of the $1bn US package; what the new government keeps of Petro’s $12bn plan. MEXICO Sheinbaum’s response to the laser engagements — especially any evidence they occurred over Mexican territory; cartel adaptation with more, cheaper drones. ECUADOR Arrival of the two US warships; the first joint operation made public; domestic political reaction. CARIBBEAN Carrier-group movements near Venezuela; the boat-strike tempo against the backdrop of negotiations with Caracas; any regional push for the Peruvian shared-fleet alternative. ARGENTINA Whether the Brazilian pitch turns into a formal requirement or tender; progress on the submarine decision and the Naval Group letter of intent. PERU Congressional findings on the April F-16 scandal; competing bids answering Lockheed’s $1.8bn package.

05 The Bottom Line

Three weeks into a new Colombian government, the hemisphere’s security map has been redrawn at speed. Colombia is bombing again — with a new high command, a new alliance and American money on the way. Ecuador has US soldiers inside its borders. The US is burning drones out of the Texas sky with a laser and sinking boats in the Caribbean, with a carrier on station to make sure everyone notices. Meanwhile, at a naval base in Mar del Plata, Brazil opened the doors of its newest frigate and submarine and quietly asked Argentina: why buy from Washington, Paris or Berlin when the neighbor builds them? That is the split running through this edition of the Latin America Defense Monitor: the US is selling protection, Brazil is selling products, and everyone else is choosing a cart. Colombia chose the US track — airstrikes, alliance, assistance. Argentina is being courted down the industrial track. Peru is discovering that after a scandal, even fighter jets must be sold with schools and factories attached. The risks stack up in the same places as always. Airstrikes in Guaviare will be measured by what happens to the civilians Calarcá was registering by force. The laser shootdowns will be measured by whether they stay north of the border line. The Escudo will be measured by its terms, not its ceremonies. Six countries flew together over the Atacama in July to prove the region’s air forces could cooperate. This week showed what they’re organizing against — and who gets to lead the fight. For now, the answer, from the Rio Grande to Guaviare, is Washington.

World.title: Mexico ‘Is Doing Very Well’, Sheinbaum Says Before Second Report as Public Investment Jumps 62.6%
World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

MEXICO · POLITICS

Key Facts —The message: “Mexico is doing very well and I am very optimistic,” Sheinbaum said days before her second report. —The date: The Segundo Informe is set for 1 September, closing a tour of states that ends at the Zócalo. —Investment: Public physical investment jumped 62.6 percent in July, according to the finance ministry’s monthly report. —Debt costs: Hacienda says the public sector’s financial cost fell 4.8 percent year on year. —The economy: The government cites record foreign investment, rising GDP and a peso near 16.97 per dollar. —The catch: The quoted numbers are July figures, and the real budget test arrives with September’s 2027 package.

Claudia Sheinbaum says Mexico is doing very well as she prepares her second annual report on 1 September. Fresh finance ministry figures hand her one striking number: public investment jumped 62.6 percent in July.

What the president said before the report

“Mexico is doing very well and I am very optimistic,” Sheinbaum said this week, according to Milenio and Excélsior. She spoke days before delivering her Segundo Informe de Gobierno on 1 September.

The president framed the report around the economy, quality of life and falling violence. A Cadena RASA survey reported her approval at 68.4 percent going into the address.

Preparations for the address have run all week, Unomásuno reported. City media even flagged changed Metro hours for 1 September, El Heraldo de México said.

The president has turned the report into a travelling exercise in accountability. Her tour of the states ends with a closing event at Mexico City’s Zócalo, El Financiero reported.

The July number behind the optimism

The standout statistic comes from the finance ministry’s July public finances report. Public physical investment, the spending that builds infrastructure, grew 62.6 percent, La Silla Rota reported.

La Silla Rota said the acceleration covers budgeted infrastructure programmes across the federal government. The ministry publishes the figures in its monthly public finances release.

That is the kind of figure Sheinbaum needs for her argument. Her government has promised visible works after years in which budget pressure squeezed capital spending.

Infrastructure outlays of that size also matter for growth. Construction crews and suppliers feel them within months, long before the projects themselves open.

Debt costs and the peso

Hacienda also reported that the public sector’s financial cost fell 4.8 percent year on year, according to La Jornada. Cheaper debt service frees room in the budget for programmes and works.

The same reporting cycle showed oil income recovering, Energy21 noted this week. That rebound has helped the treasury after a weak start to the year.

The government has also pointed to record foreign direct investment, rising GDP and a strong currency. Vanguardia put the peso near 16.97 per dollar this week.

A firm peso helps importers and holds down fuel prices. It squeezes exporters and remittance recipients, whose dollars now buy fewer pesos than a year ago.

The politics of a second informe

Mexico’s constitution requires the president to report to Congress at the start of each September. It will be her second such address in a six-year term.

Her party’s majorities in Congress mean the report will face ritual criticism rather than a real challenge. The substantive argument will come over the budget.

The opposition will contest the rosy reading, above all on security and public finances. The government answers with the approval polls and the July investment figure.

The state tour has doubled as a campaign-style showcase for local projects. Each stop let the president read out works and spending by state before the national audience.

What to watch from here

The first test is the 1 September ceremony itself at the Zócalo. The tone the president strikes there will set up the budget fight that follows.

The second is the 2027 budget package, due in September. It must show how a 62.6 percent investment jump squares with the deficit path the ministry has promised.

The third is whether the investment pace holds beyond July. For markets, a second strong month in August would turn a headline into a trend.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Sheinbaum’s second government report? On 1 September, closing a tour of the states that ends at Mexico City’s Zócalo. It is her second annual report of a six-year term. What did Sheinbaum say about Mexico’s situation? “Mexico is doing very well and I am very optimistic,” she said days before the report. She cited the economy, quality of life and falling violence. How much did public investment grow in July? Public physical investment rose 62.6 percent, according to the finance ministry’s July report, as reported by La Silla Rota. What is happening with Mexico’s debt costs? Hacienda reported the public sector’s financial cost fell 4.8 percent year on year, according to La Jornada. How popular is the president going into the report? A Cadena RASA survey put her approval at 68.4 percent in the days before the second informe.

World.title: A New Fund Wants Pension Money to Build Nigeria’s Infrastructure
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

NIGERIA · INVESTMENT

Key Facts —The vehicle: AFC Capital Partners has launched the Infrastructure Climate-Resilient Fund Nigeria, registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as a closed-end fund. —Where it sits: The Nigerian vehicle’s own target size has not been disclosed. It feeds into AFC’s wider US$750 million Infrastructure Climate-Resilient Fund. —First-loss money: The Green Climate Fund has committed US$253 million as a first-loss investor in the wider fund, with the European Investment Bank putting in US$52.48 million. —The ambition: AFC expects the US$750 million platform to mobilise up to US$3.7 billion across 10 to 12 projects. —The target investors: Nigerian pension fund administrators, insurers and asset managers, alongside the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority and development banks. —The problem it addresses: Pension industry data cited at the launch put 58.07% of Nigerian pension assets in federal government securities at the end of March 2026, against 3.95% in alternatives and real estate.

A new Nigeria infrastructure fund launched by Africa Finance Corporation is designed to pull domestic pension and insurance money into roads, power and digital assets. The Green Climate Fund has committed US$253 million as first-loss capital to the wider platform it feeds.

What the Nigeria infrastructure fund is, in plain terms

AFC Capital Partners, the asset-management arm of Africa Finance Corporation, announced the Infrastructure Climate-Resilient Fund Nigeria in Lagos on 24 August. It is registered with Nigeria’s Securities and Exchange Commission as a closed-end fund, meaning investors commit to a fixed pool for the fund’s life rather than moving money in and out daily.

The Nigerian vehicle is a feeder into a larger pool. That parent fund, the Infrastructure Climate-Resilient Fund, is sized at US$750 million; the size of the Nigerian feeder itself has not been disclosed.

The structure targets renewable energy, transport and logistics, digital infrastructure and industrial development. AFC expects the platform to mobilise up to US$3.7 billion across 10 to 12 projects.

The concessional money that makes it work

Blended finance lives or dies on who takes the first loss. Here that role falls to the Green Climate Fund, which committed US$253 million to the wider fund in 2023, its largest equity investment in Africa to date.

The European Investment Bank committed US$52.48 million in 2025. The Development Bank of Southern Africa, Italy’s Cassa Depositi e Prestiti and the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority are also named as participants.

First-loss capital is what allows a pension trustee to look at an infrastructure project without breaching a conservative mandate. It absorbs the earliest write-downs so that senior investors sit further from the risk.

Why Nigerian pension money is the real target

Nigeria’s pension industry is large, growing and overwhelmingly invested in government paper. Figures cited at the launch, from the National Pension Commission, put 58.07% of pension assets in federal government securities at the end of March 2026.

Alternatives and real estate accounted for 3.95% of the same pool, and the regulator’s own data show barely 1% sitting in infrastructure funds. That gap is the commercial thesis behind the fund.

AFC president and chief executive Samaila Zubairu said Africa holds more than US$4 trillion in domestic resources. The argument is that the continent’s savings, not only foreign money, should be building its assets.

ACP chief executive Ayaan Adam framed the Nigerian platform as a dedicated route for the country’s institutional investors into climate-resilient projects at home and across Africa. Her firm is licensed by the Nigerian SEC as a fund manager, which is what allows it to take pension money at all.

What it says about the wider financing picture

Foreign direct investment into African infrastructure has been thin and expensive since global rates rose. Sovereign borrowing costs have made the alternative unattractive too.

That pushes governments and development banks towards local institutional pools. Nigeria, South Africa, Kenya and Morocco all have pension systems big enough to matter.

The same logic is familiar to readers of our Latin American coverage. Chile, Peru, Colombia and Mexico spent two decades arguing about how much of their pension savings should sit in local infrastructure.

Chile’s funds were the pioneers, and their exposure to domestic infrastructure became a template studied across emerging markets. The argument there has since turned to whether that concentration served savers well.

Nigerian trustees will face the same question. Higher returns from infrastructure come with illiquidity that a pension book has to be able to carry through a bad decade.

The questions the announcement does not answer

The size of the Nigerian feeder fund itself has not been disclosed. Nor has the split between naira and dollar commitments, which matters a great deal in a country with Nigeria’s currency history.

No first close has been announced and no anchor Nigerian pension fund administrator has been named publicly. The 10 to 12 projects are described by sector rather than by name.

None of that makes the launch unserious, and the concessional commitments are concrete. It does mean the test is the first close, not the press conference.

Readers should also note that this is a fund launch, not a completed transaction. Figures come from the corporation and the outlets that covered the Lagos event.

Africa Finance Corporation is a multilateral development institution headquartered in Lagos, with African sovereign and institutional shareholders. It is not a commercial bank, and its own balance sheet is not the fund’s.

That distinction is worth keeping in view when reading the headline numbers. The concessional layer, rather than the corporation’s own capital, is what changes the risk profile for a pension investor.

Frequently asked questions

What is the new Nigeria infrastructure fund? It is the Infrastructure Climate-Resilient Fund Nigeria, launched by AFC Capital Partners and registered with Nigeria’s SEC as a closed-end fund. Its own size is undisclosed; it feeds into a wider US$750 million platform. Who is providing the concessional capital? The Green Climate Fund has committed US$253 million as a first-loss investor and the European Investment Bank US$52.48 million. Other named participants include the Development Bank of Southern Africa and the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority. Why is it aimed at pension funds? Figures cited at the launch put 58.07% of Nigerian pension assets in federal government securities at the end of March 2026, against 3.95% in alternatives and real estate. The fund is designed to move some of that money into infrastructure. How much investment could it mobilise? AFC expects the US$750 million platform to mobilise up to US$3.7 billion across 10 to 12 projects. The size of the Nigerian feeder fund itself has not been disclosed.

World.title: Latin America Steel Falls: SLX, Gerdau, CSN, Ternium Drop
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Key Facts — The steel fund SLX fell 0.95% to US$108.69 marking a down day for the sector as investors weighed tariff shields against weak construction demand.

— Gerdau’s New York shares slid 2.34% to US$4.59 giving back part of Thursday’s strong gain on Friday, August 28, 2026.

— CSN’s New York shares dropped 3.77% to US$1.02 the steepest fall among the region’s major listed steel names.

— Ternium, the Luxembourg-domiciled group whose largest operating market is Mexico, fell 1.77% to US$54.84 even with Mexico’s layered duties on Chinese steel.

— Brazil’s 25% above-quota tariff was renewed on May 29, 2026 yet Chinese material covers about 18% of Latin America’s steel consumption.

— Mexico added provisional anti-dumping duties on hot-rolled steel from China and Vietnam on March 23, 2026 on top of duties of up to 50% on some Chinese goods.

Today’s Focus Latin American steel shares fell across the board on Friday, August 28, 2026. The steel fund SLX lost 0.95% to US$108.69, with Gerdau down 2.34% to US$4.59, CSN off 3.77% to US$1.02 and Ternium 1.77% lower at US$54.84. The pressure comes from a familiar dynamic: cheap Chinese steel keeps arriving in Latin America despite tariff walls. Regional steel lobby Alacero puts imports at 39.7% of the region’s apparent steel consumption, with China supplying 13.2 million tonnes, about 18% of the total. Brazil shields its mills with a 25% tariff on above-quota imports, a regime extended in May for 12 months. Mexico stacks duties of up to 50% on some Chinese goods and provisional anti-dumping levies on hot-rolled steel from China and Vietnam. What matters today. Tariffs are slowing but not stopping Chinese steel, and weak construction demand in Brazil is keeping a lid on domestic producers.

The Aperam steel plant in Timóteo, Minas Gerais, one of Brazil’s major stainless steel producers. (Photo: HVL, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0)

01 The session in one read

Steel shares in Brazil and Mexico ended lower on Friday, August 28, 2026, in a session dominated by a firmer dollar. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivered a hawkish Jackson Hole address, the dollar index rose about 0.5% and gold fell 3.1% to about US$4,456, pulling the wider commodity complex down with it.

The steel fund SLX fell 0.95% to US$108.69.

Gerdau’s New York shares dropped 2.34% to US$4.59, CSN lost 3.77% to US$1.02, and Ternium slipped 1.77% to US$54.84. The moves put the whole Latin American steel complex in the red for the session.

Assessment — Tariff shields cannot rescue weak construction MEDIUM The sector’s decline on August 28 was driven mainly by dollar strength, layered on a structural squeeze between import pressure and soft construction demand. Brazil’s 25% above-quota tariff and Mexico’s layered duties have raised the cost of Chinese steel, but imports still cover more than a third of regional consumption. Watch whether Brazil’s construction activity stabilises and whether Mexico turns its provisional anti-dumping duties into final measures.

02 The board

SLX, the steel fund that tracks a global basket including Latin American names, settled at US$108.69, a decline of 0.95%. That signals broad sector weakness, not merely a local story.

Among the region’s New York-traded names, CSN was the weakest at US$1.02, down 3.77%, while Gerdau followed at US$4.59, down 2.34%. Mexico’s Ternium traded at US$54.84, a 1.77% fall.

03 What moved it

The structural overhang is Chinese steel, though Brazilian steel imports fell 17.6% in the first half of 2026 as tariff quotas and anti-dumping measures bit. Regional steel lobby Alacero estimates imports supply 39.7% of Latin American apparent steel consumption, of which Chinese material accounts for 13.2 million tonnes, about 18% of the regional total.

That keeps pressure on mill margins despite tariffs.

Policy defences have multiplied. Mexico added provisional anti-dumping duties on Chinese and Vietnamese hot-rolled steel in March, on top of duties of up to 50% on some Chinese goods and a 25% levy on steel from countries without free-trade agreements.

Chinese supply is easing at the source too: July crude steel output fell 9% year on year, the weakest July since 2017. Demand is also mixed.

Construction, the main buyer of long steel products used in building, remains soft in Brazil, leaving producers dependent on policy protection rather than end-market strength.

04 The Latin American read

Brazil applies a 25% tariff on steel imports above set quotas, a regime the trade chamber Gecex-Camex renewed on May 29, 2026. It kept the rate at 25% after rejecting a proposal to lift it to 35% on 21 tariff lines, while trimming permitted volumes on some products.

Mexico layers duties of up to 50% on some Chinese goods on top of a 25% levy on steel from countries without free-trade agreements.

Despite these walls, import penetration remains high. Domestic mills are fighting for market share even with protection, which limits how much pricing power the policy shield can deliver.

For foreign investors, the message is that Latin American steel is a policy-dependent trade. Tariffs matter, but so does the health of construction and manufacturing end-markets, and construction is doing no heavy lifting in Brazil right now.

05 The names to watch

Gerdau is the most exposed to Brazil’s construction cycle through its long-steel products, making its 2.34% drop a signal that investors see more softness ahead in civil building and infrastructure.

CSN brings together steel, mining and cement, but its 3.77% drop shows the market is focusing on the steel import squeeze rather than the diversified earnings mix.

Ternium, which operates across Mexico, Brazil and Argentina, is cushioned by Mexico’s manufacturing-linked flat steel demand. Yet its 1.77% fall suggests investors are not convinced the anti-dumping duties will quickly lift margins.

06 The outlook

The next test for the sector is whether Mexico converts its provisional anti-dumping duties on Chinese and Vietnamese hot-rolled steel into final measures. A stricter final determination could tighten supply and support domestic prices, while a softening would leave producers chasing volume against cheaper imports.

In Brazil, watch construction indicators more than any other demand signal, since long-steel demand from building is the missing piece. If construction remains weak, the 25% above-quota tariff alone may not protect earnings momentum for Gerdau and CSN.

07 What to watch

Brazil construction demand: Soft construction is the core drag on long-steel producers like Gerdau; any pickup in infrastructure or civil works would lift the sector.

Investors weighed persistent Chinese steel imports and weak construction demand against tariff shields. The steel fund SLX fell 0.95%, and the region’s New York-traded steel names dropped between 1.77% and 3.77%.
