World.title: Kazakhstan’s government steps down as newly elected Kurultai holds first session
World.content:
Kazakhstan has entered a new political season with a reshaped political system after the country’s newly established unicameral parliament, with its lawmakers gathered for its first session on Friday in Astana.

 

It comes Kazakhstan’s pro-government Adilet party won more than 71 percent of the vote in last Sunday’s parliamentary election, that was triggered by a new constitution adopted earlier this year.

The session attended by all 145 members opened with an address by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who formally declared the first session of the first convocation of the Kurultai open and described it as the beginning of an important new stage in the country’s development.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev at the first session of the Kurultai in Astana. Copyright: Aqorda Press Service

“From this day, the process of renewing the country’s political system begins. … The Kurultai will fundamentally modernise the system of government and give a powerful impetus to the work of the entire state apparatus.

By improving the quality of national legislation, the Kurultai will provide a strong foundation for the country’s legal system,” Tokayev said.

A new political system

Under the Constitution, the government is required to step down before a newly elected Kurultai. Kazakhstan’s government therefore relinquished its powers as the new parliament convened.

However, the country will not be left without a functioning government during the transition period. President Tokayev signed a decree instructing the cabinet to continue performing its duties until a new government is formed.

Under Kazakhstan’s new Constitution, which came into force on 1 July 2026, the previous bicameral parliament, consisting of the Mazhilis and the Senate, was replaced by a unicameral parliament called the Kurultai.

The term “kurultai” dates back centuries and historically referred to an assembly or council among the peoples of the Great Steppe.

The new Constitution was adopted in a nationwide referendum held on 15 March 2026.

“By coming together, our people accomplished a great deal in a very short period of time. Thanks to the nationwide referendum, the country successfully implemented a sweeping constitutional reform,” Tokayev said.

The Kurultai consists of 145 lawmakers elected for five-year terms and representing five political parties. The Adilet party, which absorbed Amanat, the successor to the long-dominant Nur Otan party, holds a commanding majority with 110 seats.

It is followed by the Auyl party with 10 seats, Respublica with nine, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party (OSDP) with eight and Ak Zhol with eight.

New speaker of the Kurultai

During the session, President Tokayev nominated Aibek Dadebai for the position of chairman of the Kurultai. Dadebai has headed the Adilet party since 7 May 2026 and has held several senior government and diplomatic posts, including serving as head of the Presidential Administration from February 2024 to May 2026.

Aibek Dadebai, Chairman of the Adilet party. Copyright: Aqorda Press Service

Tokayev said Dadebai had extensive experience in public administration and described him as an educated, patriotic and responsible citizen. “I consider him worthy of this position and ask the members of the Kurultai to support his candidacy,” Tokayev said.

Later in the day, lawmakers backed the nomination and elected Dadebai chairman of the Kurultai in a secret ballot.

Lawmakers also elected three deputy speakers: former senator Nurlan Beknazarov, former Mazhilis deputy speaker Dania Espaeva and Children’s Rights Commissioner Dinara Zakiyeva.

The Kurultai will have eight standing committees, seven of which will be chaired by representatives of the ruling Adilet party, while the remaining committee will be headed by a member of the Auyl party.

What happens next?

Kazakhstan’s new political structure will continue to take shape in the coming weeks. Once the Kurultai is fully organised, President Tokayev will put forward candidates for vice-president and prime minister, before appointing the new government following consultations with lawmakers. A deputy chairman of the Security Council will also be appointed to a newly created post.

Tokayev said he would deliver his annual address to the nation once the new parliament and government are fully formed.

The institutional changes will continue into September, with the Kazakhstan People’s Council expected to be established in the second half of the month. The new constitutional body will represent the country’s ethnic, regional, social and political diversity and will have the right to initiate legislation.

According to Tokayev, the process will renew “almost all key institutions of power” within a relatively short period.

World.title: Hundreds of foreign nationals among the missing following deadly Nepal floods
World.content:
Hundreds of foreign nationals are among the nearly 3,000 people missing following devastating floods that hit the border area between Nepal and Tibet earlier this week.

 

A tsunami-like wall of water and debris ripped through the Himalayan region on Wednesday, killing at least 682 people and sparking a huge rescue effort.

On Friday, Chinese officials said 260 foreigners remained missing following the deadly flash floods, while Nepal's disaster agency said 517 foreign nationals were missing. Nepal's tourism board put the number of tourists still "out of communication" at 622 - 471 of which were foreign tourists.

The tourism board's figures included 98 people from India, 61 Ukrainians, 51 Malaysians, 33 British, 29 Latvians, 25 Canadians, nine South Koreans, and nine Singaporeans.

Nine Russians and eight Germans were also still unaccounted for, as well as six from South Africa, five from Japan, five from New Zealand, and four from France, according to the figures.

Nepalese army soldiers load relief supplies onto a helicopter for survivors stranded in areas cut off by flash flooding in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

The other countries with people on the tourism board's missing list were Belgium, Hungary, the Netherlands, Ireland, Kazakhstan, Portugal, Italy, Belarus, Finland, Israel, Lithuania, the Philippines, Serbia, Switzerland, Sweden, and Vietnam.

The US State Department said on Thursday that 90 US citizens also remained unaccounted for, while the Australian government announced on Saturday that the number of its missing nationals had risen to 41.

The Nepal Tourism Board reported that two of the three missing Spaniards had been located, although the Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs has not commented on the matter.

China has not provided a breakdown of the nationalities of the foreign nationals it reported as missing.

Europe pledges support

The European Union has pledged its support for aid efforts in the wake of the floods, activating its Copernicus Earth observation satellite system to help monitor the aftermath.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc would also allocate €2 million in humanitarian aid for Nepal "to deliver life-saving assistance to families and communities hit hardest."

World.title: COP17 in Mongolia wraps up with 1.3 billion dollars of Green Investment Pledge
World.content:
After 12 days of debates and negotiations in the Mongolian capital, Ulaanbaatar, delegates of 197 parties (196 countries + the EU) who signed the United Nations Convention for Combating Desertification wrapped up the soConference of Parties (COP17) with note-worthy results.

 

Like in all previous COPs it proved difficult to achieve unanimity over a legally binding all-encompassing documents, especially at the time when the big powers question the mere principle of multilateralism.

But, the Convention is a process and from the beginning of COP17 the host country Mongolia and the UN have appealed for it to try to produce tangible results.

“Today, the time has come for us to ask ourselves a bold and candid question – we have spoken at length and made many declarations, but have we been able to turn our words into action?

The previous events all brought meaningful outcomes. But, the truth is that the world has never lacked goals and commitments.

What we need more urgently are the resources, financing, technology and institutional environment to turn those commitments into tangible results,” said Mongolian Prime Minister Nyam-Osoryn Uchral.

So, did the COP17 produce tangible results?

One of the sessions within COP17 Euronews

Raising awareness

40% of usable, arable land on the planet is affected by land degradation. That is, it is slowly turning into a barren desert. The problem already affects 3.2 billion people in the world. From the very opening of COP17 its officials and delegates from different countries warned that the world often fails to see that the more obvious issues such as migration, wild fires and draughts are often consequences of the land not being able to sustain vegetation and human habitation.

“Desertification can simply be a food crisis because once your land is degraded you will not be able to plant and you will have both food and water security problem and migration and displacement.

Here, the people are not being given a choice whether they will leave their land, yes or no, but they have nothing to sustain their livelihood and give them resilience. Add to that the impact of draught, the climate change and the loss of biodiversity and it all adds to the problem of desertification,” says Yasmine Fouadh, Executive Secretary of the UNCCD.

Our languages, cultures, ethnic backgrounds and religions may differ, but we share a common determination to safeguard the future in which we can all continue to live in harmony with Mother Earth. Nyam-Osoryn Uchral Prime Minister of Mongolia

“We will not be able to resolve any of our issues without working on the land. 90% of our food comes from the land, 99.8% of our calories come from the land, our cities and on land, our villages and farms are on land, rivers, lakes, all the freshwater lie on the land. And that land also stores three times more carbon dioxide than there is in the atmosphere,” warned dr Osama Faqeeha, advisor to COP16 in Riyadh.

Raising funds

During COP16 in Riyadh in Saudi Arabia, mechanisms were initiated to gather financial institutions, bank and private equity to invest in projects that protest land from degradation. It is possible because those projects can be profitable, especially if they tackle water utilization and sustainable agriculture.

The Convention estimates that inaction on land costs the world almost 900 billion dollars a year while investment in healthy land could generate up to 1.8 trillion through food production, water provision and carbon storing. Yet, the investment so far remains modest.

“If you look at how much money goes into artificial intelligence, it is the same amount of money that goes into climate financing – 2 trillion dollars a year.

But, when you double-click on climate financing, less than 3% goes into land and water. It is way under-invested.

And the white-paper we published puts forward reasons why businesses can actually invest into land and water. It can bring returns, every dollar you put into land brings 8 to 30 dollars in exchange,” says Gim Huay Neo, Managing Director World Economic Forum.

77% of land in Mongolia is already degraded and needs funds for restauration Euronews

This is why the governments, development banks and private investors were able to announce one of the biggest successes of COP17 - the $1.3 billion in new and pipeline financing for land restoration and drought resilience across 23 countries on five continents.

Of the $1.3 billion announced, $644.5 million has been identified as new finance, while $216.4 million has already been confirmed and is moving towards implementation, the UNCCD noted.

The announcement came against the backdrop of perceived huge financing gaps for meeting global land restoration commitments.

“There is a huge gap in the funding for land preservation. Annualy, about 355 billion dollars is needed but we have only about 70 billion, so we miss around 280 billion,” says deputy Prime Minister of Mongolia Togmid Dorjkhand who chaired the ministerial session on finance.

“The governments have raised over a billion dollars for projects and in the afternoon session we got the private sector involved and another 1.3 billion were discussed so all in all about 2.1 billion dollars are on the bale. COP17 has been a success in that financial part,” explains Dorjkhand.

A lot of fundraising was done in direct talks between the financial institutions and governments. Mongolia as used the opportunity to offer favourable conditions for opening data centres across its vast territory.

The advantages it presented are the low cost of energy, 40% of savings on cooling owing to Mongolias harsh winters and the fact that 98% of land in Mongolia is state-owned which simplifies construction.

“But this is not the only thing that Mongolia offers, there are also legal advantages. We have just proposed a so-called data law which guarantees data sovereignty. It basically turns data centre into a data embassy in which both data and connectivity, networking guarantee safety and security.

So, we hope that this will be attractive to those who want to build data centres to serve the largest market, China, but still keep their data outside China,” explains Mongolian Minister of Digital Development Chinbat Nomin.

Networking, planning and making commitments

COP17 saw hundreds of events and many countries had their pavilions on the its grounds. Big projects were presented, like the Chinese “Green Wall of China” a mega project of planting billions of trees over several decades to stop the spreading of deserts.

Countries most affected by desertification had the biggest presence. Among them the host country, Mongolia, where 77% of land is already degraded and where Gobi desert “swallows” thousands of hectares every year.

Folklore programme at COP17 Euronews

“There are many problems that countries share and we all learn from each other here,” says Bakhtiyor Pulatov, Rector of the Central Asian University of Environmental and Climate Change Studies. “Uzbekistan has established scientific approach to solving the problem of the land degradation because it is serious in our country, more than 70% of the territory is already a desert or turning into one.

So, we established many systems like early warning system for sand and dust storms. There is also the initiative of our president Shavkat Mirziyoyev to plant a billion saksaul trees in deserts that works well.

We also opened the only university that studies the environmental issues, because we believe I science and we are ready to share, out pavilion here is open to their countries that have similar problems,” says Pulatov.

The Mayor of Ulaanbaatar hosted the first Mayor’s Forum during COP17. It gathered participants from 30 countries, including around 30 mayors, governors and other local and regional leaders.

They signed a joint declaration, exchanged experience and agreed that they would be involved in the negotiations by their national governments in the future because they will be the ones implementing the solutions to combat desertification.

Also, within 90 days they will create a network of cities in dryland and extreme climate areas.

COP17 Green Zone Euronews

All the countries of UNCCD have made national agendas. More of them than ever came to Ulaanbaatar with their own initiatives.

In Riyadh we had 35 initiatives and real national agendas and we continued after that in 2025 and 2026 and we came here to Mongolia and we have 200, or to be exact 198 initiatives under the Riad action agenda, says dr Osama Faqeeha, advisor to COP16 in Riyadh.

During 12 days in Ulaanbaatar alliances were forged, like the one between China and the League of Arab States who made a joint 5-year plan of cooperation to restore land. Countries shared experience in fighting desertification.

Where politics meets life

Summits of this kind can often feel distant from real life of the people whose problems are being discussed. Negotiations are mostly behind closed doors and end in documents whose bureaucratic and expert language is difficult to understand.

A day into the conference, it opened the so-called Green Zone, part of the event open to the general public. More than 400 events were held in its halls, stages and meeting points. It was visited by thousands of people who could see exhibitions of around 60 different organisations.

This is where visitors met representatives of businesses, civil society, scientists, young people, entrepreneurs and government agencies and see their projects, solutions, screenings, workshops and cultural performances.

World.title: Uzbekistan marks 35 years of independence as president outlines plans for next decade
World.content:
Uzbekistan has begun marking the 35th anniversary of its independence with a large-scale celebration in New Tashkent, days before the country’s official Independence Day on 1 September.

 

Uzbekistan proclaimed independence from the Soviet Union on 31 August 1991.

The ceremony brought together Uzbek officials, foreign guests and performers from Uzbekistan and abroad. Spanish tenor José Carreras, British soprano Sarah Brightman and Italian tenor Alessandro Safina were among the international artists taking part, alongside Uzbek singers and dancers. The programme also included 3D projections, lighting effects, robots and a drone show.

The choice of venue was significant. New Tashkent is a major urban development being built alongside the existing capital on a site of around 20,000 hectares. It is ultimately designed for a population of two million, while its first phase, covering 6,000 hectares, is intended to accommodate 600,000 residents. Plans include housing, universities, cultural and scientific institutions, government buildings, business districts and new transport infrastructure.

President Shavkat Mirziyoyev used the anniversary address both to look back at the country’s development since independence and to set out priorities for the next decade.

The reform agenda

Mirziyoyev framed independence as a restoration of national identity, paying tribute to the Jadids, a reformist movement of Central Asian intellectuals who promoted modern education and social change, and to Uzbekistan’s first president, Islam Karimov.

“Independence gave us back our honour and dignity, our mother tongue and our national values,” he said.

Much of his speech, however, focused on the reforms pursued over the past decade as Uzbekistan has sought to open its economy and strengthen relations with its neighbours and international partners.

He pointed to the end of systemic forced and child labour in the cotton harvest, the lifting of restrictions on currency conversion and the easing of restrictions on residence registration.

The president also cited changes in taxation, customs and investment policy as evidence of the country’s economic opening. He said annual foreign investment had increased from around $2 - 3bn (€1.7 - 2.6bn) to $40 - 50bn (€34.5 - 43.2bn).

Mirziyoyev said Uzbekistan had initially aimed to raise gross domestic product to $160bn (€138bn) by 2030 but now expected to exceed that level in 2026.

The president also said poverty had fallen from 35% in 2017 to 4% this year.

Seven programmes for the next decade

President Mirziyoyev described the coming ten years as a new period of national development and announced seven programmes covering education, healthcare, the economy, the environment, the rule of law, local government and foreign policy.

Among the main ambitious economic targets is a plan to attract $450bn (€388bn) in foreign investment over the next decade and increase GDP to $300bn (€259bn) by 2030. The government also aims to create two million high-income jobs in industry and make start-ups, venture capital and artificial intelligence priority areas for development.

In education, Uzbekistan plans to provide preparatory education to all six-year-olds, introduce international standards across technical colleges, train up to one million young people for higher-income professions and place at least ten Uzbek universities among the world’s top 1,000.

Healthcare spending is planned to rise to 5% of GDP over the next five years, alongside the expansion of preventive medicine and state health insurance.

Another programme targets water scarcity and environmental pressures, with the government aiming to introduce water-saving technologies across all cultivated land within five years.

Plans also call for stronger judicial independence and legal protections for citizens and businesses.

The mahalla, Uzbekistan’s traditional neighbourhood-based system of local community organisation, is also set to play a greater role. District budgets, investment programmes and infrastructure projects are intended to be shaped increasingly by priorities identified at neighbourhood level.

A bigger international role

The seventh programme focuses explicitly on Uzbekistan’s international position.

The President said the country would continue what he described as an open, pragmatic foreign policy, prioritising close relations within Central Asia while expanding partnerships with the European Union, the Americas, Asia-Pacific, Africa and the Arab and Muslim world.

Uzbekistan is also due to chair the Non-Aligned Movement for the first time from 2027 to 2029. The grouping brings together more than 120 countries, making it one of the world’s largest groupings of states.

After the president’s address, the anniversary ceremony moved from speeches to spectacle. As darkness fell over New Tashkent, the programme culminated in a major concert, choreographed light and visual displays and drones forming images above the venue, bringing the anniversary ceremony in New Tashkent to a close.

World.title: Heavy gunfire in Niger capital as clashes reported at presidential palace
World.content:
Gunfire rang out across parts of the Niger capital of Niamey overnight amid reports of an attack on the presidential palace.

 

The cause of the shooting was not immediately clear.

Bana Wagana Ibrahim, a member of Niger's Consultative Council, shared a statement on Saturday saying: "In light of current events, let us remain calm and avoid sharing unverified information."

"Our defence and security forces have been mobilised for the defence of the homeland," the statement read.

Ibrahim had earlier condemned what he called "another cowardly attack" on the Base 101 military airbase but added that the situation was "under control."

"Once again our defence and security forces have risen to the challenge," he wrote in a post on social media.

It comes as a security source told the AFP news agency that Niger's presidential guard had fought off "insurgents from within the armed forces" who attempted to make their way into the presidential palace in Niamey on Saturday.

The west African nation's state TV was also off air on Saturday, locals told AFP, with a black screen showing in place of regular programming.

One local said they had heard "heavy gunfire and explosions" at Base 101. Several other witnesses corroborated the report.

Another resident said he heard "bursts of gunfire" at around 7 am local time.

"I went to get credit for my phone. I saw a military vehicle heading towards the base that had to turn back," he added. "The weapons we're hearing are not the kind that terrorists on motorbikes can carry. The fighting has been non-stop since last night."

A military junta has ruled Niger for three years but has struggled to contend with jihadist violence.

Jihadists have already targeted Niamey airport twice this year. The Islamic State in the Sahel group attacked in January, before the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims attacked in June.

World.title: Nepal flood highlights growing risk of glacier disasters in the Alps
World.content:
Authorities in Nepal suspect that the recent devastating flash flood was triggered by a glacial lake outburst or a glacier collapse in the Himalayas - something experts say could also threaten the Alps.

 

A torrent of water, mud and debris surged almost 170 kilometres through southwest Tibet and into central Nepal earlier this week, killing hundreds of people.

Such disasters are also possible in Europe, particularly in the Alps, explains glaciologist Olaf Eisen, a professor at the Alfred Wegener Institute for Polar and Marine Research and at the University of Bremen.

As an example, Eisen cites an incident in the Swiss village of Blatten in May 2025, where a rock and glacier collapse occurred. The village had been evacuated beforehand, but a 64-year-old man was killed.

However, Eisen considers it unlikely that such an event in the Alps could reach the same scale as in Nepal.

"The disaster in Nepal was, in terms of the volume of the avalanche, around 10 to 20 times larger than Blatten, according to current estimates," Eisen said.

"Europe is among the continents warming the fastest, driven by human-made climate change. Rapidly retreating glaciers and thawing permafrost are destabilising high mountain regions," he added.

The areas most at risk are those at about 2,500 to 3,000 metres, including parts of France, Italy, Austria and Switzerland.

"In combination with extreme weather events such as heatwaves or heavy rainfall, similar natural disasters are becoming more likely there too," Eisen continued.

Risk of glacier collapse in Switzerland

Around 1,000 glaciers have disappeared in Switzerland since 1850. In total, an area of about 1,000 square kilometres has lost its ice cover, according to SRF.

One glacier that has been monitored for years is Weisshorn East, which saw three small glacier collapses earlier this week.

"This glacier has been monitored for years and there are repeated movements – sometimes more, sometimes less," Frederic Imboden, the mayor of Randa, the municipality bordering the glacier, told SRF.

Several hundred thousand cubic metres could potentially break away from the glacier. While there is no danger for local residents at present, according to Imboden, hiking trails and cycling routes have nevertheless been closed.

Causes of glacier collapses

There are several causes of glacier collapses: on the one hand they can be normal, cyclical processes, Eisen told Euronews.

Increasingly, though, they are being driven by human-induced climate change.

Glacial lake in Zermatt, Switzerland, 19 September 2025 © KEYSTONE / JEAN-CHRISTOPHE BOTT

The situation is particularly critical in regions that have historically remained permanently below freezing.

These contain so-called permafrost, ice that has stayed frozen continuously for at least two years.

"As temperatures rise, permafrost begins to thaw and a glacier starts to melt at its base. As a result, it no longer 'sticks' as firmly to the ground," Eisen says.

"In some cases, the formation of a pocket of water has been observed beneath a glacier that was still frozen at its snout," he continued.

During heatwaves or rainfall, this pocket can exert such intense pressure that the still-frozen front of the glacier gives way.

That would then cause the entire ice mass to be released in one go, Eisen explains.

Such an incident occurred in 2022 on Italy's Marmolada glacier in the Dolomites, when a huge block of ice broke away from the glacier, killing 11 mountaineers.

"Climate protection is glacier protection. Every tenth of a degree less counts. If average temperatures were to fall again, glaciers could adapt and grow," Eisen says.

Mechanical protection would only have a short-lived effect and is used solely in certain ski areas, requiring a great deal of energy and labour.

World.title: India news: PM Modi in Uzbekistan on way to SCO summit
World.content:
08/29/2026 August 29, 2026 Congress slams Penguin India for backing out of Sonia Gandhi's memoir

Sonia Gandhi's memoir reportedly addresses her decision to turn down the position of Prime Minister of India in 2004 [FILE: June 2024] Image: Sondeep Shankar/Pacific Press/picture alliance

Leaders of India's largest opposition party, the Indian National Congress (INC), alleged that publishing house Penguin India was pressured to back out of publishing veteran politician Sonia Gandhi's memoir due to portions related to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Hindu nationalist group, and China's alleged occupation of Indian territory under Modi's rule.

Sonia Gandhi has been a leading figure in Indian politics for decades. She was the president of the INC from 1998 to 2017 and is the party's longest-serving chief.

Earlier this month, Alfred A. Knopf announced that Gandhi's "Belonging: A Journey of Love" will be published on November 10. Knopf is a publishing imprint under Penguin Random House.

"Suppressing the book of Sonia Gandhi, a person of such stature, a senior leader of the nation, and former Leader of the Opposition, under pressure is tantamount to the murder of freedom of Expression," senior INC leader Ashok gehlot said in a post on X.

"The real issue is that pressure was put on Penguin India to remove the portions related to Modi, the RSS, and the occupation of Indian territory by China during Modi's rule. This is the murder of democracy," he said.

In another post, Gehlot said "there's some kind of pressure. It could be from the PMO [Prime Minister's Office] or someone else — that time will tell."

This comes a day after Penguin India released a statement of clarification: "Any suggestion that Penguin Random House India decided not to publish 'Belonging' because the author declined editorial changes does not accurately reflect the circumstances."

The statement was referring to a report by The Indian Express which said the publishing house would not publish the book in India because "editorial changes and deletions" were turned down by the author.

"As a publisher, it is both our prerogative and our responsibility to fact check and provide authors with recommendations that are in best interests of their books," Penguin India said in its statement, adding that it "remained willing and keen to publish the book."

World.title: Russian strike on ammunition depot near Kyiv kills dozens
World.content:
Hundreds were also forced to flee after a Russian attack near Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, sparked a huge fire and explosions. The strike was the second to hit an arms depot near Kyiv in less than two months.

At least 37 people were killed after a Russian drone strike on a ammunition depot near Kyiv late Friday, one of the deadliest attacks in Ukraine this year.

The drone strike was the second attack to hit an arms depot near the Ukrainian capital in less than two months.

"A terrible situation and terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a video address on X.

"Another such crime — after what happened in Vyshneve — is absolutely unacceptable," he added. Zelenskyy was referring to an attack on an ammunition warehouse last month that set off secondary explosions in the small town on Kyiv's western outskirts, killing ten people.

Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified long-range strikes, increasingly hitting civilian infrastructure such as logistics warehouses and oil and port facilities. These attacks have resulted in more civilian casualties.

What else do we know about the Russian drone attack near Kyiv?

The strike sparked a major fire and explosions at the arms depot in the Bucha district, close to the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, forcing more than 370 people to evacuate the region. Dozens were injured.

Among those killed was Taras Didych, head of the Dmytrivka community, who was one of the first to rush to the scene to rescue people, according to Kyiv region governor Tymur Tkachenko. He also said the attack damaged at least 50 residential buildings.

Zelenskyy earlier said that criminal proceedings had been opened on charges of official negligence.

"There are regulations in place — ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas," Zelenskyy said.

Kyiv under jet-powered drone attacks

Friday's drone attack followed ​two days of constant air raids aimed at the Ukrainian capital and the surrounding region.

"Kyiv is under virtually nonstop attack from jet-powered drones. Ukraine cannot be left alone in finding solutions to defend against such strikes," said Zelenskyy, adding that Russia also struck nine other regions overnight.

It's been more than four and a half years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbor.

World.title: Death toll from Nepal-Tibet floods rises to over 600
World.content:
Heavy rain is complicating an already difficult rescue effort, as hundreds remain missing three days after deadly flash floods hit the Nepal-Tibet border region.

The latest death toll from the devastating flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border was reported on Saturday to be over 600, as frantic rescue operations to search for hundreds of missing people entered a fourth day.

Figures from both countries put the number of missing close to 3,000, with 682 bodies recovered and reports of corpses swept as far downstream as India.

According to Nepal's disaster agency, the death toll there now stands at 675, with 2,426 people — including foreigners — still missing.

Across the border in Tibet, China's state news agency, Xinhua, has confirmed seven deaths and reported 554 missing individuals.

A glacial collapse on Wednesday sent rock, ice, mud and debris surging through the Himalayan mountain river systems below.

The flood swept through areas near the Chinese border, ravaging entire towns and damaging hydropower plants.

What is the status of rescue efforts in Nepal?

Rainy weather conditions are hindering aerial rescue operations in Nepal.

Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told the media on Saturday that helicopter operations were on hold until the weather improved.

Rescuers are battling thick layers of mud in the affected areas, which is making it difficult for helicopters to land and take off.

Tunnels in the mountainous region are also a challenge, Basnet said.

The army has located people trapped in a tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project in Nepal's Rasuwa District. Over 100 people are believed to be inside the tunnel filled with mud.

Basnet said that rescuers were struggling to locate the entry points of the tunnel and had made use of baskets and ropes to reach some people. There are also limited places for helicopters to land in the area.

Members of the Nepal Army load relief material as a helicopter containing relief supplies takes off Image: Athit Perawongmetha/REUTERS

On Friday, Nepal's Army shared visuals of some people being rescued from the tunnel. The survivors were seen stuck in the mud, while officials crawled through the sludge and held out their hands to them.

On Saturday, Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal said a specialized tunnel rescue team had arrived from neighboring India and was ready to start work.

Nepalese authorities said the bodies of many flood victims have also been found dozens of kilometers from the disaster zone in Chitwan District in southern Nepal, which borders India.

Meanwhile, Indian authorities said they recovered the bodies of seven people who were swept downstream from Nepal and believe them to be flood victims.

More than 1,000 believed missing after Nepal flash floods To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nepal needs help in technical areas, says foreign minister

Late on Friday, Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told the Reuters news agency that his country needed equipment, along with technical knowledge in tunnel rescue operations.

Khanal also told Reuters that Nepal did not need help with search and rescue operations but needed assistance in opening transport and communication lines in places where bridges were destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storage of bodies for a longer timeframe.

"We have already made requests for such ⁠specialized ​services and technical assistance in areas where we don't have enough expertise and technical know-how," ​Reuters quoted Khanal as saying.

Nepal's Foreign Ministry had on Friday declined foreign involvement in search and rescue.

Nepal's post-flood rebuilding estimated at $4-$5 billion

In another Reuters interview, Nepal's Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said that the Himalayan nation may need $4 billion (€3.5 billion) ⁠to $5 billion ⁠to rebuild after the flood.

The estimate is equivalent ​to nearly a tenth of Nepal's economy.

"The initial estimate is ​between $4-$5 billion. Just an estimate," Wagle told Reuters, adding that the bill would be much less than what was needed in reconstruction after the disastrous 2015 earthquake — Nepal's worst ‌ recorded disaster.

"Loss and damage is being assessed," he said.

People carry salvaged belongings from damaged houses following the flash floods and mudslide Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

What do we know about rescue operations in Tibet?

In Gyirong, one of the hardest-hit areas in Tibet along the China-Nepal border, Beijing had temporarily halted its rescue efforts due to the risk of renewed flooding before announcing that the threat had waned.

China's Xinhua agency reported on Saturday morning that two villagers had been rescued in the Gyirong area.

Rescue workers operate excavators and loaders to repair a damaged road leading to Gyirong Port Image: China Daily/REUTERS

The glacial collapse on Wednesday led to the formation of a barrier lake upstream due to debris dams. Experts warned that the lake had started to overflow.

On Saturday, Chinese authorities announced that the lake had begun to shrink.

China's state broadcaster, CCTV, cited the Ministry of Water Resources as saying that satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake in the Tsangpo River basin on Saturday morning showed a reduction of around 21,000 square meters compared to images from Thursday.

Authorities have also identified a larger body of water at the bottom of the glacier collapse.

"We estimate its area to be over 120,000 ⁠square ​meters, but its depth is currently unknown," Reuters quoted Chen Hongqi, a senior engineer at ​the Ministry of Natural Resources' Geological Disaster Technical Guidance Center, as saying.

Reuters also reported an official of Nepal's Disaster ​Management Authority as saying that flood risks will remain until the two lakes have fully drained.

World.title: Niger's defense ministry says soldiers attempted mutiny
World.content:
Gunfire and explosions were heard across Niamey overnight. The attack posed the latest threat to Niger's military junta, led by Abdourahamane Tchiani, who seized power in a 2023 coup.

Niger's Ministry of National Defense ‌on ⁠Saturday said ⁠that ​a group of soldiers shot at "sensitive" locations in the capital Niamey in an apparent mutiny.

Gunfire and explosions had been heard across Niger's capital, Niamey, overnight into the early hours of Saturday morning.

Attackers had targeted Diori Hamani International Airport, which also houses a military air base, and attempted to breach the security perimeter around ​the presidency.

"Another cowardly attack on Base 101 and once again our defense and security forces ensured ... Situation under control," said lawmaker Bana Wagana Ibrahim, who serves on the Consultative Council.

Niger military 'gradually regaining control'

The military said it was "gradually regaining control" after mutineers took soldiers hostage at a base near the airport in Niamey, AFP news agency reported.

Authorities urged the public to "remain calm and freely go about their business" in a statement read out on public television and signed by Defense Minister General Salifou Mody.

The attack posed the latest threat to Niger's military junta, led by Abdourahamane Tchiani, who seized power in a 2023 coup.

Niger, like its Sahelian neighbors Mali and Burkina Faso, has for years been ruled by a military junta that has struggled to stem a jihadi insurgency.

National TV signal reportedly cut after gunfire

The shooting began around 1 a.m. local time (0000 GMT) and continued until daybreak.

Locals said that the country's national television had gone off air.

Tele Sahel's satellite and online programming was replaced with a black screen at 9 a.m. local time (0800 GMT), AFP reported. It was restored around one hour later.

Niamey has been targeted by jihadists twice this year: once by the so-called "Islamic State in the Sahel" group (EIS) and again in June by their rivals from the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM).

World.title: Germany news: Sick leave wage bill doubles in 15 years
World.content:
Skip next section Sick leave now costs Germany twice as much as in 2010

08/29/2026 August 29, 2026 Sick leave now costs Germany twice as much as in 2010

The average number of sick days taken by German workers has risen sharply Image: Sergey Mironov/Zoonar/IMAGO

The total amount of wages German firms paid in sick and maternity leave has more than doubled over the past 15 years, a study from the Cologne-based German Economic Institute (IW) shows.

IW estimated that German companies paid a record-high €85.6 billion ($111 billion) in wages to employees who were out sick last year. This compares to €36.9 billion in 2010.

Of the larger figure, €72.5 billion represented gross wages, while €13.1 billion was earmarked for social security contributions.

IW said several factors have contributed to the rise, including wage hikes and inflation in other employee costs.

The institute said the total number of employed people has also grown since 2010, meaning more workers are eligible for sick leave.

IW, however, said it had noted a "significant" rise in recorded sick leave since Germany moved to electronic medical certificates in 2022.

Separate research by the Berlin-based IGES Institute in January showed that German workers now take an average of 19.5 working days as sick leave per year, a noticeable increase from about 13 days in 2018.

In an effort to stem the rise, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government will from January ban patients from receiving sick notes from doctors by phone.

In Germany, employers are generally required to pay workers' salaries for up to six weeks before the statutory health insurance fund takes over by paying sickness benefits.

World.title: US, Ecuador forces strike alleged drug smuggling boat
World.content:
Tackling drug trafficking in Latin America is a key priority for Washington. In March, Ecuador joined a US-led coalition to combat the drug trade in the region.

The US military said on Friday it had destroyed an alleged drug trafficking boat in a coordinated operation with Ecuador.

In a post on X, US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said that its forces intercepted a vessel "operating as a floating refueling station" in the Eastern Pacific.

According to SOUTHCOM, the vessel was operating "in support of the Los Choneros violent narco-terrorist organization," referring to one of Ecuador's most powerful criminal gangs, which Washington has designated as a Foreign Terrorist Organization .

"Working together with our Ecuadorian partners, our coalition dealt a decisive blow to a narco-terrorist operation responsible for moving significant amounts of drugs through the region," SOUTHCOM said.

US, Ecuador combat drug cartels

In March, Ecuador joined President Donald Trump's "Shield of the Americas" — a US-led coalition focused on combating drug trafficking across the region.

Ecuador's strategic location between Colombia and Peru — the world's two largest producers of cocaine — makes the country a key transit hub for drug-trafficking gangs.

The US military launched Operation Southern Spear in September 2025 as part of a fight against drug trafficking in the region.

The Trump administration, however, has not presented definitive evidence that the vessels targeted in its operations were carrying or transporting illegal drugs.
