World.title: SCO's role in Kazakhstan's multi-vector policy - ahead of Bishkek Summit
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. For Kazakhstan, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) is primarily of practical importance: through it, the country engages with Eurasia's largest economies, expands trade ties, promotes investment cooperation and transport projects.

Kazakhstan has been one of the founding members of the SCO since the organization was established in 2001. The member states are directly important to Kazakhstan as trading partners and participants in major regional projects.

This is well reflected in Kazakhstan's foreign trade statistics. In January-June 2026, China accounted for 18.6% of Kazakhstan's exports, while Russia accounted for 8.6%. In the structure of imports, Russia accounted for 30.9%, while China accounted for 29.1%.

Thus, a significant share of Kazakhstan's foreign trade turnover is accounted for by SCO member states. According to Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, the country's trade turnover with the organization's member states approached $70 billion in 2024.

For Astana, the SCO serves both as a platform for political dialogue and as a mechanism for promoting economic ties with the major markets of its member states.

The composition of the organization is also important. China and India are among the world's largest economies, while Russia remains one of Kazakhstan's key trading partners. As a result, Kazakhstan has an opportunity to develop relations simultaneously with several major economic centers without focusing exclusively on a single partner. This directly corresponds to Astana's multi-vector approach to foreign policy.

The SCO's transport potential is particularly important for Kazakhstan. The country is located between China and European markets and also has access to the Caspian Sea.

According to available estimates, Kazakhstan accounts for about 85% of overland freight traffic between China and Europe. This makes the development of rail and other transport infrastructure one of the key tools for strengthening the country's economic role in the region.

For Kazakhstan, the growth of transit traffic is important not only in itself. It enables the development of logistics centers, warehousing infrastructure, processing and higher-value-added manufacturing, turning the country's transit position from a geographical advantage into a source of economic activity.

Kazakhstan is seeking not only to use the existing opportunities offered by the SCO, but also to create new mechanisms for cooperation.

In particular, at the previous summit, Tokayev supported China's initiative to establish an SCO Development Bank and stated Kazakhstan's readiness to participate in the implementation of this project. A political decision to establish the SCO Development Bank was made on September 1, 2025.

Another proposal from Kazakhstan is to establish an SCO Office for the Support of Promising Investment Projects at the Astana International Financial Centre. Such a structure could bring together financial, legal and consulting capabilities to promote projects.

This is an important signal: Astana is interested in ensuring that cooperation within the SCO leads not only to increased trade, but also to the emergence of new joint ventures, investment projects and sources of financing.

In addition, last year, at the SCO Council of Heads of State meeting in Tianjin, Tokayev supported the establishment of four SCO centers to combat security challenges and threats. The President also proposed strengthening cooperation between the SCO and the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia and using the potential of the UN Regional Centre for the Sustainable Development Goals for Central Asia and Afghanistan to coordinate regional cooperation.

In other words, Kazakhstan is seeking to use the SCO to address specific issues directly related to its interests, ranging from security and sustainable development to transport, trade and investment.

Against this backdrop, the SCO summit in Bishkek, marking the organization's 25th anniversary, is important for Kazakhstan primarily in terms of further filling the economic component of cooperation with concrete projects. For Astana, the most interesting areas may include further promoting the SCO Development Bank, increasing trade among the organization's member states, developing transport routes and attracting investment.

The SCO is important to Kazakhstan because it brings together, in a single framework, countries that are already crucial to its trade, investment, transit and regional security. This is particularly important for Astana's multi-vector policy, as Kazakhstan can simultaneously develop relations with several major centers of power without tying its foreign economic strategy to a single direction.

World.title: Baku-Nakhchivan flights postponed due to weather conditions
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. A number of Azerbaijan Airlines (AZAL) Baku-Nakhchivan-Baku flights scheduled for August 29, 2026, have been postponed due to thunderstorm activity.

According to the Press Service of Azerbaijan Airlines CJSC, flights will resume once weather conditions stabilize. Passengers will be provided with detailed information regarding any possible changes.

AZAL added that due to the geographical location and mountainous terrain of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic, meteorological conditions in the region can directly affect flight operations. In particular, strong winds, sudden changes in wind direction and thunderstorm activity create additional risks during takeoff and landing.

“The decision to postpone or cancel flights due to weather conditions is not based solely on the weather conditions observed by passengers at the airport. Decisions are made based on existing and forecast meteorological conditions along the route, as well as at the departure and destination airports.

As such meteorological conditions can seriously affect flight safety, crews and operational services make appropriate decisions in accordance with international aviation safety standards,” the Azerbaijan Airlines statement said.

World.title: Kyrgyz President inspects Manas airport’s readiness to receive SCO summit delegations
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov visited Manas International Airport on August 29 to check its readiness to receive foreign delegations arriving for upcoming international events.

According to the Kyrgyz president’s press service, Sadyr Japarov inspected the airport grounds as well as the halls designated for receiving Kyrgyz citizens and foreign delegations.

"President of the Kyrgyz Republic Sadyr Japarov made an unscheduled visit to Manas International Airport today, August 29, to inspect its condition following a major reconstruction," the statement said.

Sadyr Japarov also reviewed the airport complex’s readiness to receive high-ranking guests arriving in Kyrgyzstan to participate in the meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), the World Nomad Games and other events.

The president instructed the relevant officials to ensure the full readiness of the airport and adjacent areas, with particular attention to order and security, the proper organization of protocol procedures and the quality of services provided to arriving delegations.

Sadyr Japarov also stressed the need to ensure a high level of preparation for the upcoming international events.

Meanwhile, the SCO was established in 2001 and initially comprised China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Over the past 25 years, its membership has expanded to 10 countries. The 26th SCO summit will be held in Bishkek on August 31-September 1, 2026, under Kyrgyzstan’s chairmanship.

The meeting will focus on the organization’s further development, strengthening economic and transport cooperation, and security cooperation.

Following the summit, the leaders are expected to consider a number of documents related to the development of the SCO’s financial and economic mechanisms, including initiatives to expand settlements in national currencies and establish new cooperation institutions.

World.title: Xi Jinping calls for deeper trade and transport ties with Kyrgyzstan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. China and Kyrgyzstan should continue deepening bilateral relations, with a focus on trade, transport connectivity, infrastructure and new technologies.

This was stated in an article by Chinese President Xi Jinping published on August 28 on the official website of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the People’s Republic of China ahead of his state visit to Kyrgyzstan, where he will also attend the 26th meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).

"Cooperation should be strengthened in traditional areas such as trade and investment, infrastructure connectivity and green minerals, while cooperation in emerging sectors, particularly the digital economy, clean energy and artificial intelligence, should be expanded," Xi Jinping said.

According to Xi Jinping, the two sides should step up the alignment of development strategies and deepen exchanges of experience in state governance, creating conditions for further economic cooperation.

He placed particular emphasis on transport connectivity. The construction of the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway is underway in Kyrgyzstan, while transport links between the two countries are also expanding.

"It is important, with a long-term perspective, to make high-quality Belt and Road cooperation the main direction and promote practical cooperation in terms of both scope and level," Xi Jinping noted.

He called for stronger cooperation in trade and investment, infrastructure connectivity and green minerals, as well as expanded cooperation in the digital economy, clean energy and artificial intelligence.

The Chinese president also stressed the need to accelerate implementation of the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway project and modernization of border checkpoints.

"Meanwhile, connectivity should be enhanced not only in terms of infrastructure, but also in terms of rules and standards, so as to create favorable conditions for the smooth movement of people and goods," he said.

According to Xi Jinping, the development of humanitarian ties remains an important area of cooperation. China and Kyrgyzstan should expand cooperation in culture, tourism, arts, education, healthcare and archaeology, as well as interaction between media outlets, think tanks and youth organizations.

Xi Jinping noted that humanitarian exchanges between the two countries have increased in recent years. In particular, the number of mutual visits by citizens of China and Kyrgyzstan exceeded 400,000 last year.

He also highlighted the importance of multilateral cooperation between the two countries within the UN and SCO, noting the need for joint efforts on regional security and international cooperation.

Speaking about bilateral relations, Xi Jinping noted that China and Kyrgyzstan have progressed from establishing diplomatic relations to a comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era.

According to him, in February 2025, the two sides reached agreements on further deepening their comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era and building a China-Kyrgyzstan community with a shared future.

Xi Jinping’s upcoming visit will be his third visit to Kyrgyzstan. During the visit, he will meet with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov and attend the meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the SCO, which will be held in Bishkek on September 1.

Kyrgyzstan is celebrating the 35th anniversary of its independence this year. Xi Jinping conveyed his congratulations and best wishes to the Kyrgyz people on the occasion.

World.title: SCO summit could give fresh impetus to Kyrgyzstan-Azerbaijan transport links – expert (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. The upcoming summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) could give fresh impetus to transport cooperation involving Kyrgyzstan, Temirlan Razbaev, chief expert at the Analytics and Coordination Department of the National Institute for Strategic Initiatives under the President of the Kyrgyz Republic, told Trend.

According to him this includes the integration of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway with the Middle Corridor via the Caspian Sea and Azerbaijan. “The first promising area is logistics. It would be advisable to link the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway with the Middle Corridor via the Caspian Sea and Azerbaijan. According to official Azerbaijani data, the capacity of the Alat Port is planned to be increased from 15 million to 25 million tons per year, while cargo volumes along the Middle Corridor via Azerbaijan have increased by nearly 90% since 2022. For Kyrgyzstan, the practical benefit will come not from the route simply being mapped out, but from a regular container service, a single electronic document and a competitive end-to-end tariff,” he said.

The expert added that investment was another promising area. In particular, in July 2026, the capital of the Azerbaijan-Kyrgyzstan Development Fund was increased from $100 million to $200 million. At the same time, three joint projects were opened and eight initiatives were launched. “The next stage should involve moving toward measurable production projects in agro-processing, logistics, green energy and digital services. These are areas with potential rather than sectors in which agreements have already been finalized for specific projects,” he added.

At the same time, Razbaev said tourism and people-to-people ties represented a third area of potential cooperation. “On July 31 this year, the five-star Baku Resort & Spa complex, built by the Azerbaijani side, opened in the village of Kara-Oy on Lake Issyk-Kul. According to the official announcement, the complex covers more than 17 hectares, includes 111 rooms and 10 cottages, and can accommodate 330 guests. At the initial stage, it is expected to provide employment for 255 people. This is a concrete example of a project whose impact can be assessed in terms of the facility itself, employment and the quality of its infrastructure. Overall, the success of cooperation should be measured not by the number of memorandums signed, but by cargo volumes, investment, operational enterprises and jobs created,” the chief expert said.

Razbaev also emphasized that Kyrgyzstan’s role in the SCO is currently determined primarily by its ability to advance Central Asian interests within the broader Eurasian organization. “The SCO comprises 10 countries with a combined population of more than 3.4 billion people, accounting for about a quarter of global GDP and more than 15% of international trade. By comparison, when Kyrgyzstan held the SCO chairmanship in 2019, the organization had eight members – Iran and Belarus joined later. Therefore, the current chairmanship is taking place within a larger and more complex organization.

Over 2025-2026, Bishkek has identified specific priorities, including streamlining trade procedures, developing the digital economy and transit potential, expanding renewable energy, and improving security mechanisms. A practical indicator was the SCO Investment and Business Forum held on June 24, 2026, which brought together more than 600 participants. The Universal SCO Center currently being established is also set to include a Center for Combating Transnational Organized Crime in Bishkek.

It is therefore more accurate to say that over the past year, the country has strengthened its role as a coordinator and initiator of the Central Asian agenda. The final assessment will be determined by the package of decisions adopted at the Bishkek summit,” he concluded.

The SCO was established in 2001 and initially comprised China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Over the past 25 years, its membership has expanded to 10 countries. The 26th SCO summit will be held in Bishkek on August 31-September 1, 2026, under Kyrgyzstan’s chairmanship. The meeting will focus on the organization’s further development, strengthening economic and transport cooperation, and security cooperation. Following the summit, the leaders are expected to consider a number of documents related to the development of the SCO’s financial and economic mechanisms, including initiatives to expand settlements in national currencies and establish new cooperation institutions.

World.title: Kyiv warehouse explosion kills 37 in third night of aerial assault
World.content:
At least 37 people have been killed after a Russian drone strike on a Kyiv-area warehouse sparked a detonation, officials say, as Moscow's air attacks on the Ukrainian capital and surrounding region dragged into a third straight day.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy vowed to punish those responsible for the warehouse explosion late on Friday, which caused one of the highest death tolls in months and appeared to be the second such occurrence in two months.

Dozens were injured and more than 370 people evacuated from the area of the strike in the village of Myla, Mr Zelenskyy said.

Nearby infrastructure suffered "significant damage", he added, including residential buildings and a facility providing care for the elderly.

"Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions," Mr Zelenskyy wrote on X.

"There are regulations in place — ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas. Appropriate conclusions will certainly be drawn."

The warehouse explosion is the second of its kind in recent months. (Reuters/State Emergency Service of Ukraine)

Russia has escalated its air war on Ukraine, using more ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones that are difficult to shoot down.

Drone swarms aimed at Kyiv

Nine other regions had been targeted in overnight strikes by Russia, Mr Zelenskyy added, saying Kyiv in particular was under "virtually non-stop attack" from high-speed drones.

Trump and Putin are running out of options Conflicting stories about the CIA chief's Moscow trip throw Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin's positions into stark relief.

On Saturday, sirens blared throughout the morning for a third straight day as Ukraine's air force warned of new waves of drones approaching the capital.

The sound of air defences could be heard booming across the sky.

Kyiv region governor Tymur Tkachenko said a 14-year-old girl was killed in a morning drone strike on the Boryspil district. In Kyiv, a 2-year-old girl was killed by a downed drone, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Saturday.

Strikes in and around Kyiv on Thursday and Friday had damaged warehouses and homes, part of what some Ukrainian officials said was a campaign aimed at "paralysing" the city of several million.

Second recent strike-related detonation

Friday's blast follows a similar incident in the Kyiv-area town of Vyshneve last month, when 10 people were killed and hundreds of houses damaged after a strike triggered secondary explosions.

"In the fifth year of full-scale war, we have no right to allow a repetition of tragedies like the one that occurred in Vyshneve, and this one in the Bucha district," said Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi, who visited the site of Friday's blast, posted on Telegram.

Mr Zelenskiy said criminal cases had already been opened on charges of official negligence. Ukrainian officials rarely disclose damage to military ⁠targets from Russian attacks.

Reuters

World.title: One Nation secures historic victory in Secret Harbour by-election
World.content:
One Nation has scored a historic win in Western Australia, securing its first lower house seat in the state.

The ABC's chief elections and data analyst Casey Briggs called the outer suburban seat of Secret Harbour for One Nation's Luke Herdegen a little over four hours after votes began to be counted.

One Nation's WA leader Rod Caddies claimed victory at 9.30pm local time, although Labor had yet to concede.

Luke Herdegen will be the next MLA for Secret Harbour. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Labor's candidate was political staffer-turned-Woodside lobbyist Georgia Tree.

The area was traditionally safe Labor territory, having been held in different shapes and under different names since 1989, including most recently by Paul Papalia on an 11.5 per cent margin.

'Fight for our lives'

WA Labor Premier Roger Cook had repeatedly described the by-election as a "fight for our lives", given the threat posed by One Nation.

That the minor party was able to achieve such a large swing in Labor heartland will be watched closely around the country, both as an indication of the support behind One Nation and to learn lessons in how it can be campaigned against.

Mr Herdegen said his victory sent a loud message.

"There are no safe Labor seats in this state or in this country anymore," he said.

"The people have spoken today.

"A message that will send shock waves across the entire country ... and put every MP in this entire country on notice.

"None of these MPs are safe from the orange tsunami."

Mr Caddies said Australia's two-party political system was "dead".

Rod Caddies (left) says most people thought a One Nation win was impossible. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"You're witnessing a result they said was impossible," he said.

"Labor owned this part of Perth.

WA by-election puts One Nation's growing appeal to the test Next Saturday's Secret Harbour by-election will be the first clear test of whether One Nation's popularity on the east coast extends across the Nullarbor.

"The working families out here would always vote Labor.

" But a safe seat does not stay safe if you ignore it long enough. "

The area is home to a mix of older West Australians and young families, with new housing developments dotted along the coast, and shares many similarities with areas in other states where One Nation has performed well in recent elections.

Mr Herdegen is a gym owner who said he moved to Western Australia three years ago because there were better business opportunities.

He campaigned on a wide array of issues including how often red bins were being collected in the area, local housing pressures and migration.

Mr Herdegen campaigned on a variety of issues from rubbish collection to migration. (ABC News: Ashleigh Davis)

After being pre-selected, an old social media post emerged in which he spoke about heavy cocaine use and being connected to the Albanian mafia while living in London a decade ago.

"That's a story I put out there to try and help inspire people to live happier and healthier lives and I think it really did help a lot of people," Mr Herdegen said at the time.

Speaking on News24, formerly known as Sky News, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said people were turning to her party for hope.

One Nation supporters watch Pauline Hanson on screen as they celebrate their strong showing in the Secret Harbour by-election. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"They're wanting someone who's really going to listen to them and really go out and fight for them to change the direction this country is going in," she said.

"And I give them my solemn oath I'm trying to get the right people on the floor of parliament to do that for the Australian people, to give them back our country that's been stripped away from us every which way."

Secret Harbour fast facts: The beachside outer suburban seat south of Perth is very safe Labor territory with the party holding it with a 11.5% swing.

It's been vacant since the resignation of Labor's Paul Papalia in July who held the seat and its predecessors since 2007. 16 candidates have nominated for election.

Secret Harbour is home to many young, working families and ranks fourth out of WA's 59 electorates for residents who nominate British or Australian as their ancestry

Speaking before the result was known, WA Premier Roger Cook said Ms Tree had "delivered a hell of a fight".

"This campaign has been a reminder that Western Australians are doing it tough," he said.

"People are concerned about their lifestyle and their futures."

Roger Cook and Georgia Tree at the Labor Party function for the Secret Harbour by-election. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Mr Cook urged the party faithful to use the disappointment of the result to work harder.

"Seize those emotions and build on them, let it galvanise us for the fight of the future."

Voters wanted change

Many voters the ABC spoke to before the election highlighted a desire for change and a frustration with local, state and federal governments.

Many voters have said that they are disappointed in Labor in what was once a safe seat for the party. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Labor will be able to take some heart from the fact that by-elections can often produce results which differ from general elections, because the government of the day won't change no matter the outcome.

But the result remains a significant blow for the party which has been dominant in WA for nearly a decade.

Liberal leader Basil Zempilas stands with the party's candidate Ryan Robertson. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Leader of the WA opposition Basil Zempilas had claimed a win for One Nation would be a win for his Liberal party, because it would show falling support for Labor.

It prompted a fierce rebuke from federal MP Andrew Hastie who accused Mr Zempilas of accepting defeat.

His seat of Canning overlaps with Secret Harbour and is expected to be targeted by One Nation at the next federal election, making any lessons from this by-election particularly pertinent for him.

World.title: Blues' resurgence continues with stirring wildcard win over Demons
World.content:
Carlton will play an elimination final against Geelong after winning a wildcard clash against Melbourne at the MCG.

Despite conceding the first four goals of the game, the Blues improved steadily throughout the game to grind the Demons down, before finally emerging 19-point winners.

Ben Ainsworth kicked three goals for Carlton, while Sam Walsh and rising star Jagga Smith were sensational in the midfield.

The Blues had multiple opportunities to put the game to bed in the last quarter, but it wasn't until Smith converted a set shot for his second of the evening when the result was put to bed.

World.title: Jai Arrow makes emotional return for South Sydney
World.content:
Jai Arrow has made an emotional return for South Sydney, leading the side out and officially playing his 99th match for the club against Gold Coast.

Arrow, who was diagnosed with MND earlier this year, has received special dispensation from the NRL to play the opening seconds of the Rabbitohs' final two matches for the year.

He was substituted before kick-off for Cameron Murray and left the field at Skilled Park to a standing ovation.

Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett and former stalwart Jason Clark helped Arrow put his boots on before the match.

The Titans wore a commemorative jersey with Arrow's face on the front.

He played 56 matches for the club from 2018 to 2020.

Arrow will lead South Sydney out again next week in their final game of the regular season against the Sydney Roosters.

Arrow was in tears as he left the field. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

It will mark his 100th game for the club and the 180th and final match of his career.

Arrow was in the room when elated Souths players were told about the plan during their team review session on Monday morning.

"We all play a tough sport and we all mean so much to so many people, but it's so special to see what players mean to other players when things are going tough," said Rabbitohs fullback Matt Dufty.

"[Jai] brings a smile to everyone's face. Whatever we can do to give back to him, even if it's a little bit, it's just what we need to do. We're all behind him."

The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.

Murray replaced Arrow before kick off. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of his jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.

Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.

Players from all clubs showed their support by marking tries with 'arrow' celebrations during July.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Nepali families' desperate search for news of missing loved ones
World.content:
Photographs of unidentified dead plaster the walls of a major hospital in Kathmandu.

The pictures are printed on A4 paper, displayed in the hope someone will recognise them.

But the rain regularly arrives before a loved one can — streaking and washing away the faces, forcing them to be reprinted.

Rescuers in the areas hardest hit in Nepal's catastrophic flash flooding have to prioritise survivors. They cannot bring all the bodies back, so photos are taken instead.

Nepal flash floods updates: Follow this story as it unfolds with our live blog.

A woman searches for information about her family members at the Maharajgunj Medical Campus in Kathmandu. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Hanging alongside the pictures of the lost is a noticeboard with lists of survivors and the injured.

Crowds of people gather at the gates of the Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital desperately hoping they will find their loved ones on the latter.

Almost 2,500 people are now missing in Nepal after a glacial collapse sent a wall of water, mud and debris tearing through the valley on the border with Tibet, wiping out communities.

Some 517 bodies have been recovered on the Nepali side.

Family members are posting their own pictures rather than relying on authorities. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Hung next to the pictures of the deceased are smiling photos of those who are missing — remnants of better days.

Friends and family are taking matters into their own hands, posting pictures of the people they are searching for.

Police and volunteers are set up at desks taking the names and numbers of those who have missing relatives.

Some people come here multiple times a day in the desperate hope they will receive good news.

'His phone is not connecting'

Mud-covered properties following a flash flood at Trishuli in Nepal. (Reuters: Navesh Chitrakar)

Among the crowd at the hospital is Tilmaya Gurung. She has been visiting hospitals and morgues in the city searching for news of her sister's husband.

Meg Bahadur was working at a hydropower plant in Rasuwa when the flood hit. The 49-year-old has two children.

"We tried his phone several times but his phone is not connecting," she wept.

" We came here to hospital to check the list pasted here but not found his name on the list. "

A missing person's QR code is scanned at the Maharajgunj Medical Campus. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Her husband Jai Bahadur Gurung explained that the relatives split into groups to go to different sites to search for information.

He is trying to remain hopeful, but as the days stretch on the fear is building.

"We are here at hospital looking among dead," he said.

New methods for treatment developed

Doctors are treating survivors who were covered from head to toe after being buried in mud. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

More than 400 injured people, airlifted from the disaster area, have been brought here.

Chief of the emergency medicine department Ramesh Kumar Maharjan said most of those patients had been buried in mud.

"People were buried from head to toe and they have chest injuries and limb injuries, fractures, as well as head injuries and aspiration," he said.

" They were crushed. Their chests were crushed. They had become trapped. "

This QR code directs families to information about unidentified and unclaimed bodies. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

He said some of the people that had recovered from suffocation had "mud trapped inside them".

Staff have never treated patients like this before and are having to develop new methods, including a "decontamination shower" to remove the mud.

People adding missing person details to lists at the Maharajgunj Medical Campus. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

One of his patients is a five-year-old girl who had lost all of her family members. She is in critical care with a head injury.

This region is prone to natural disasters. It's been hit with earthquakes and more standard flooding before. But Dr Maharjan said this was a "different type of natural disaster" altogether.

Difficulty in accessing key locations

The flooding has destroyed roads and bridges, meaning the worst hit areas are only accessible by helicopter.

It is not only making it difficult to get injured people out, it is also making it difficult to get aid in.

Some young survivors have lost all their family members. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Less than 10 kilometres from the hospital, at a specialist hub, people are loading trucks with supplies like hygiene kits, food, water, and protective equipment.

Hangers are lined up, filled with donations from all over the world.

The humanitarian staging area was already set up, built on experiences with previous natural disasters, and in some areas allowed supplies to arrive within five hours of the emergency being declared.

Almost 3,000 people are still unaccounted for in Nepal and Tibet. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

But getting aid to those most in need is incredibly difficult.

UN World Food Programme country director Riaz Lodhi said road access being cut to the worst hit areas was "very restrictive" and made it difficult to assess the situation.

"We still don't know what the needs are out there," he said.

Some 93,000 people are believed to have been impacted by the disaster. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Aid supplies are currently being trucked a certain distance before being transferred to helicopter to be flown in.

"It's an enormous challenge given the magnitude of the disaster," he said.

World.title: Child stars say fame gives a 'wound' regulation has failed to prevent
World.content:
At just 16, Hayden Panettiere was handed a pill that would propel her "downfall of addiction".

The US star — who died last week aged 36 — wrote she was given the drug as a teen to boost her energy ahead of a red carpet appearance.

It was just one of the candid disclosures she made in the weeks before her death, in a memoir that laid bare the challenges of child stardom, substance abuse and postpartum depression.

Early coronial reports from Panettiere's death say she suffered a cardiac arrest, while police dispatchers said they were resuscitating the star after a possible "overdose".

The US Drug Enforcement Agency has also reportedly joined the investigation.

And while it's still unknown if drugs or alcohol played a factor in her death, Panettiere has joined the tragic roll call of former child stars who have died prematurely over the last year or so.

Hayden Panettiere (centre) wrote of how the traumatic storylines she portrayed led her to associate "catastrophe with adoration". (AP: Kevork Djansezian/File)

Her Ice-Princess co-star Michelle Tratchenberg died aged 39 last February, as a result of complications from diabetes — with co-star Rosie O'Donnell later alleging Tratchenberg struggled with addiction before her death.

Daveigh Chase, of The Ring and Lilo & Stitch fame, died in June aged 35 of AIDS, after suffering from drug abuse and homelessness.

Ice Princess director Tim Fywell paid tribute to his dual leads, Hayden Panettiere and Michelle Trachtenberg, saying he would remember them as "two shining talents, gone far too soon". (Getty Images: Alli Harvey/Stuart Weitzman)

Child stars have long been a vital facet of Hollywood, but this latest triad of deaths has reignited calls for better protections.

Anna Paquin, who was 11 when she won her Oscar, has joined the calls for better support for child actors. (Reuters: File)

In an essay following Panettiere's death, Even Stevens star Christy Carlson Romano said stars like herself powered "one of the most profitable storytelling machines in the world, while their mental needs are treated as inconvenient or irrelevant".

"Those of us who make it are given the adoration of saints — and then, if we don't climb to A-list fast enough, we're torn down as if we've committed some unspeakable mortal sin. All before our frontal lobes have fully formed," she wrote for Elle.

"Is it any wonder so many of us struggle with addiction?

" The industry gives us the wound and then acts surprised when we reach for something to treat it. "

Anna Paquin, who was 11 when she won her Oscar for The Piano, said the deaths were more than coincidence, in a separate statement about Panettiere's death.

"We are not as protected by the 'systems' that look great on paper, as we are supposed to be," she wrote on Instagram.

The first child star who almost lost it all

There is one key piece of US law that enshrines the rights of child stars — and it is nearing 100 years old.

The 1939 Coogan Law is named after Jackie 'The Kid' Coogan, arguably Hollywood's first child star.

At age four, he was foisted onto the screen by Charlie Chaplin to star 1921's The Kid.

Coogan became a hit, making millions but still only received a weekly allowance of $6.25 from his family.

Hours after Coogan (right) filed his lawsuit, the child star act was rushed through legislation. (Wikimedia Commons: Unknown photographer)

Then when he turned 21, he found his mother and manager-turned-stepfather would not give him a cent more.

Coogan eventually won the subsequent lawsuit he waged, albeit recovering only a small portions of his earnings.

As Coogan Law currently stands, it ensures 15 per cent of a child actor's earnings are set aside in a blocked trust, and also codifies issues such as schooling, work hours, and time off.

In her final months, Hayden Panettiere chose to be 'brutally honest' The actress, who died on Sunday aged 36, spoke openly about the hardships she experienced throughout her decades in the spotlight.

Yet despite decades of regulation, the extent of Hollywood's alleged 2000s lawlessness has been made fully apparent.

The child stars from Nickelodeon's heyday have grown up, and now they're speaking out against the machine and long-time producer Dan Schneider.

The 2024 documentary Quiet on Set delved into how dialogue coach Brian Peck was brought onto Disney's The Suite Life of Zack & Cody after previous convictions for the sexual abuse of Nickelodeon stars.

Meanwhile, Disney star Alyson Stoner says unsafe working conditions left her malnourished and chronically stressed, despite the labour laws in place.

And just this week, former child star Raquel Lee Bolleau has sued Disney, alleging a middle-aged employee repeatedly raped her on a 2001 set while other visible adults failed to intervene.

These are the same spaces Panettiere grew up in.

And now, some fear a new era of child stars could face similar problems with even less oversight.

Hayden Panettiere said her mother was a "momager" more often than not. (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)

Fame arrives from 'the first ultrasound'

In 2024, former Disney star Demi Lovato shone a light on a new child star industry, booming and unregulated.

She was ushering in two new Californian bills that brought kidfluencers in line with the financial restraints of Coogan Law.

Risks of promoting children as influencers remain largely unregulated around the world, including in Australia where there is no specific legislation around kidfluencing, despite being a multi-million industry.

Demi Lovato lamented how her young fame had made her the family "breadwinner". (Supplied: Gavin Newsom )

Social media communication researcher Catherine Archer says she has seen how some kids are famous "from the first ultrasound".

What follows can be enormous pressure to gather large followings that may result in thousands of dollars in earnings for the family — with no guardrails.

"If it's your source of income and you're also their parent, there's a bit of a conflict of interest there, isn't it?" Dr Archer notes.

"It's going to be that pressure to continue, particularly if (your child is) getting the likes, the shares and the comments."

Jerome is a four-year-old model who makes thousands. But his fame has a dark side Children are gathering large followings and earning thousands of dollars through social media influencing — but some warn it comes with a dark side.

No case is a better example of the risks of unregulated family vloggers than Utah mother Ruby Franke, who created a "concentration camp-like setting" for two of her four children.

Her daughter Shari Franke later testified to politicians as a "victim of family vlogging".

"If I could go back and do it all again, I'd rather have an empty bank account now and not have my childhood plastered all over the internet," she said.

" No amount of money I received has made what I've experienced worth it. "

Complicating the issue is a general "reluctance to regulate what goes on in people's homes" Dr Archer adds, while acknowledging the entertainment relies on that very access.

"You see the kids in their bathrooms getting ready for bed. You'll see them in their bedrooms getting ready," she says.

"There's this lack of privacy."

Ruby Franke (centre) was arrested after her 12-year-old son escaped through a window, malnourished and badly bruised. (Washington County Attorney's Office via AP)

Saving stars from 'a lawless area'

France now regulates the hours under-16s can work online, their earnings — and their right to be removed from online platforms at their wish.

MP Bruno Studer said the bill was France's duty to protect children from the internet "which must not be a lawless area".

Disturbing rumours have followed Dan Schneider for years. Now people are speaking out The child stars from Nickelodeon's heyday have grown up, and now they're speaking out against the machine and long-time producer Dan Schneider.

Panettiere's death and those of Tratchenberg and Chase have reignited a debate about the treatment of children on movie sets.

Yet the rise of the kidfluencer shows the new and insidious ways child entertainers continue to face harm.

These are children who often just started with a dream to be creative, as Dr Archer says.

"I don't want to say it is 100 per cent all bad because there are things to enjoy," she says.

"But there's definitely another dark side to it too."

As Anna Paquin says, it can be "possible to holistically look after the kids on set and tell complex and upsetting stories".

World.title: Walker's season in jeopardy, Cowboys lock in top eight with Tigers win
World.content:
An inspired defensive effort has seen the Dolphins hold on for a 26-12 victory over the Roosters, who lost star halfback Sam Walker to an ankle injury early in the second half.

Walker will go for scans for a suspected syndesmosis injury.

In Townsville, the Cowboys became the eighth and final team to lock in a finals berth with a 24-10 victory over Wests.

Earlier, South Sydney beat the Titans 42-22 to lock in a finals spot after a pre-game tribute to retiring Jai Arrow.

Arrow, who was forced into retirement after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, started the game on the field before subbing off for Cameron Murray and will do the same next week to ensure he notches 100 games for the Rabbitohs.

World.title: Three teenagers arrested over alleged burglary spree in Melbourne
World.content:
Three teenage boys have been arrested following an alleged crime spree in Melbourne's north-eastern suburbs yesterday morning.

A 17-year-old from the Greater Shepparton area, and a 15-year-old and a 17-year-old, both from the Manningham area, were arrested by detectives at an address in Darebin.

The 17-year-old from the Greater Shepparton area was charged with four counts of aggravated burglary, two counts of burglary, an attempted theft from a motor vehicle, among other charges.

The 15-year-old and the 17-year-old from Manningham were both charged with four counts of aggravated burglary, attempted theft from a motor vehicle and theft of a motor vehicle, among other charges.

Youth crime has been a key election topic ahead of Victoria's November state election. (AAP: James Ross)

Victoria Police said the charges followed several alleged incidents in the early hours of August 28, including two separate aggravated burglaries in Balwyn North; an attempted theft from a motor vehicle in Templestowe; and aggravated burglaries in Bulleen and Templestowe.

The trio were remanded to appear before a children's court today.

It comes as crime, particularly youth crime, dominates debate between the Labor government and Coalition opposition ahead of Victoria's November state election.

Stepping into the top job after Jacinta Allan was ousted in late July, Premier Ben Carroll vowed to "continue the same hardline approach to tackling crime."

Last month, the Coalition pledged to add new offences to the state's Adult Crime, Adult Time laws if elected, including car theft and attempted carjacking.

According to the most recent statistics, youth crime fell last year in Victoria for the first time in four years, but adult crime rose by more than 10 per cent over the same time frame.

The Crime Statistics Agency (CSA) released its figures for the 12 months to March 2026, showing Victoria's overall crime rate fell by just under 2 per cent.

The CSA said the figures showed youth crime falling for the first time since the COVID pandemic.

There were 22,654 alleged offences involving young people, which was a fall of 6 per cent on the previous year.

However, adult crime rose by 10 per cent, which the CSA attributed to increases in breaches of bail, retail theft and breaches of family violence orders.

World.title: One Nation claims victory in Secret Harbour as last-minute votes seal Labor’s fate
World.content:
One Nation has converted its popularity in opinion polls into electoral success in Western Australia, with a 30.6 per cent swing making gym owner Luke Herdegen the party’s first-ever lower house MP and nixing Labor’s efforts to retain Secret Harbour in a bruising byelection. By 10.30pm, with 80 per cent of the vote counted, Herdegen had amassed a primary vote of 39 per cent, ahead of Labor candidate Georgia Tree’s 24.4 per cent and Liberal candidate Ryan Robertson’s 17.3 per cent. WA One Nation Leader Rod Caddies and Secret Harbour candidate Luke Herdegen claim victory on Saturday night. Michael Philipps The preference count showed Herdegen was ahead of Tree, with a two-party preferred count showing a 3.9 per cent margin. One Nation claimed victory on Saturday, with WA leader Rod Caddies introducing Herdegen to the crowd of supporters gathered at a party function as “the next member for Secret Harbour”.



Labor refused to concede earlier in the night as it awaited vote counts from the early polling booth, but those dropped just after 10pm and sealed One Nation’s historic victory. Related Article WA election Secret Harbour byelection as it happened: ‘There are no safe Labor seats in this country any more’: One Nation claims historic WA lower house victory; Labor yet to concede “You’re witnessing a result they said was impossible,” Caddies told the crowd of One Nation supporters in Karnup. “A safe seat does not stay safe if you ignore it long enough. Tonight, Labor found it out the hard way. Secret Harbor did not send a protest, it sent a verdict. “Western Australia just told the rest of the nation the two-party system is dead.”



Herdegen was full of praise for the roomful of volunteers that had helped the campaign. “[Tree’s campaign] came with the big Labor machine,” Herdegen said. Pauline Hanson celebrates Luke Herdegen takes a lead in Secret Harbour. Facebook/Pauline Hanson's Please Explain “They came with their scare tactics. They came with their handlers on the polling booths, and we marched right through it. “The days of WA Labor having a stranglehold on the outer southern suburbs; those days are over.”



Herdegen told the crowd: “There are no safe Labor seats in this state, or in this country any more.” Tree arrived at her function at the Secret Harbour Surf Lifesaving Club just after 9pm alongside WA Premier Roger Cook. Cook said his government had a responsibility not to shirk the message sent by Secret Harbour voters. “It is easy to be a small target, to be a party that deals in grievances, but delivery, delivery, the grind of getting hard things done is how Labor handles that responsibility,” he said. “The voters of Secret Harbor have spoken and regardless of the outcome tonight, we will listen.



“This campaign has been a reminder that Western Australians are doing it tough. “We know that this is a time of high interest rates and fuel prices. People are concerned about their lifestyles and their futures, and this campaign has been a reminder about how key our priorities are to this state: jobs, health, housing, and cost of living relief.” Labor candidate Georgia Tree and WA Premier Roger Cook at Secret Harbour polling booths on Saturday. Colin Murty Tree said it was always going to be a tough night for Labor. “We always said this campaign was going to be a fight, and it has been a fight,” she said.



“We don’t know the result now, but I’ve been humbled by the support that I’ve received from everyone in the community; it’s been so amazing. Related Article WA election Cook says he would be ‘heartbroken’ if Labor loses Secret Harbour “No matter what, we’ve run such a good race, and I’m so proud of what we’ve done.” The byelection was triggered by the resignation of former Corrective Services minister Paul Papalia in July, when he quit politics to spend more time with an ill family member. Papalia won the seat with a margin of 11.5 per cent in 2025.



The result represents a significant erosion of support for Labor in what was considered one of its safest seats, which the party has held in its various iterations since the 1980s. The byelection was being considered by many pundits as a test of the recent surge in support for One Nation in opinion polls and how significantly that would translate to votes away from both Labor and Liberal parties. Secret Harbour sits firmly in the mortgage belt of Perth’s south and, federally, sits across Liberal MP Andrew Hastie’s electorate of Canning and Labor MP Madeleine King’s electorate of Brand. It is also considered a litmus test for all outer suburban seats nationwide where cost of living issues are manifesting as voter discontent for the Albanese government. Earlier in the day, Hasluck Labor MP Tania Lawrence, whose federal electorate shares similarities in demographics to Secret Harbour, said her party would take into account the results.



“I think the national secretary will always have regard to every election and understand what the constituency is saying on different issues because at the end of the day, every policy we work on is framed around what the community is looking for and what they need,” she said. Editor's pick Courts Mining millionaire’s legal fight against Perth yacht club sinks in court At the start of the day, Cook said he would be heartbroken if Tree lost the seat, while Herdegen said the electorate was hungry for change. No major party candidates could vote for themselves this campaign – because none of them actually lived in the electorate. Tree lives the furthest away at 61 kilometres, which the Liberals took great delight in reminding voters with their political signage.



Behaviour at booths was mostly cordial, but Labor volunteers did wake up to some of their signs at Secret Harbour Primary School slashed by a masked man on an e-scooter in the early hours of the morning. Police were notified.

World.title: Demons v Blues player ratings: From a future Brownlow medallist, to the Dees who ran out of fuel
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Demons v Blues player ratings: From a future Brownlow medallist, to the Dees who ran out of fuel

Loading

It’s barely believable that Carlton were 1-8 and 16th on the ladder after round nine – staring down the barrel of another wasted season. In the weeks and months since, the transformation under Josh Fraser has the Blues looking every bit the powerhouse they were for generations, and after their win over the Demons in front of more than 91,000 fans on Saturday night, who knows just how many more chapters their fairytale has to play out. Our experts, Jon Pierik (Demons) and Danny Russell (Blues) rate every player’s performance from the second wildcard final. Patrick Cripps and the Blues’ leaders put their team on their backs. Getty Images



Melbourne (4) Harvey Langford: Has had a super year, but this wasn’t one of his best. He emptied the tank on a wing when running alongside Ollie Hollands. He appeared gassed, at times, in the first half and should have made a better contest when Matt Cottrell marked on the lead. He won’t want to watch a replay of that. 5/10 (5) Xavier Lindsay: The mid-sized defender and former Morrish medallist had a solid night, spending time on Cottrell. Found plenty of the ball, and is another youngster the Demons are building around. 5.5/10 (6) Caleb Windsor: Had a quiet first half with only five disposals and 67 metres gained, and struggled to have an impact at stoppages. 5/10 Should Melbourne have recalled vice captain Jack Viney for a cut-throat final? Getty Images



(7) Jack Viney: It was a questionable decision for the Demons to bring in their vice captain for his first senior appearance of the season. He was given a rousing ovation when he took to the field for the first time with 11 minutes left in the first term. He had five disposals to half-time but already appeared out of petrol tickets. 2/10 (9) Jack Steele: The former St Kilda captain had a team-high nine disposals in the first term, and continued to work diligently through the midfield, finishing with 23 disposals. While it was a bruising departure from the Saints, Steele had the last laugh. 6.5/10 (10) Daniel Turner: The disciplined full-back had the job on Harry McKay and struggled with the size of the Blues’ forward, McKay booting two goals and being an active threat. He really missed injured fellow defensive pillar Jake Lever, and was switched to Brodie Kemp late in the game. 6.5/10 A dejected Max Gawn (right). AFL Photos (11) Max Gawn: The reigning All-Australian captain had eight first-term touches and pushed forward whenever he could. He was rewarded when he converted after a slick Melksham pass, but was quiet in the second term when Marc Pittonet responded. Had 18 touches and 31 hitouts, but appeared regularly unhappy with several umpiring calls. 7/10



(12) Koltyn Tholstrup: The emerging defender was sent to Francis Evans, and made sure the Blues’ cult figure was unable to reproduce his five-goal return of last week. It was a surprise Steven King did not move him to Jagga Smith late when the young Blue took control. 6.5/10 (14) Changkuoth Jiath: Demons fans are never too sure if the former Hawk will pick off more than he can chew. The rebounding half-back was sent to Mitch McGovern and eclipsed the veteran Blue, but left the field with a leg issue in the first term. He soon returned, and continued to test the Blues – and the hearts of the red and blue – with his run. 6/10 (15) Ed Langdon: The hard-running wingman is a marathon man and had 160 metres gained to half-time. He finished with 299. There weren’t any match-defining moments, but Langdon is one of the Demons’ more unassuming stars. 6.5/10 (16) Bailey Laurie: The robust half-forward was on the end of a chain of handballs in the first term, converting the Demons’ third. But that was his only highlight on a disappointing night, for he finished with only five disposals, and no marks. 2/10 (17) Jake Bowey: The robust small defender ran out for his 100th game and provided plenty of drive, delivering 231 metres gained in the first half. He was chippy all night, unafraid to exchange a few words, but was lucky a botched tackle on Patrick Cripps late didn’t cost a goal when Brodie Kemp wasted a set shot. 7/10



(18) Jake Melksham: In what proved to be the final game of his career, the recalled forward hit up Max Gawn with a slick pass in the first term. But it was a rather cold night from there, the one-time Bomber finishing goalless and with only six touches. 4/10 View post on X (19) Xavier Taylor: The young defender had the job on Brodie Kemp and won the battle in the first half. He had a solid night, and was later shifted to McKay with Turner struggling. There was much to like about his game. 6.5/10 (24) Trent Rivers: The hard-running defender provided attacking drive, finishing with 430 metres gained. He spent time on Francis Evans and continued to work hard, including a desperate spoil on the goal-line to deny Jagga Smith a late goal. 6/10 (25) Tom McDonald: In the final game of his career, the veteran utility was sent forward, where he was manned by either star rookie Harry Dean or Jacob Weitering. He slotted a key goal on the half-time siren, but never really got into the game. 3/10



Jake Melksham and Tom McDonald after their final AFL games. AFL Photos (30) Harry Sharp: Had a moment to forget when his late hit on Dean led to Harrison Petty’s shot at goal being reversed in the first term. But he made amends minutes later by kicking the Demons’ first. He was in the thick of the action early, but faded as the game unfolded. 6 /10 (31) Bayley Fritsch: A man who knows all about delivering in finals, the explosive forward had a night he would rather forget. He was manned by Nick Haynes and had no direct scoreboard impact in the first half. That changed when he snapped the Demons’ second goal of the third, but this was a game of frustration for a man the Demons really needed to deliver. 3/10 (32) Tom Sparrow: The key onballer was averaging 23 disposals per game but had arguably his worst game of the season, having just the six touches, one clearance and 77 metres gained to half-time. Had only four more touches for the game, but did lay nine tackles. 3/10 (35) Harrison Petty: It wasn’t the best of nights for the strong-marking forward, given Weitering marshalled the Blues’ defence well. He wasn’t afraid to push into defensive 50 to help out, and did begin the third term with a mark and goal. But the Demons needed more. 6 /10



(36) Kysaiah Pickett: The dynamic match-winner delivered a team-high 201 metres gained in the first term, exciting all with his typical dashing run. He almost hauled in a late bid for the mark of the year in the third term but was unable to provide a game-defining moment in a desperate final quarter, botching an open running shot on goal with the Demons trailing by nine points. 7/10 (37) Kade Chandler: The speedy small forward provided a strong tackle to start the third term, the Demons going forward. Had Billy Wilson and Ollie Florent as opponents, and was disappointed to miss a long shot late in the third term. Had six clearances. 5/10 (47) Joel Fitzgerald: The tough-as-teak tagger spent time on George Hewett, finishing with 15 disposals and four clearances of his own. He worked hard, but Hewett had 20 disposals. 6/10 Carlton



(2) Lachlan Cowan: Carlton’s poster boy for tatts – not that he has much competition in the ink department at Ikon Park – was a key cog in the Blues’ defensive machine. He laid a brilliant run-down tackle on Fritsch in the second term. 6/10 (4) Oliver Hollands: Surely secured his future at Carlton after one of the best games of his career. While he looked to have his hands full early with Langford, he ran himself into the ground. He set up several goals and kicked one of his own. 7/10 (5) Adam Cerra: Tried to bite off more than he could chew by missing pinpoint passes in the first term before finding his groove. He wasn’t alone as Carlton struggled to break through Melbourne’s defence. Then he became a valuable playmaker out of defence. 7/10 (7) Jagga Smith: We are not usually about outlandish statements, but this guy has future Brownlow medallist written all over him. When Melbourne shot out to a near-four-goal, first-quarter lead, Smith and Sam Walsh dragged them back. He had 29 disposals. 8/10 View post on X



(9) Patrick Cripps: Not the big-possession game from Cripps that we come to expect. Instead, he did a stack of the grunt work as Sam Walsh and Smith got busy. Looked to have a sore knee during the game, but typically soldiered on. 6/10 (10) Harry McKay: It was not a night for big forwards, as the Blues were so conscious of keeping the ball away from Gawn, they forgot to kick long to McKay. He managed two opportunistic goals – one from a touchy free kick, the other a handball over the top. 5/10 (11) Mitch McGovern: Forgot to pack the Grippo. He worked up and down the ground and presented on the lead, but struggled to hold his marks. Towelled up early by Jiath. 4/10 (12) Ben Ainsworth: The best thing to come out of the Gold Coast since Trevor Hendy paddled a surf ski – OK, maybe with apologies to Tom Lynch. Ainsworth was Carlton’s best forward with three goals and had 21 disposals. 7/10 Ben Ainsworth played one of the most important games of his career. AFL Photos



(13) Blake Acres: Did he look slow early when Melbourne jumped out of the blocks? Maybe. Just a touch. He was swapped off Langford onto Langdon and then worked his way into the game. He had the last kick of the game for a behind. 6/10 (14) Ollie Florent: Gave the term “too cute” a work over in the first half by picking tough targets and missing them. Still, he had plenty of the ball and showed why he has helped Carlton’s turnaround this year. 6/10 (15) Billy Wilson: He started the game on the pine before being swung into the action midway through the first term and was serviceable in the defensive half. He kicked well. 5/10 (17) Brodie Kemp: After being well-held across the first three quarters, he missed two easy shots in the final term that should have swung the game firmly in Carlton’s favour. Not good enough for a key focal point. 5/10 (18) Sam Walsh: He doesn’t have the polish of Nick Daicos, or the omnipresence of Marcus Bontempelli, but he is one of the elite players of the competition. He provided hard running and sure ball use time and time again. Had 39 disposals. Best on ground. 9/10



Sam Walsh (right) had plenty to say to Harry Sharp, and ended up having the last laugh, too. AFL Photos (23) Jacob Weitering: Anyone who ever suggested the Blues should entertain letting go of their key defender should wash their mouth out with soap. He was supreme in defence for the Blues alongside Dean. Took 12 marks, and saved numerous goals. 8/10 (26) Nick Haynes: Huge in defence early when the Blues were under siege, marking everything that came his way while keeping an eye on the dangerous Fritsch. He did need treatment on an ankle twice during the game. 7/10 (27) Marc Pittonet: How do you judge a ruckman who plays against Gawn? Of course he lowered his colours, but there’s more to it than that. He toiled admirably and kept Gawn from being a matchwinner. That’s a victory in itself. 6/10 (29) George Hewett: Started on the bench as the second-change midfielder. Had 20 disposals and worked hard without having a huge influence. 5/10



(33) Lewis Young: In the side as the back-up ruckman, which prevents Cripps and McKay from getting beaten up in the centre square or around the ground. So he’s worth his place, but turned the ball over in some nervous moments. 4/10 (35) Harry Dean: You can see why this father-and-son gem has become a fan favourite in his first year at Carlton. He looks like his dad, premiership player Peter, and is just as brave and dependable. A brilliant key defender who plays through the pain barrier. 8/10 Loading (36) Cooper Lord: Forget his stats – remember the job he did on Kozzy Pickett. The task looked beyond him in the first term as Pickett had four shots on goal and five for the night – all missed – but, gee, he found his feet after that. 7/10 (39) Talor Byrne: He brought pressure to the Blues’ forward line but little else. Not tall enough to be a marking presence, and did not have the blistering pace to break free. Still, he’s only 18 and has plenty of time. 3/10



(44) Francis Evans: The Dees paid him the compliment of sending their best shut-down player, Tholstrup, to his side to keep him quiet. As a result, he struggled to gain any traction. 4/10 (46) Matthew Cottrell: Carlton’s harmonica man had some enormous moments, including a big hit on Jiath, and could have had a sensational night had he taken every chance. He hit the post three times and butchered a snap in the final term. 6/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Demons v Blues player ratings: From a future Brownlow medallist, to the Dees who ran out of fuel
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Demons v Blues player ratings: From a future Brownlow medallist, to the Dees who ran out of fuel

Loading

It’s barely believable that Carlton were 1-8 and 16th on the ladder after round nine – staring down the barrel of another wasted season. In the weeks and months since, the transformation under Josh Fraser has the Blues looking every bit the powerhouse they were for generations, and after their win over the Demons in front of more than 91,000 fans on Saturday night, who knows just how many more chapters their fairytale has to play out. Our experts, Jon Pierik (Demons) and Danny Russell (Blues) rate every player’s performance from the second wildcard final. Patrick Cripps and the Blues’ leaders put their team on their backs. Getty Images



Melbourne (4) Harvey Langford: Has had a super year, but this wasn’t one of his best. He emptied the tank on a wing when running alongside Ollie Hollands. He appeared gassed, at times, in the first half and should have made a better contest when Matt Cottrell marked on the lead. He won’t want to watch a replay of that. 5/10 (5) Xavier Lindsay: The mid-sized defender and former Morrish medallist had a solid night, spending time on Cottrell. Found plenty of the ball, and is another youngster the Demons are building around. 5.5/10 (6) Caleb Windsor: Had a quiet first half with only five disposals and 67 metres gained, and struggled to have an impact at stoppages. 5/10 Should Melbourne have recalled vice captain Jack Viney for a cut-throat final? Getty Images



(7) Jack Viney: It was a questionable decision for the Demons to bring in their vice captain for his first senior appearance of the season. He was given a rousing ovation when he took to the field for the first time with 11 minutes left in the first term. He had five disposals to half-time but already appeared out of petrol tickets. 2/10 (9) Jack Steele: The former St Kilda captain had a team-high nine disposals in the first term, and continued to work diligently through the midfield, finishing with 23 disposals. While it was a bruising departure from the Saints, Steele had the last laugh. 6.5/10 (10) Daniel Turner: The disciplined full-back had the job on Harry McKay and struggled with the size of the Blues’ forward, McKay booting two goals and being an active threat. He really missed injured fellow defensive pillar Jake Lever, and was switched to Brodie Kemp late in the game. 6.5/10 A dejected Max Gawn (right). AFL Photos (11) Max Gawn: The reigning All-Australian captain had eight first-term touches and pushed forward whenever he could. He was rewarded when he converted after a slick Melksham pass, but was quiet in the second term when Marc Pittonet responded. Had 18 touches and 31 hitouts, but appeared regularly unhappy with several umpiring calls. 7/10



(12) Koltyn Tholstrup: The emerging defender was sent to Francis Evans, and made sure the Blues’ cult figure was unable to reproduce his five-goal return of last week. It was a surprise Steven King did not move him to Jagga Smith late when the young Blue took control. 6.5/10 (14) Changkuoth Jiath: Demons fans are never too sure if the former Hawk will pick off more than he can chew. The rebounding half-back was sent to Mitch McGovern and eclipsed the veteran Blue, but left the field with a leg issue in the first term. He soon returned, and continued to test the Blues – and the hearts of the red and blue – with his run. 6/10 (15) Ed Langdon: The hard-running wingman is a marathon man and had 160 metres gained to half-time. He finished with 299. There weren’t any match-defining moments, but Langdon is one of the Demons’ more unassuming stars. 6.5/10 (16) Bailey Laurie: The robust half-forward was on the end of a chain of handballs in the first term, converting the Demons’ third. But that was his only highlight on a disappointing night, for he finished with only five disposals, and no marks. 2/10 (17) Jake Bowey: The robust small defender ran out for his 100th game and provided plenty of drive, delivering 231 metres gained in the first half. He was chippy all night, unafraid to exchange a few words, but was lucky a botched tackle on Patrick Cripps late didn’t cost a goal when Brodie Kemp wasted a set shot. 7/10



(18) Jake Melksham: In what proved to be the final game of his career, the recalled forward hit up Max Gawn with a slick pass in the first term. But it was a rather cold night from there, the one-time Bomber finishing goalless and with only six touches. 4/10 View post on X (19) Xavier Taylor: The young defender had the job on Brodie Kemp and won the battle in the first half. He had a solid night, and was later shifted to McKay with Turner struggling. There was much to like about his game. 6.5/10 (24) Trent Rivers: The hard-running defender provided attacking drive, finishing with 430 metres gained. He spent time on Francis Evans and continued to work hard, including a desperate spoil on the goal-line to deny Jagga Smith a late goal. 6/10 (25) Tom McDonald: In the final game of his career, the veteran utility was sent forward, where he was manned by either star rookie Harry Dean or Jacob Weitering. He slotted a key goal on the half-time siren, but never really got into the game. 3/10



Jake Melksham and Tom McDonald after their final AFL games. AFL Photos (30) Harry Sharp: Had a moment to forget when his late hit on Dean led to Harrison Petty’s shot at goal being reversed in the first term. But he made amends minutes later by kicking the Demons’ first. He was in the thick of the action early, but faded as the game unfolded. 6 /10 (31) Bayley Fritsch: A man who knows all about delivering in finals, the explosive forward had a night he would rather forget. He was manned by Nick Haynes and had no direct scoreboard impact in the first half. That changed when he snapped the Demons’ second goal of the third, but this was a game of frustration for a man the Demons really needed to deliver. 3/10 (32) Tom Sparrow: The key onballer was averaging 23 disposals per game but had arguably his worst game of the season, having just the six touches, one clearance and 77 metres gained to half-time. Had only four more touches for the game, but did lay nine tackles. 3/10 (35) Harrison Petty: It wasn’t the best of nights for the strong-marking forward, given Weitering marshalled the Blues’ defence well. He wasn’t afraid to push into defensive 50 to help out, and did begin the third term with a mark and goal. But the Demons needed more. 6 /10



(36) Kysaiah Pickett: The dynamic match-winner delivered a team-high 201 metres gained in the first term, exciting all with his typical dashing run. He almost hauled in a late bid for the mark of the year in the third term but was unable to provide a game-defining moment in a desperate final quarter, botching an open running shot on goal with the Demons trailing by nine points. 7/10 (37) Kade Chandler: The speedy small forward provided a strong tackle to start the third term, the Demons going forward. Had Billy Wilson and Ollie Florent as opponents, and was disappointed to miss a long shot late in the third term. Had six clearances. 5/10 (47) Joel Fitzgerald: The tough-as-teak tagger spent time on George Hewett, finishing with 15 disposals and four clearances of his own. He worked hard, but Hewett had 20 disposals. 6/10 Carlton



(2) Lachlan Cowan: Carlton’s poster boy for tatts – not that he has much competition in the ink department at Ikon Park – was a key cog in the Blues’ defensive machine. He laid a brilliant run-down tackle on Fritsch in the second term. 6/10 (4) Oliver Hollands: Surely secured his future at Carlton after one of the best games of his career. While he looked to have his hands full early with Langford, he ran himself into the ground. He set up several goals and kicked one of his own. 7/10 (5) Adam Cerra: Tried to bite off more than he could chew by missing pinpoint passes in the first term before finding his groove. He wasn’t alone as Carlton struggled to break through Melbourne’s defence. Then he became a valuable playmaker out of defence. 7/10 (7) Jagga Smith: We are not usually about outlandish statements, but this guy has future Brownlow medallist written all over him. When Melbourne shot out to a near-four-goal, first-quarter lead, Smith and Sam Walsh dragged them back. He had 29 disposals. 8/10 View post on X



(9) Patrick Cripps: Not the big-possession game from Cripps that we come to expect. Instead, he did a stack of the grunt work as Sam Walsh and Smith got busy. Looked to have a sore knee during the game, but typically soldiered on. 6/10 (10) Harry McKay: It was not a night for big forwards, as the Blues were so conscious of keeping the ball away from Gawn, they forgot to kick long to McKay. He managed two opportunistic goals – one from a touchy free kick, the other a handball over the top. 5/10 (11) Mitch McGovern: Forgot to pack the Grippo. He worked up and down the ground and presented on the lead, but struggled to hold his marks. Towelled up early by Jiath. 4/10 (12) Ben Ainsworth: The best thing to come out of the Gold Coast since Trevor Hendy paddled a surf ski – OK, maybe with apologies to Tom Lynch. Ainsworth was Carlton’s best forward with three goals and had 21 disposals. 7/10 Ben Ainsworth played one of the most important games of his career. AFL Photos



(13) Blake Acres: Did he look slow early when Melbourne jumped out of the blocks? Maybe. Just a touch. He was swapped off Langford onto Langdon and then worked his way into the game. He had the last kick of the game for a behind. 6/10 (14) Ollie Florent: Gave the term “too cute” a work over in the first half by picking tough targets and missing them. Still, he had plenty of the ball and showed why he has helped Carlton’s turnaround this year. 6/10 (15) Billy Wilson: He started the game on the pine before being swung into the action midway through the first term and was serviceable in the defensive half. He kicked well. 5/10 (17) Brodie Kemp: After being well-held across the first three quarters, he missed two easy shots in the final term that should have swung the game firmly in Carlton’s favour. Not good enough for a key focal point. 5/10 (18) Sam Walsh: He doesn’t have the polish of Nick Daicos, or the omnipresence of Marcus Bontempelli, but he is one of the elite players of the competition. He provided hard running and sure ball use time and time again. Had 39 disposals. Best on ground. 9/10



Sam Walsh (right) had plenty to say to Harry Sharp, and ended up having the last laugh, too. AFL Photos (23) Jacob Weitering: Anyone who ever suggested the Blues should entertain letting go of their key defender should wash their mouth out with soap. He was supreme in defence for the Blues alongside Dean. Took 12 marks, and saved numerous goals. 8/10 (26) Nick Haynes: Huge in defence early when the Blues were under siege, marking everything that came his way while keeping an eye on the dangerous Fritsch. He did need treatment on an ankle twice during the game. 7/10 (27) Marc Pittonet: How do you judge a ruckman who plays against Gawn? Of course he lowered his colours, but there’s more to it than that. He toiled admirably and kept Gawn from being a matchwinner. That’s a victory in itself. 6/10 (29) George Hewett: Started on the bench as the second-change midfielder. Had 20 disposals and worked hard without having a huge influence. 5/10



(33) Lewis Young: In the side as the back-up ruckman, which prevents Cripps and McKay from getting beaten up in the centre square or around the ground. So he’s worth his place, but turned the ball over in some nervous moments. 4/10 (35) Harry Dean: You can see why this father-and-son gem has become a fan favourite in his first year at Carlton. He looks like his dad, premiership player Peter, and is just as brave and dependable. A brilliant key defender who plays through the pain barrier. 8/10 Loading (36) Cooper Lord: Forget his stats – remember the job he did on Kozzy Pickett. The task looked beyond him in the first term as Pickett had four shots on goal and five for the night – all missed – but, gee, he found his feet after that. 7/10 (39) Talor Byrne: He brought pressure to the Blues’ forward line but little else. Not tall enough to be a marking presence, and did not have the blistering pace to break free. Still, he’s only 18 and has plenty of time. 3/10



(44) Francis Evans: The Dees paid him the compliment of sending their best shut-down player, Tholstrup, to his side to keep him quiet. As a result, he struggled to gain any traction. 4/10 (46) Matthew Cottrell: Carlton’s harmonica man had some enormous moments, including a big hit on Jiath, and could have had a sensational night had he taken every chance. He hit the post three times and butchered a snap in the final term. 6/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.
